questions.q: According to the lecture, elements are believed to be formed from three processes. Which set is correct?
o: The Big Bang, fusion reactions in stars, artificial synthesis
The Big Bang, radioactive decay, electrolysis
questions.e: The lecture names exactly three origins of elements: the Big Bang theory, fusion reactions in stars (the Stellar hypothesis), and artificial/laboratory synthesis.

questions.q: The Big Bang theory describes the universe beginning as an explosion of what?
o: A cold, sparse cloud of dust drifting through empty space
An infinitely hot and dense ball of primordial matter
A collapsing black hole pulling matter into a single point
A supernova remnant scattered from a single dying star
questions.e: The slides describe an explosion of an 'infinitely hot and dense ball of primordial (pre-existing) matter' some billions of years ago.

questions.q: Which two elements were formed immediately after the Big Bang explosion, before any stars existed?
questions.e: Only hydrogen and helium formed right after the Big Bang; no stars or light existed yet at that stage.

questions.q: What was notably absent from the universe during the earliest period right after the Big Bang?
questions.e: The lecture states that no stars or light existed during that very early period — light could not yet shine because charged particles scattered it.

questions.q: What ultimately pulled clouds of gas together to collapse into vast galaxies of billions of stars?
questions.e: Gravitational forces brought the clouds of gas together, and they eventually collapsed into galaxies.

questions.q: How many stages does the lecture's Big Bang timeline diagram identify, from 'Time Begins' to 'Present Day'?
questions.e: The slide explicitly lists 'the seven stages of the Big Bang', running from time 10⁻⁴³ sec to 15 billion years (present day).

questions.q: At the very first instant ('Time Begins', ~10⁻⁴³ sec), what is the cosmos doing?
o: Cooling into the first solid planets that later orbit newborn stars
Undergoing a superfast 'inflation', expanding from atom-size to grapefruit-size
Forming the first stars from collapsing clouds of hydrogen gas
Radiating visible light freely across all of observable space
questions.e: Stage 1 describes the cosmos going through a superfast 'inflation', expanding from the size of an atom to that of a grapefruit in a tiny fraction of a second.

questions.q: Around the 'one second' mark in the Big Bang timeline, what key event occurs?
o: Galaxies fully form and begin clustering together under gravity
Quarks first appear and clump together into protons and neutrons
Electrons combine with protons and neutrons to form atoms, and light can finally shine
Iron is synthesised deep within the core of a massive dying star
questions.e: At stage 5 (around one second/300,000 years in the diagram), electrons combine with protons and neutrons to form atoms — mostly hydrogen and helium — and light can finally shine.

questions.q: During the 'rapidly cooling cosmos' stage (~10⁻⁶ sec), what happens to quarks?
o: They decay rapidly into a shower of photons
They clump into protons and neutrons
They form full atoms with orbiting electrons
They form galaxies bound together by gravity
questions.e: Stage 3 describes a rapidly cooling cosmos that permits quarks to clump into protons and neutrons.

questions.q: Why could light not shine during the earliest, hottest stages of the Big Bang?
o: There was no energy in the universe yet for any particles to move
Charged electrons and protons prevented light from shining in the superhot fog
Light had not yet been invented as a physical phenomenon
Black holes absorbed all light before it could travel any distance
questions.e: The slide states that charged electrons and protons prevented light from shining — the universe was a 'superhot fog' until atoms could form.

questions.q: By the 'Present Day' stage of the Big Bang timeline (~15 billion years), what has happened?
o: The universe is still a hot dense fog of quarks with no atoms or starlight yet formed at all
Galaxies have clustered together under gravity, and dying first stars have spewed heavy elements into space
All stars have gone dark permanently, and no new elements are ever formed again anywhere
Elements heavier than iron can no longer form anywhere in the whole of the observable cosmos
questions.e: Stage 7 describes galaxies clustering together under gravity; the first stars die and spew heavy elements into space, which eventually form new stars and planets.

questions.q: The lecture recommends a video, 'Origin of the Universe 101', produced by which channel?
o: BBC Earth's nature and science strand
PBS Space Time's physics web series
questions.e: The slide cites 'Origin of the Universe 101 by the National Geographic Channel' as a supplementary resource.

questions.q: According to the Stellar hypothesis, where were all elements other than hydrogen and helium formed?
o: In the outer atmosphere of planets orbiting young stars
In the centre of stars, released upon their explosion
In interstellar dust clouds drifting between star systems
In the vacuum of deep space far from any stars
questions.e: The Stellar hypothesis states that all elements other than H and He were formed in the centre of stars and released upon their explosion.

questions.q: What two conditions does the Stellar hypothesis say are required for the formation of elements in a star's core?
o: Low temperature and low pressure throughout the stellar core
Very high temperatures and high concentrations of reactants
Vacuum and darkness with no reactants present at all
Strong magnetic fields only, with no heat required
questions.e: Very high temperatures and high concentrations of reactants are both required in the core of stars for new elements to form.

questions.q: Why are extremely high temperatures necessary for nuclear fusion to occur in stars?
o: To evaporate excess hydrogen so that only the heaviest nuclei remain able to fuse together
To overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nuclei that must fuse
To cool the reactants before they combine together into new, heavier atomic nuclei
To ionise the surrounding vacuum completely so that fusion reactions can begin at all
questions.e: The high temperatures are needed to overcome the electrostatic (like-charge) repulsion between positively charged nuclei so they can fuse together.

questions.q: In the fusion example shown in the lecture, deuterium (D) fuses with tritium (T) to form helium plus which two other products?
questions.e: The diagram shows D + T fusing to release helium (He), a neutron, and energy.

questions.q: Fusing helium nuclei requires a much higher temperature than fusing hydrogen because helium nuclei have:
o: Half the mass of a hydrogen nucleus
Twice the positive charge of hydrogen
No neutrons at all in the nucleus
A negative charge on every nucleon
questions.e: Helium nuclei carry twice the positive charge of hydrogen nuclei, so a much higher temperature (~20 × 10⁶ K) is needed to overcome the stronger repulsion.

questions.q: Which of the following fusion reactions listed in the lecture correctly produces carbon-12?
questions.e: The slide lists 'He + Be → ¹²C' as one of the example fusion reactions, alongside 2He → ⁸Be and He + C → ¹⁶O.

questions.q: What is the largest atom that can be formed directly through nuclear fusion reactions inside stars?
questions.e: The lecture states that iron (Fe) is the largest atom that can be formed from nuclear fusion reactions in stars.

questions.q: How are elements larger than iron actually formed?
o: By electron loss from iron atoms during a supernova explosion
When the nuclei of iron atoms capture neutrons released from a star's explosion
By simple radioactive decay of hydrogen nuclei over time
Through condensation of stellar dust into new planetary bodies
questions.e: Atoms larger than Fe form when Fe nuclei capture neutrons released during the explosion of a star.

questions.q: According to the Oddo-Harkins rule mentioned in the lecture, elements with even atomic numbers are generally:
o: Rarer than elements with odd atomic numbers overall
Far more abundant than odd-mass-numbered elements, except H and Be
Always radioactive regardless of their mass number
Exclusively formed by artificial synthesis in laboratories
questions.e: The Oddo-Harkins rule states that elements with even atomic numbers are far more abundant than odd-mass-numbered elements, with H and Be as exceptions.

questions.q: In the star-lifetime table shown in the lecture, what is associated with the 'Supernova' stage?
o: Core temperature ~1.5 × 10⁷ K, forming only helium from hydrogen fusion reactions
Core temperature ~1 × 10¹¹ K, with multiple neutron captures forming elements with Z > 28
No nuclear reactions at all are occurring anywhere within the collapsed stellar core
Formation of only hydrogen and helium at comparatively low core temperatures throughout
questions.e: At the Supernova stage the core temperature reaches about 1 × 10¹¹ K, and multiple neutron-capture reactions form elements with atomic number (Z) greater than 28.

questions.q: Elements with atomic numbers beyond 92 (the transuranium elements) are produced through which method described in the lecture?
o: Naturally in Earth's crust over geological time
Photosynthesis in plants converting sunlight to matter
Simple heating in a furnace at atmospheric pressure
questions.e: Transuranium elements (Z > 92) are synthesised in the laboratory via fusion reactions, using cyclotrons to accelerate high-energy particles into target nuclei.

questions.q: What is the role of a cyclotron in artificial element synthesis?
o: It cools particles to absolute zero before they are safely stored away
It accelerates high-energy particles to high speed so they can fuse with target nuclei
It separates isotopes by mass only, without changing their speed
It measures radioactive half-life of naturally occurring isotopes
questions.e: Cyclotrons accelerate particles to high speed, enabling them to fuse with target nuclei and create new, heavier elements.

questions.q: Seaborg and colleagues (1950) synthesised californium by firing helium nuclei (alpha particles) at which target?
questions.e: The lecture states that Seaborg et al. (1950) formed californium using a cyclotron, firing alpha particles (helium nuclei) at curium-242.

questions.q: About how many elements are recognised as essential to living cells, per the lecture?
questions.e: The slide states that 'about 32 elements are recognised as essential to cells.'

questions.q: According to the body-composition table in the lecture, which element makes up the largest percentage of the human body by mass?
questions.e: Oxygen is listed at 65.0% — by far the largest single contributor to human body mass.

questions.q: Which element is the second-most abundant by percentage in the human body according to the lecture's table?
questions.e: Carbon comes in second at 18.5% of body mass, after oxygen's 65.0%.

questions.q: Which element is listed at about 3.2% of body mass in the lecture's table?
questions.e: Nitrogen is listed at 3.2% of body mass, ranking fourth after oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen.

questions.q: In the lecture's percentage table, magnesium is listed at what percentage of body mass?
questions.e: Magnesium is listed at 0.1% of body mass — the lowest of the explicitly percentaged elements before the 'trace elements' group.

questions.q: Which two elements together already account for more than 80% of the human body's total mass?
questions.e: Oxygen (65.0%) plus carbon (18.5%) together make up 83.5% of the body's mass.

questions.q: Which six elements are described as the 'major/bulk' elements, making up over 99% of the mass of most cells?
o: C, H, O, N, P, S
C, H, O, Na, K, Cl
Ca, P, K, S, Na, Mg
C, O, Fe, Si, Mg, Ca
questions.e: The major/bulk elements named in the lecture are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur (C, H, O, N, P, S).

questions.q: Which element is specifically described in the lecture as 'the most versatile and predominant' element in the cell?
questions.e: The slide states directly: 'Carbon is the most versatile and predominant in the cell.'

questions.q: Where in the cell are the major (bulk) elements mainly found, according to the lecture?
o: In the organic compounds of the cell
questions.e: The lecture notes that the major elements are found in the organic compounds of the cell, whereas minor elements are mainly in the fluids that bathe the cells.

questions.q: Where are the minor/trace elements mainly located, according to the lecture?
o: In the organic compounds of the cell
Mainly in the fluids that bathe the cells
Only in bone tissue and tooth enamel
In the cell's genetic material and chromosomes
questions.e: Minor (trace) elements are mainly found in the fluids that bathe the cells, unlike the major elements found in organic compounds.

questions.q: In the colour-coded periodic table shown in the lecture, what does the colour yellow represent?
o: Trace elements essential for bacteria, plants, or animals
Bulk biological elements that make up most of body mass
Possibly essential trace elements for some species
Radioactive elements that occur rarely in living tissue
questions.e: The legend on the periodic-table slide marks yellow squares as 'Bulk biological elements.'

questions.q: In the colour-coded periodic table, what does green represent?
o: Bulk biological elements that make up most of body mass
Trace elements believed to be essential for bacteria, plants, or animals
Possibly essential trace elements for some species
Non-essential inert elements with no known biological role
questions.e: Green squares in the legend denote 'Trace elements believed to be essential for bacteria, plants or animals.'

questions.q: Which block of the periodic table do most of the major biological elements belong to?
questions.e: The lecture states that the major elements are 'mostly p-block elements.'

questions.q: What type of chemical bond do the major biological elements typically form?
questions.e: A notable feature of the major elements listed in the lecture is that 'they can form covalent bonds.'

questions.q: Are the major biological elements (C, H, O, N, P, S) generally metals or non-metals?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'they are non-metals' as one of the notable features of the major elements.

questions.q: In terms of reactivity, how are the major biological elements best described?
o: Neither too reactive nor too inert
Radioactive and unstable in most known isotopes
questions.e: The slide describes the major elements as 'neither too reactive nor too inert (unreactive)' — a balance that suits biological chemistry.

questions.q: According to the lecture's diagram of mineral functions in the body, which mineral is linked to 'brain function and alertness'?
questions.e: The body diagram links zinc to 'brain function and alertness' (as well as smell/taste and prostate/hormone function).

questions.q: Which minerals are linked in the lecture's diagram to 'tooth and bone formation'?
questions.e: Phosphorus and calcium are shown linked to tooth and bone formation in the mineral-function diagram.

questions.q: Which mineral is linked to thyroid function in the lecture's diagram (alongside manganese)?
questions.e: Iodine is linked to thyroid function in the diagram; manganese is separately linked to thyroid function as well.

questions.q: Which mineral is described in the diagram as helping the body 'fight infection'?
questions.e: Copper is linked to 'fights infection' in the mineral-function diagram (it is also linked to lung and kidney function).

questions.q: Which mineral is linked to 'heart regulation' in the lecture's body diagram?
questions.e: Magnesium is linked to heart regulation, as well as alleviating constipation and relaxing muscles.

questions.q: Which mineral is described in the diagram as helping to 'reduce blood pressure'?
questions.e: Potassium is linked to reducing blood pressure, sending oxygen to the brain, and relieving anxiety/insomnia in the diagram.

questions.q: Which mineral is linked in the diagram to 'blood production and disease resistance'?
questions.e: Iron is linked to blood production and disease resistance in the mineral-function body diagram.

questions.q: What does 'properties of the biosphere' refer to, as a factor for inclusion of elements in cells?
o: Comparing the composition of the Earth and its atmosphere with the human body
Measuring atmospheric pressure at sea level across the globe
The number of species on Earth catalogued by biologists
The distance of Earth from the sun and its orbital period
questions.e: The lecture defines this factor as comparing the composition of the Earth and its atmosphere with that of the human body.

questions.q: Which elements, abundant in the Earth's crust, are noted in the lecture as being similarly prominent in the human body?
questions.e: The lecture lists O (48.9%), Fe (18.8%), Si (14.0%), Mg (12.4%), and C (0.10%) in the Earth's crust as being 'like the human body.'

questions.q: The similarity in ion concentrations (Cu²⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Na⁺, K⁺) between seawater and blood plasma is said in the lecture to suggest what?
o: That the ocean is contaminated by biological waste
That man has his ancestry from the sea
That blood and seawater are chemically identical
That minerals dissolve faster in blood than in water
questions.e: The lecture states: 'This phenomenon shows that man has his ancestry from the sea,' based on similar primary-ion concentrations in seawater and blood plasma.

questions.q: What is meant by 'chemical democracy' in the context of elements found in cells?
o: All elements are equally toxic regardless of their concentration
Almost every group on the periodic table has a representative in living cells
Only metals are represented in cells, with no non-metals present
Cells vote on which elements to absorb through active transport
questions.e: 'Chemical democracy' describes how almost every group of the periodic table has at least one representative found in living cells.

questions.q: How many of the 18 groups of the periodic table are found represented in cells, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that 15 out of the 18 groups of elements on the periodic table are found in cells.

questions.q: Besides the f-block (lanthanides and actinides), which blocks of elements have representatives in the cell?
o: Only the s-block elements are represented
Only the p-block elements are represented
The s-block, p-block, and d-block elements
No other blocks are represented in the cell
questions.e: The lecture notes that except for f-block elements, all the other blocks — s, p, and d — have their representatives in the cell.

questions.q: Elements with atomic numbers above 92, such as technetium, astatine, and francium, are excluded from cells mainly because of their:
questions.e: The lecture lists these as excluded due to their 'artificial nature' — they are essentially man-made rather than naturally biologically available.

questions.q: Rare gases such as He, Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe are excluded from biological roles in cells mainly because of their:
questions.e: The lecture attributes their exclusion to 'inert nature' — noble gases (and scarce elements like lanthanides/actinides) are largely unreactive.

questions.q: According to the lecture, lead (Pb²⁺) is toxic to the body primarily because it:
o: Interferes with the functions of magnesium
Damages the liver, kidney, and brain
Causes schizophrenia and other neurological symptoms
questions.e: The lecture states that lead (Pb²⁺) can cause anaemia by inhibiting haem synthesis.

questions.q: Mercury (Hg) toxicity is described in the lecture as primarily damaging which organs?
questions.e: The lecture states that mercury (Hg) causes liver, kidney, and brain damage.

questions.q: Beryllium (Be²⁺) is described as toxic because it interferes with the functions of which ion?
questions.e: The lecture states that beryllium (Be²⁺) interferes with the functions of Mg²⁺.

questions.q: Why can carbon form stable covalent bonds, according to the lecture?
o: It has an ideal atomic size, neither too small nor too big
It is a metal with freely delocalised electrons
It has no valence electrons available for bonding
It is radioactive and decays over geological time
questions.e: The lecture explains that carbon's 'ideal size (neither too small nor too big)' allows it to form stable covalent bonds.

questions.q: What is the specific term for carbon's ability to bond with itself to form straight chains, branches, or rings?
questions.e: 'Catenation' is defined in the lecture as carbon's ability to form bonds with itself in straight chains, branches, or rings.

questions.q: Besides catenation, what other bonding ability of carbon gives rise to a huge variety of organic compounds?
o: The ability to form multiple bonds with itself or other elements
The ability to lose all its electrons easily during reactions
The ability to become a noble gas configuration immediately
The inability to bond with hydrogen or any other element
questions.e: The lecture states that carbon can form multiple bonds either with itself or with other elements, providing a wide variety of organic compounds.

questions.q: What term describes carbon's ability to form four bonds?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'tetravalency' as one of the features that makes carbon unique among elements.

questions.q: Which three elements, besides carbon, are noted in the lecture as being able to produce three or more bonds and potentially form chains of covalent bonds?
questions.e: The lecture names Si, N, and B as elements that can produce three or more bonds and have the potential to form chains of covalent bonds.

questions.q: Silicon is described as a 'congener' of carbon, but Si–Si bonds are weaker than C–C bonds mainly because:
o: Silicon has a smaller atomic size than carbon, which strengthens orbital overlap between atoms
Silicon has a larger atomic size, so atoms cannot approach closely enough for adequate orbital overlap
Silicon cannot form any covalent bonds with itself or with any other atoms whatsoever
Silicon has no valence electrons available at all for forming any kind of covalent bond
questions.e: The lecture explains that silicon's larger atomic size prevents two Si atoms from approaching close enough to allow adequate orbital overlap, weakening Si–Si bonds.

questions.q: How many valence electrons does boron have, and what compounds does this tend to produce?
o: Five valence electrons; highly stable compounds with no reactivity
Three valence electrons; electron-deficient compounds that limit stability
Seven valence electrons; noble-gas-like compounds that resist bonding
One valence electron; ionic salts only with no covalent character
questions.e: The lecture states that boron has three valence electrons, forming electron-deficient compounds, which limits the stability of those compounds.

questions.q: How many valence electrons does nitrogen have, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states plainly that 'nitrogen has five valence electrons.'

questions.q: Why is the bond energy of N–N relatively lower than that of C–C, according to the lecture?
o: Nitrogen atoms are heavier than carbon atoms, which weakens their orbital overlap
Repulsion between lone pairs of electrons remaining on the bonded nitrogen atoms weakens the bond
Nitrogen cannot form covalent bonds at all with any other nitrogen atoms whatsoever
Carbon has more protons than nitrogen, strengthening its nuclear attraction
questions.e: The lecture explains that the lone pair of electrons remaining on each bonded nitrogen atom repels the lone pair on the other, markedly reducing the N–N bond energy.

questions.q: What overall effect does lone-pair repulsion have on the bond energy between two bonded nitrogen atoms?
o: It slightly increases the bond energy
It markedly reduces the bond energy
It converts the bond into an ionic bond
questions.e: The lecture states directly: 'The repulsion between the lone pairs on the bonded nitrogen atoms markedly reduces the bond energy.'

questions.q: According to the lecture, life is a process, feature or phenomenon capable of which three things?
questions.e: The lecture defines life as capable of self-sustenance, replication and mutation — self-sustenance replaces damaged/lost material, replication ensures continuity of life across generations, and mutation allows progeny to change under natural selection.

questions.q: In the lecture's definition, what does 'self-sustenance' ensure?
o: That genetic information is passed to offspring
That organisms can migrate to new environments
That damaged or lost material is replaced
questions.e: Self-sustenance ensures that some damage or loss of material may occur, and these must be replaced, as stated on the 'Origin of Life' slide.

questions.q: What does 'replication' ensure, according to the lecture?
o: That cells can repair DNA damage accumulated during replication and normal metabolic activity
The continuity of life so it does not become extinct, passing genetic information through generations
That organisms can adapt instantly to new environments without any genetic change occurring
That energy is conserved during metabolism so that no energy is ever lost to the surroundings as heat
questions.e: Replication ensures the continuity of life so that it does not become extinct; genetic information is passed through generations.

questions.q: What does 'mutation' permit, per the lecture's definition of life?
o: The emerging progeny to change under the pressure of natural selection to compete efficiently for matter and energy
Cells to remain completely genetically identical across every successive generation without any variation at all
The complete cessation of reproduction across every population of organisms on the planet entirely and forever
Organisms to avoid all forms of environmental stress without needing any physiological adaptation whatsoever
questions.e: Mutation permits the emerging progeny to change under the pressure of natural selection to compete efficiently for matter and energy in an increasingly changing environment.

questions.q: The lecture's second definition of life distinguishes living things from inanimate objects based on what processes?
questions.e: Life is described as a feature distinguishing physical entities having biological processes (signalling and self-sustaining processes) from those that do not (inanimate).

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the 'life forms' in the lecture?
o: Only animals and plants, excluding all microorganisms entirely
Animals, plants, protists, fungi, bacteria and archaea
Only eukaryotic organisms with membrane-bound nuclei and organelles
Only bacteria and viruses, excluding all eukaryotic life forms
questions.e: The lecture lists life forms as animals, plants, protists, fungi, bacteria and archaea.

questions.q: Another definition given in the lecture states that organisms maintain homeostasis, are composed of cells, undergo metabolism, and do what else?
o: Grow, adapt to their environment, respond to stimuli, and reproduce
Only exist in aquatic environments and never survive on dry land
Convert all matter into energy instantly without producing any waste
Only reproduce sexually, never through asexual budding or fission
questions.e: The lecture states organisms maintain homeostasis, are composed of cells, undergo metabolism, grow, adapt to their environment, respond to stimuli, and reproduce.

questions.q: Living systems, as described in the lecture, are maintained by flows of which three things?
questions.e: Living systems are open, self-organising things that interact with their environment and are maintained by flows of information, energy and matter.

questions.q: Who developed the Gaia hypothesis mentioned in the lecture?
questions.e: The Gaia hypothesis, theory or principle was developed by James Lovelock, proposing that organisms interact with their inorganic surroundings to form a self-regulating system that maintains conditions for life.

questions.q: What does the Gaia hypothesis propose?
o: All life forms are chemically identical in their composition, molecular structure and metabolic pathways, with no meaningful biochemical differences
Earth's temperature has remained completely unchanged since the planet first formed billions of years ago, with no climatic variation whatsoever at all
Organisms interact with their inorganic surroundings to form a synergistic, self-regulating complex system that maintains and perpetuates conditions for life on the planet
Life arrived on Earth entirely from outer space, carried here by comets, asteroids and meteorites arriving from distant, unknown star systems far away
questions.e: Per the lecture, the Gaia hypothesis proposes a self-regulating, synergistic system formed by organisms and their inorganic surroundings that helps maintain and perpetuate conditions for life on Earth.

questions.q: What is Complex Systems Biology (CSB), as defined in the lecture?
o: A method for classifying species by total genome size, chromosome number, and complete karyotype structure
A branch of physics studying planetary orbits, gravitational interactions and very detailed orbital mechanics
A subfield of biochemistry focused only on enzyme kinetics, catalysis and very detailed reaction mechanisms
A branch of mathematical and theoretical biology concerned with the complexity of structure and function in biological organisms
questions.e: CSB is defined as a branch of mathematical and theoretical biology concerned with the complexity of both structure and function in biological organisms, focusing on emergence, evolution and complex interactions within bionetworks.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why does life not occur on all planets?
o: Every planet lacks a solid surface capable of supporting complex prebiotic chemistry
Conditions on most planets do not support life — Earth has the right moisture, air and temperature
Life requires no specific conditions at all and can arise spontaneously anywhere
All planets are too far from any star to receive sufficient warmth or light energy
questions.e: The lecture states that life does not occur on all planets because conditions on most planets do not support life; conditions on Earth are right for the occurrence, sustenance and perpetuation of life, with proper moisture, air and temperature.

questions.q: What does the Habitable Zone Distance (HZD) measure?
o: The exact surface temperature of a planet measured in degrees Celsius
How far an exoplanet is from the center of its star's habitable zone, in habitable zone units
The number of moons orbiting a planet within its own planetary system
The mass of a planet relative to the total mass of the planet Earth itself
questions.e: The lecture defines HZD as measuring how far an exoplanet is from the center of the star's habitable zone (HZ), in habitable zone units (HZU), with zero being the exact center and values from -1 to +1 for planets inside the HZ.

questions.q: What does the Standard Primary Habitability (SPH) scale measure, and what is considered optimum?
o: Distance from the sun measured in astronomical units, which is unrelated to surface climate conditions
Thermal-water climate suitability for land vegetation on a scale of 0 to 1, with 25°C as the optimum growth temperature
Ocean salinity measured on a scale of 1 to 10, which is entirely unrelated to land vegetation growth
Atmospheric oxygen percentage relative to the total atmospheric gas composition of a whole planet
questions.e: SPH measures the thermal-water climate suitability of a planet for land primary producers (vegetation) on a scale from zero to one; planets with mean surface temperatures near 25°C (the optimum growth temperature for most vegetation) score close to one, while temperatures below -10°C or above 50°C are non-habitable.

questions.q: According to the 'Special Creation' view discussed in the lecture, life requires what to be generated?
o: A supernatural force beyond natural explanation
Radioactive decay of unstable heavy elements
A chemical reaction in a primordial pond
Volcanic heat released from deep within the crust
questions.e: The special creation view holds that life is so complex that it requires a supernatural force to generate it — a position associated with the Christian, Muslim and African traditionalist views mentioned in the lecture.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: What problem do some scientists have with the special creation view, per the lecture?
o: It requires too much laboratory equipment to ever test
It contradicts the fossil record directly and consistently
It is mystical, cannot be proved, and does not obey natural laws
It was disproved by Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiment
questions.e: The lecture states scientists' problem with special creation is that it is mystical and cannot be proved, and it does not obey the natural laws.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: What does the term 'Panspermia' literally mean, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that Panspermia means 'seeds everywhere,' suggesting that life seeds came from outer space and planets exchanged life.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Which two scientists proposed that intelligent forces may have directed the transport of life from elsewhere (directed panspermia)?
questions.e: The lecture credits Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel with proposing that some intelligent forces may have directed the transport of life from elsewhere.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Who among the following proposed that life came from meteorites, according to the lecture?
o: Francesco Redi, who tested spontaneous generation
H.E. Richter, who proposed life came from meteorites
Sales Gyon de Montlivant, who proposed life came from the moon
Svante Arrhenius, who proposed directed panspermia
questions.e: The lecture lists H.E. Richter as a proponent who suggested that life came from meteorites, while Sales Gyon de Montlivant proposed life came from the moon and Svante Arrhenius proposed panspermia.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: According to the lecture, roughly what percentage of rocks from Mars are estimated to reach Earth, and how long can that journey take?
o: About 50%, travelling less than 1 year to arrive
About 7.5%, travelling between 100 and 16,000 years or more
About 1%, travelling millions of years to arrive
questions.e: The lecture states that statistics have shown about 7.5% of rocks from Mars reach Earth, and the rocks would travel between 100 and 16,000 years or more to arrive.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Which piece of evidence for panspermia relates to bacteria's survival ability, as noted in the lecture?
o: Bacteria can survive the harsh environment of space, including UV radiation, proton bombardment and cold, living in a sleeping state until awakened
Bacteria require oxygen to remain dormant, and quickly die within mere seconds of exposure to the vacuum of outer space itself
Bacteria cannot survive outside a host cell and die rapidly the very moment they are exposed to the open vacuum of space entirely
Bacteria are destroyed almost instantly by vacuum conditions, cosmic radiation and the extreme cold found throughout deep space
questions.e: The lecture states bacteria can survive the harsh environment of space (UV radiation, proton bombardments, and cold), living for a long time in a sleeping state until awakened — cited as evidence for panspermia.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: What evidence regarding meteorites supports the panspermia hypothesis, according to the lecture?
o: Meteorites never survive atmospheric entry and burn up completely
Meteorites contain amino acids, bacteria, and carbon protected inside rocks
Meteorites are composed entirely of ice with no rocky material
Meteorites contain no organic molecules of any kind whatsoever
questions.e: The lecture notes evidence that meteorites contain life: amino acids (left-handed in helicity), bacteria, and carbon protected inside rocks.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Why does the lecture suggest Mars might be 'safer' than Earth for early life?
o: Mars has a much thicker atmosphere than Earth, trapping far more heat near its surface
Mars is much closer to the sun than Earth, receiving far greater amounts of solar radiation
Mars has much stronger gravity than Earth, always holding a much denser atmosphere in place
Mars had fewer bombardments and less gravity, was not as hot as early Earth, and had oxygen when Earth did not
questions.e: The lecture states Mars is safer than Earth (fewer bombardments and gravity), was not as hot as Earth in its early development, and had oxygen when Earth did not.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: The spontaneous generation theory, as presented in the lecture, asserts that life arose how?
o: Only from pre-existing life, never arising spontaneously
Abiogenically, arising spontaneously from non-living matter
Through radioactive decay of elements deep within rocks
Through directed panspermia sent by another civilisation
questions.e: The spontaneous generation theory asserts that life arose abiogenically — from non-living matter — a view historically attributed to Aristotle and supported later by Van Velmont, John Needham and Felix Pouchet.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: According to the lecture, which ancient philosopher (384–322 BC) suggested that organisms could emerge freely from soil, straw or refuse left for a period under the right conditions?
o: Aristotle, philosopher who inspired spontaneous generation
Francesco Redi, who tested spontaneous generation
Louis Pasteur, who disproved spontaneous generation
Lazarro Spallanzani, who repeated Redi's experiments
questions.e: The lecture credits Aristotle (384-322 BC) with suggesting that organisms could emerge freely from soil, straw, or refuse free of life if conditions were right — a foundational idea behind spontaneous generation.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Whose work delivered 'the first blow' to the spontaneous generation idea, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states the first blow to spontaneous generation came from the work of Francesco Redi (1626-1697), relating to biogenesis, later reinforced by Rudolph Virchow in 1858.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: Who invented the microscope in 1675, paving the way for studying spontaneous generation of microbes, per the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states the invention of the microscope by Anton van Leeuwenhoek in 1675 paved the way for studying the spontaneous generation of microbes.
questions.t: Views on the Origin of Life

questions.q: How does the lecture distinguish chemical evolution from biological evolution?
o: Chemical evolution occurs only within animals over the course of their individual lifetimes, while biological evolution occurs only within separate plants and fungi over many generations instead
Chemical evolution and biological evolution are considered by most scientists to be entirely identical processes that occur at exactly the same steady rate everywhere across the universe

Chemical evolution is the formation of complex organic molecules from simple molecules, while biological evolution is the formation of a self-sustaining, self-replicating system from complex organic molecules
Biological evolution precedes chemical evolution in every single documented case, always occurring before any organic molecules have ever had any chance whatsoever to form naturally at all
questions.e: The lecture states chemical evolution is the formation of complex organic molecules from simple molecules, whereas biological evolution is the formation of a self-sustaining, self-replicating system from complex organic molecules.

questions.q: What is the first of the three steps of chemical/biological evolution listed in the lecture?
o: Formation of complete multicellular organisms directly from simple inorganic compounds alone
Aggregation of biopolymers into prototypes of cells with primitive enclosing lipid membranes
Formation of vital monomers like sugars, amino acids, and organic bases from simple compounds like CH4, NH3, H2O
Development of reproductive machinery capable of accurate genetic self-replication systems
questions.e: The lecture lists the steps as: (1) formation of vital monomers from simple compounds such as CH4, NH3 and H2O, (2) polymerisation of monomers into proteins/nucleic acids and aggregation into cell prototypes, and (3) development of reproductive machinery.

questions.q: Which two 20th-century scientists suggested, in long-term spontaneous generation theory, that life once evolved from non-living matter?
questions.e: The lecture credits JBS Haldane, a British biochemist, and AL Oparin, a Russian biochemist, with independently suggesting in the 20th century that life once evolved from non-living matter.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what was the largest source of energy for chemical evolution on primitive Earth?
o: Sunlight, the dominant energy source for early chemistry
questions.e: The lecture states that the largest source of energy for chemical evolution was sunlight, with electrical discharges from lightning cited as another source.

questions.q: Which molecules does the lecture list as present in the primitive atmosphere?
o: Hydrogen, methane, water vapour, ammonia and probably hydrogen sulphide
Helium and neon exclusively, with no other trace gases
Ozone and chlorine only, with no reducing gases present
Oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide only, as found today
questions.e: The lecture states the primitive atmosphere included hydrogen, methane, water vapour, ammonia and probably hydrogen sulphide.

questions.q: What organic molecules does the lecture say carbonaceous meteorites contain, similar to those in biological systems?
o: Only water ice with no other chemical compounds present
Only metallic iron with no organic compounds at all
Only inorganic salts with no carbon-based molecules
Alcohols, aldehydes, amines, amino acids, purines and pyrimidines
questions.e: The lecture states carbonaceous meteorites contain organic molecules like those found in biological systems, such as alcohols, aldehydes, amines, amino acids, purines and pyrimidines.

questions.q: How does the lecture describe the formation of the 'prebiotic' or 'primordial soup'?
o: Biologically vital compounds formed in the absence of oxygen, were spared oxidative alteration, and were washed by rain into the oceans to build up in concentration
Compounds formed exclusively through photosynthesis inside early cyanobacteria colonies long before any oceans on Earth ever existed at all
Vital compounds formed only inside active volcanic craters and were never transported anywhere else on the surface of the planet at all, whatsoever
Compounds were synthesised only inside laboratory flasks under artificial conditions that never occurred anywhere in nature at all, under any circumstances
questions.e: The lecture explains that compounds formed in the absence of oxygen were spared oxidative alteration, persisting and being washed by rain into the oceans, building up concentrations that formed the prebiotic/primordial soup.

questions.q: Roughly how long ago does the lecture say the primordial soup theory places the beginning of life?
questions.e: The lecture states the primordial soup theory places the beginning of life at least 4.5 billion years ago, in a pond or ocean where chemicals from the atmosphere combined with energy to make amino acids.

questions.q: Who independently conceived the primordial soup idea in 1920, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states Oparin and Haldane conceived this idea, both developing the primordial soup theory independently in 1920.

questions.q: What does current evidence suggest about the first organisms, contrary to the earlier heterotroph-first idea presented in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture notes that while it was once thought the first organisms were simple heterotrophs that later became autotrophs by mutation, evidence now suggests the first organisms were actually autotrophs.

questions.q: Which two scientists performed the famous 1950 experiment testing the primordial soup theory, according to the lecture?
o: Chemist Stanley Miller and physicist Harold Urey
questions.e: The lecture states that chemist Stanley Miller and physicist Harold Urey performed a famous experiment in 1950 to test the primordial soup theory.

questions.q: In the Miller–Urey experiment described in the lecture, which gases were mixed (without oxygen) to simulate the primitive Earth?
questions.e: The lecture states Miller and Urey mixed gases thought to be present on primitive Earth — methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), water (H2O) and hydrogen (H2) — without oxygen.

questions.q: What did Miller and Urey do to the gas mixture to simulate lightning, and what was the result?
o: They exposed it to gamma radiation, producing no measurable change at all
They boiled the mixture for a week and it produced sugars only, nothing else
They froze the mixture and it produced no products of any kind whatsoever
They electrically sparked the mixture, producing amino acids, the building blocks of proteins
questions.e: The lecture states they electrically sparked the mixture to signify lightning, and the results were amino acids — the building blocks of proteins.

questions.q: Besides electricity, which other energy sources does the lecture say can excite gases to produce all 20 amino acids?
o: Only magnetism applied continuously to the gas mixture
Only sound waves passed through the gas mixture
Only gravity acting on the gas mixture over time
UV light, heat, and shock waves applied to the mixture
questions.e: The lecture states it was later discovered that electricity, UV light, heat, and shock can all excite gases and produce all 20 amino acids.

questions.q: What reaction network does the lecture cite as an example of the prebiotic synthesis of monosaccharides?
o: The formose reaction network, starting from formaldehyde
The Krebs cycle, which oxidises acetyl groups for energy
The urea cycle, which detoxifies ammonia in the liver
The Calvin cycle, which fixes carbon dioxide in plants
questions.e: The lecture presents an excerpt of the formose reaction network — beginning from formaldehyde and proceeding through reactions like the Cannizzaro reaction, aldol reaction, isomerisation and others — as the route to prebiotic monosaccharide synthesis.

questions.q: Which synthesis route does the lecture describe for prebiotic amino acid formation?
o: The citric acid cycle, which oxidises acetyl groups for energy
Photophosphorylation, which generates ATP using light energy
Strecker synthesis, in which an aldehyde reacts with hydrogen cyanide
Beta-oxidation of fatty acids, which releases acetyl-CoA units
questions.e: The lecture states amino acids could be formed via Strecker synthesis, in which an aldehyde reacts with hydrogen cyanide (HCN).

questions.q: What are the three steps of Strecker synthesis as outlined in the lecture?
o: Water is added to an alkene; the resulting alcohol is then oxidised; the acid formed is finally esterified with another alcohol
Ammonia reacts with an aldehyde to form an imine; cyanide adds to the imine to form aminonitrile; hydrolysis of the aminonitrile gives an amino acid
Glucose is first phosphorylated; it is then isomerised; the resulting product is finally cleaved into two three-carbon sugars
An amine attacks a carbonyl group; a Schiff base forms; it is then reduced by NADH to give a completely new amine product entirely
questions.e: The lecture lists the Strecker synthesis steps as: ammonia reacts with an aldehyde to form an imine, cyanide addition to the imine forms an aminonitrile, and hydrolysis of the aminonitrile gives an amino acid.

questions.q: According to the lecture's prebiotic nucleotide synthesis diagram, what starting molecule polymerises to eventually form adenine, hypoxanthine, xanthine and guanine?
o: Glucose, the simple sugar broken down in glycolysis
Hydrogen cyanide, which polymerises toward purine bases
Acetic acid, a simple two-carbon carboxylic acid
Formaldehyde, the simplest possible aldehyde molecule
questions.e: The lecture's slide on prebiotic synthesis of nucleotides shows polymerisation of hydrogen cyanide (HCN), passing through diaminomaleonitrile, to ultimately yield purine bases such as adenine, hypoxanthine, xanthine and guanine.

questions.q: What conditions does the lecture say were required to synthesise fatty acids under one proposed prebiotic route?
questions.e: The lecture states high temperature and hydrogen pressures were required to synthesise fatty acids, though it notes a problem: such elevated temperatures could not have been sustained in primitive times over an extended period.

questions.q: In the lecture's fatty acid synthesis pathway diagram, formic acid and oxalic acid undergo thermal decomposition to produce which gases, which then undergo Fischer-Tropsch thermal processes?
o: Only nitrogen and hydrogen released from ammonia breakdown
CO, H2O, H2 and CO2, feeding later Fischer-Tropsch chemistry
Only methane released from carbonate mineral decomposition
Only oxygen released from mineral oxidation reactions
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows formic acid and oxalic acid undergoing thermal decomposition to CO, H2O, H2 and CO2, which then undergo Fischer-Tropsch thermal processes to yield n-alkanes, alkenes, alkanols, alkanoic acids (fatty acids), and alkyl formates.

questions.q: How does the lecture define polymerisation?
o: Removing hydrogen atoms from a molecule through repeated oxidative dehydrogenation reactions
Combining several monomers to form more complex molecules, such as polysaccharides, polypeptides and polynucleotides
Breaking large molecules into smaller subunits through repeated hydrolysis of chemical bonds
Converting monosaccharides into fatty acids through repeated enzymatic condensation reaction steps
questions.e: Polymerisation is defined as combining several monomers to form more complex molecules; through polymerisation, polysaccharides, polypeptides and polynucleotides could be formed.

questions.q: In the example of two glucose molecules joining, what must be removed for the disaccharide to form, and what is this forward reaction called?
o: Oxygen must be removed; the forward reaction is oxidation
Water must be removed; the forward reaction is a condensation reaction
Carbon must be removed; the forward reaction is decarboxylation
Nitrogen must be removed; the forward reaction is reduction
questions.e: The lecture explains Glucose + Glucose ⇌ Disaccharide + H2O: the elements forming water must be removed from the two glucose molecules; the forward reaction is a condensation reaction, and the backward reaction is a hydrolytic reaction.

questions.q: What makes a condensation reaction thermodynamically favoured, per the lecture?
o: If the water formed can be removed by evaporation or by using condensing agents
If no catalyst is present anywhere in the surrounding solution
If the reaction occurs strictly in a vacuum with no solvent present
If the temperature is kept below 0°C throughout the entire reaction
questions.e: The lecture states a condensation reaction would be thermodynamically favoured if the water formed by condensation can be removed by evaporation or by using condensing agents.

questions.q: What chemical feature do condensing agents typically have, according to the lecture?
o: A single hydroxyl group attached to an otherwise unreactive carbon chain
Carbon atoms linked by energetic double bonds to two nitrogen atoms, e.g. carbodiimide
An aromatic amine group only, with no other reactive functional groups
A benzene ring fused to a simple saturated hydrocarbon chain structure
questions.e: The lecture states condensing agents typically have carbon atoms linked by energetic double bonds to two nitrogen atoms (-N=C=N-), exemplified by carbodiimide of the general formula R-N=C=N-R.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in the lecture as a condensing agent that could have existed in the prebiotic soup?
o: Oxygen gas released during early photosynthesis
Glucose, a simple six-carbon sugar molecule
Carbon dioxide fixed later by autotrophic organisms
questions.e: The lecture lists cyanogen (N≡C-C≡N), cyanamide (N≡CNH2), diaminomaleonitrile and cyanoacetylene (N≡C-C≡CH) as other possible condensing agents in the prebiotic soup, alongside carbodiimide.

questions.q: What polyphosphate compound does the lecture cite as a condensing agent and energy source used by organisms?
o: NADH, the reduced electron carrier of respiration
Pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis
ATP, the universal energy currency of the cell
questions.e: The lecture states polyphosphates, such as ATP, act as condensing agents, driven by the free energy of hydration of the condensing agent, and these polyphosphates were also energy sources used by organisms.

questions.q: What effective way to concentrate pre-biological molecules does the lecture mention, besides dry heating?
o: Exposing them to constant darkness for long periods of time
Freezing them slowly inside ancient glacier ice sheets
Dissolving them further into dilute ocean seawater
Adsorption onto the surfaces of minerals such as micas, clays and kaolin
questions.e: The lecture states another effective way to concentrate pre-biological molecules was adsorption onto the surfaces of minerals such as micas, clays (made of silicates attached to cations), and kaolin, which also served as primitive catalytic centres.

questions.q: Regarding whether protein or nucleic acid is more primitive, what 'more plausible reason' does the lecture propose?
o: Nucleic acids evolved millions of years before any proteins had ever existed anywhere at all, historically
Neither molecule type could have evolved at all without cell membranes forming completely first
Proteins evolved millions of years before any nucleic acids had ever existed anywhere at all, historically
Proteins and nucleic acids evolved in parallel, with polynucleotide replication coupled to polypeptide catalytic power
questions.e: The lecture proposes that proteins and nucleic acids evolved in parallel: the ability of a polynucleotide to replicate could be coupled to the power of a polypeptide to act as a catalyst, with polynucleotides specifying polypeptides via translation while polypeptides catalyse polynucleotide replication.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the simplest structure that shows evidence of life?
o: A strand of RNA capable of limited self-replication alone
A crystal lattice that grows through simple mineral accretion
A single protein molecule with no genetic material at all
A cell, which must have a membrane separating it from its surroundings
questions.e: The lecture states the simplest structure that shows evidence of life is a cell — a compartment that must have a membrane to separate it from its surroundings so it is not diluted out of existence.

questions.q: What did Oparin call his early 'cells,' and what process formed them?
o: Protobionts, formed through a process of coacervation
questions.e: The lecture states Oparin called his 'cells' protobionts, which were formed through a process of coacervation, suggested to emerge when a boundary or membrane formed around molecules with catalytic activity, most probably proteins.

questions.q: What was the shortcoming of Oparin's coacervate droplets, per the lecture?
o: They were formed from materials such as gum arabic, histone and albumin, which living systems had already produced
They dissolved almost instantly in water and left behind no trace of any lasting structure
They could not form any stable spherical shapes under any laboratory conditions ever tested at all
They contained no catalytic molecules at all capable of driving any chemical reactions forward
questions.e: The lecture notes the shortcoming of Oparin's coacervate droplets is that they were formed from materials such as gum arabic, histone and albumin — substances that living systems had already formed, undermining their use as a prebiotic model.

questions.q: What are Fox's 'thermal proteinoids' described as in the lecture?
o: Large multicellular colonies formed by aggregating separate proteinoid microspheres together
Micro-spheroidal aggregates that, under suitable conditions, form microspheres which grow and eventually bud
Crystalline mineral structures with no organic content or catalytic activity whatsoever
RNA-only structures with no protein content or any catalytic activity whatsoever at all
questions.e: The lecture describes Fox's thermal proteinoids as micro-spheroidal aggregates; under suitable conditions the proteinoids form microspheres, which grow and eventually bud, and these microspheres have a two-layer membrane like that of bacteria.

questions.q: What was the problem with the membranes of Fox's proteinoid microspheres, according to the lecture?
o: They contained no lipids at all
They were too rigid to grow
They could not form in water
questions.e: The lecture explicitly states the problem with the membranes of Fox's proteinoids was that they were too leaky.

questions.q: In the lecture's diagram of self-reproducing catalytic micelles as protocell precursors, what process follows 'homeostatic growth' before compositional reproduction occurs?
o: Fission, splitting the micelle into two daughter vesicles
Translation of stored genetic information into new protein
Photosynthesis, converting captured light into chemical energy
Endocytosis, engulfing material from outside the micelle
questions.e: The diagram shows a mixed micelle library undergoing catalysed accretion, then homeostatic growth, then fission leading to compositional reproduction (with possible compositional mutations), and further evolution toward a vesicular protocell.

questions.q: What ultimately develops from the sequence of catalysed accretion, homeostatic growth, and fission of micelles, according to the lecture's diagram?
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows that through further evolution beyond compositional reproduction, the micelle system develops into a vesicular protocell.

questions.q: What drove the development of metabolic pathways, according to the lecture?
o: Competition for nutrients in the cell
questions.e: The lecture states that competition for nutrients in the cell led to the development of metabolic pathways.

questions.q: What energy-rich compounds does the lecture say powered early polymerisation reactions in developing metabolism?
o: Only water supplying hydrogen atoms for reduction reactions
Only carbon dioxide fixed directly from the atmosphere
ATP or polyphosphates, energy-rich phosphate compounds
Only glucose broken down through simple glycolysis
questions.e: The lecture states that evolved polymerisation reactions depended on the environment to supply monomeric units and energy-rich compounds such as ATP or polyphosphates.

questions.q: As components of the prebiotic soup became scarce, what did organisms develop, according to the lecture?
o: The ability to survive without needing any energy source of any kind whatsoever
Enzymatic systems that could synthesise these substances from simpler, more abundant precursors
A complete dependence on radioactive decay as the sole source of usable energy
Complete immunity to all environmental change of any kind whatsoever, permanently
questions.e: The lecture states that as essential components in the prebiotic soup became scarce, organisms developed enzymatic systems that could synthesise these substances from simpler but more abundant precursors, giving rise to energy-producing metabolic pathways.

questions.q: Why did the photosynthetic system evolve, according to the lecture?
o: Because water was extremely scarce on early Earth and could not support any other reaction pathways
Because pre-existing energy-rich substances became increasingly scarce, while the sun's energy supply was inexhaustible
Because oxygen was already abundant throughout the atmosphere before photosynthesis ever evolved
Because organisms wanted to stop reproducing and instead conserve all their available stored energy
questions.e: The lecture states that as pre-existing energy-rich substances became increasingly scarce, the photosynthetic system evolved to take advantage of the sun, whose energy supply was inexhaustible.

questions.q: What reducing agent was initially used in photosynthesis before being replaced, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that in photosynthesis, reducing agents such as H2S were initially used until this reductant was exhausted, leading to refinement of the photosynthetic apparatus to utilise the ubiquitous reducing agent, H2O.

questions.q: What reactive by-product resulted once water (H2O) became the photosynthetic reducing agent, and what did organisms adopt to avoid its damage?
o: Excess ammonia was produced as a toxic by-product; organisms then adopted the urea cycle to detoxify it
Highly reactive nitrogen gas was produced; organisms then adopted denitrification pathways to remove it
Toxic methane gas was produced as a by-product; organisms then adopted methane fixation pathways to remove it
Highly reactive O2 was produced; organisms adopted a more efficient form of energy metabolism using O2 as an oxidising agent
questions.e: The lecture explains that using water brought the production of highly reactive O2 as a by-product; to circumvent oxidative damage from O2 accumulation, a much more efficient form of energy metabolism using O2 as an oxidising agent was adopted.

questions.q: According to the lecture's summary timeline of the evolution of life, approximately how old is the oldest zircon crystal, and what does it mark?
o: 4.4 billion years old, among the earliest evidence tied to Earth's formation timeline
440 million years old, marking the early rise of the first dinosaurs on land
44,000 years old, marking the appearance of the first hard-shelled animals in the oceans
4.4 million years old, marking the appearance of the very first early humans
questions.e: The lecture's summary timeline places the oldest zircon crystal at 4.4 billion years old, shortly after Earth's formation at 4.56 billion years ago, making it among the earliest physical evidence in the timeline of life's evolution.

questions.q: Who first suggested the particulate nature of matter around 500 BC, calling the basic units of elements 'atoms'?
questions.e: About 500 BC, Democritus suggested the particulate nature of matter and called the basic units of elements 'atoms'.

questions.q: Which philosopher proposed that matter was continuous and not composed of smaller particles, naming it 'Hyle'?
o: Rutherford, who proposed the nuclear atomic model
Aristotle, who proposed the four classical elements
Democritus, who proposed the concept of the atom
Bohr, who proposed quantised electron energy levels
questions.e: Aristotle proposed that matter was continuous and was not composed of smaller particles, naming it 'Hyle'.

questions.q: John Dalton's atomic theory was based on which two laws?
o: Law of definite proportion and law of conservation of mass
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and Pauli's exclusion principle
Law of octaves and law of triads, from Newlands and Döbereiner
Law of multiple proportion only, without any other laws
questions.e: Dalton's proposals were based on the law of definite proportion (Proust) and the law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier).

questions.q: According to Dalton's atomic theory, atoms of the same element are:
o: Different in mass but identical in charge
Identical in mass/size and physical and chemical properties
Always negatively charged, regardless of the element
Always radioactive, decaying spontaneously over time
questions.e: Dalton's theory states atoms of the same element are identical: identical mass or size and the same physical and chemical properties.

questions.q: Which aspect of Dalton's atomic theory was proven incorrect by the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons?
questions.e: The existence of sub-atomic particles (protons, neutrons, electrons) disproved Dalton's claim that atoms are indivisible.

questions.q: Hydrogen-3 isotopes (protium, deuterium, tritium) disprove which part of Dalton's theory?
questions.e: The presence of isotopes — atoms of the same element with different masses, e.g. ¹₁H protium, ²₁H deuterium, ³₁H tritium — showed Dalton's theory was incomplete.

questions.q: J. J. Thomson's atomic model (1904) is commonly known as the:
questions.e: J. J. Thomson proposed the 'slum pudding' or watermelon model of the atom.

questions.q: Thomson's atomic model was developed from which experiment?
questions.e: Thomson's plum-pudding model came from his cathode ray experiment.

questions.q: Ernest Rutherford's nuclear atom model (1911) resulted from which experiment?
questions.e: Rutherford's nuclear atom model came from the alpha scattering or gold foil experiment.

questions.q: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, what did the occasional back-scattering of an alpha particle indicate?
o: The atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense core
The atom has a small, dense, positively-charged nucleus
Electrons are quantised into discrete energy levels
Electrons have wave properties, like light does
questions.e: That an alpha particle occasionally travelled straight back from the foil showed it hit something small, dense and positively charged — the nucleus.

questions.q: Niels Bohr's atomic model is also called the:
questions.e: Neil Bohr's model is the planetary model, based on the atomic spectrum.

questions.q: Bohr explained that electrons do not spiral into the nucleus because their energy is:
o: Always zero, regardless of the electron's position
Continuous, taking on any value without restriction
Randomly distributed across all possible energy values
Quantised, restricted to discrete/permissible energy levels
questions.e: Bohr used quantum theory to show electrons are restricted to permissible energy levels — they are quantised, so they do not lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.

questions.q: What is observed when hydrogen atoms are given energy by passing an electric current through them at low pressure or heating them in a flame?
o: An electron cloud surrounding the nucleus
A line spectrum of discrete wavelengths
A continuous spectrum across all wavelengths
An orbital region of high electron probability
questions.e: A line spectrum is observed under these conditions, and it was this spectrum that Bohr studied to develop his model.

questions.q: In Bohr's model, what is the name given to the whole number (1 to infinity) assigned to each electron orbit?
questions.e: In Bohr's model, each orbit was assigned a number called the principal quantum number, a whole number from 1 to infinity.

questions.q: Who suggested that an electron has wave properties in addition to being a particle?
questions.e: Louis de Broglie, a French graduate student, suggested that apart from having a particle nature, the electron also had wave properties (momentum and wavelength).

questions.q: The uncertainty principle, which states it is difficult to determine an electron's position and momentum at the same time, is attributed to:
questions.e: The uncertainty principle was postulated by Werner Heisenberg.

questions.q: Who derived the equation describing the behaviour of an electron in a hydrogen atom by combining de Broglie's equation with equations for wave motion?
questions.e: Erwin Schrödinger combined de Broglie's equation with others for wave motion to derive the Schrödinger equation.

questions.q: What does ψ² (psi squared) represent?
o: The total energy of an electron occupying a given atomic orbital
The intrinsic spin of an electron about its own internal quantum axis
The number of protons contained within the atomic nucleus itself
The mathematical expression of the probability of finding an electron in a small volume
questions.e: ψ² is a mathematical expression of the probability of finding an electron in a small volume that varies from place to place.

questions.q: How many quantum numbers are there in total?
questions.e: There are four quantum numbers: principal (n), orbital/azimuthal (l), magnetic (ml) and spin (ms).

questions.q: What does the principal quantum number (n) determine?
o: The shape of an orbital within a given subshell
The energy level and closeness of electrons to the nucleus
The orientation of orbitals in three-dimensional space
The spin direction of an electron within its orbital
questions.e: The principal quantum number (n) determines the energy level and closeness of electrons to the nucleus.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy a shell with principal quantum number n?
questions.e: The maximum number of electrons per shell is 2n², where n is the number of energy levels.

questions.q: The orbital (azimuthal) quantum number (l) defines:
o: The energy level of an electron
questions.e: The orbital or azimuthal quantum number (l) defines the shape of an orbital.

questions.q: For n = 1, what is the only possible value of l, and what orbital shape does it correspond to?
questions.e: l starts from 0 to n−1; for n=1, l=0, which is the s-orbital, symmetrically spherical and able to hold two electrons.

questions.q: The magnetic quantum number (ml) describes:
o: The orientation of orbitals in space
The energy level of a shell
questions.e: The magnetic quantum number (ml) describes the orientation of orbitals in space; it ranges from −l to +l including zero.

questions.q: What range of values can the magnetic quantum number (ml) take?
questions.e: The magnetic quantum number starts from −l to +l, including zero (0).

questions.q: The spin quantum number (ms) represents:
o: The particular shape of the orbital occupied by the electron
The number of protons contained within the atomic nucleus
The ability of electrons to spin about their axis, clockwise or anti-clockwise
The orientation of an orbital within three-dimensional space
questions.e: The spin quantum number (ms) represents the ability of electrons to spin about their axis, either clockwise or anti-clockwise; values range from −½ to +½.

questions.q: For n = 3, how many possible l values are there, and what are they?
questions.e: For n=3, l = n−1 gives possible values of 0, 1 and 2, corresponding to the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells.

questions.q: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in atoms, following how many approaches?
questions.e: There are two approaches: considering only the principal quantum number (octet rule), and considering all four quantum numbers.

questions.q: Which three rules guide the writing of electronic configuration?
o: Aufbau's rule, Pauli's exclusion principle, Hund's rule
Heisenberg's principle, de Broglie's rule, Bohr's rule
Octet rule, Law of triads, Law of octaves from early chemists
Law of conservation of mass, Law of definite proportion, Octet rule
questions.e: Three rules guide electronic configuration: Aufbau's rule, Pauli's exclusion principle, and Hund's rule.

questions.q: Aufbau's rule states that electrons must first fill orbitals of:
o: The same energy level only, in any order
questions.e: Aufbau's rule: the electrons must first fill the orbitals of lower energies before the orbitals of higher energies.

questions.q: According to the Aufbau filling order, which orbital is filled immediately after 3p?
questions.e: The filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s... so 4s fills before 3d, immediately after 3p.

questions.q: Using the first approach (octet rule), what is the electronic configuration of sodium (₁₁Na)?
questions.e: Using the first approach obeying the octet rule, ₁₁Na = 2, 8, 1.

questions.q: Using the second approach (all quantum numbers), what is the electronic configuration of sodium (₁₁Na)?
questions.e: Using the second approach, ₁₁Na = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.

questions.q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that an orbital can be filled by a maximum of how many electrons, and with what spin arrangement?
questions.e: Pauli's exclusion principle: the total number of electrons that can fill an orbital must be two, and these electrons must have opposite spins.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of boron (₅B) according to Aufbau's rule and Pauli's exclusion principle?
questions.e: ₅B = 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py 2pz — the fifth electron occupies a 2p orbital singly.

questions.q: Hund's rule states that degenerate orbitals are first filled:
o: Only after the next shell begins filling
In pairs with opposite spins immediately
Singly, with parallel spins, before pairing up
questions.e: Hund's rule: degenerate orbitals (of the same energy) are first filled singly and with parallel spins before pairing up with opposite spins.

questions.q: According to Hund's rule, what is the correct electron arrangement for nitrogen's (₇N) three 2p electrons?
questions.e: ₇N = 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹ — Hund's rule requires the three 2p electrons to occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins.

questions.q: What is the electronic configuration of oxygen (₈O), which has one paired 2p orbital?
questions.e: ₈O = 1s² 2s² 2px² 2py¹ 2pz¹ — after nitrogen's half-filled p-orbitals, the fourth p-electron must pair up in one orbital.

questions.q: Why do chromium (₂₄Cr) and copper (₂₉Cu) deviate from the standard Aufbau filling order?
o: Half-filled and fully-filled 3d/4s subshells confer extra stability
They have no 4s electrons occupying any orbital
They are noble gases with completely filled shells
They are radioactive and decay spontaneously over time
questions.e: Chromium ([Ar] 3d⁵4s¹) and copper ([Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹) show extra stability when the 3d and 4s subshells are half-filled or fully filled, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of chromium (₂₄Cr)?
questions.e: Chromium's configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, noted for the stability of a half-filled 3d and half-filled 4s.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of scandium (₂₁Sc) in noble-gas shorthand?
questions.e: Scandium (Z=21) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹ 4s², shortened to [Ar] 3d¹ 4s².

questions.q: Who put forward the modern form of the periodic table of the elements?
o: Rutherford, who proposed the nuclear atomic model
Dalton, who proposed that atoms are indivisible
Bohr, who proposed quantised electron energy levels
Mendeleev, who put forward the modern periodic table
questions.e: Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, put forward the modern form of the periodic table of the elements.

questions.q: The modern periodic table arranges elements according to their:
o: Discovery date, the year each element was first isolated
Melting point, measured under standard atmospheric pressure
Atomic number, based on periodicity of electronic structure
Atomic mass only, ignoring electronic structure entirely
questions.e: The arrangement is based on the periodicity of the electronic structure of atoms; elements are arranged according to their atomic numbers.

questions.q: Into how many categories can the periodic table's elements be divided?
o: Five, including groups, periods, blocks and subshells
Two: groups and periods, ignoring blocks entirely
Three: groups, periods and blocks of the table
Four: groups, periods, blocks and families
questions.e: The elements of the periodic table can be divided into groups, periods and blocks.

questions.q: A 'group' on the periodic table refers to a:
questions.e: A group is a vertical arrangement of elements on the periodic table.

questions.q: Elements within the same group share the same:
o: Number of neutrons, which varies between isotopes
Principal quantum number, describing the outer shell
Atomic mass, which differs across every element
Valence electrons or similar atomic configurations
questions.e: Elements in a group have the same valence electrons or similar atomic configurations.

questions.q: How many main groups are there on the periodic table?
questions.e: There are 8 main groups on the periodic table.

questions.q: For most elements, the number of valence electrons is the same as:
questions.e: In most elements, the number of valence electrons is the same as the group number.

questions.q: Which group is noted as an exception that does NOT form a true chemical 'family'?
questions.e: Exceptions: Group 4 is not a family — it includes carbon and silicon, which do not share similar chemical behaviour despite being in the same group.

questions.q: A 'period' on the periodic table refers to a:
questions.e: This is the horizontal arrangement of elements on the periodic table.

questions.q: What does the period number refer to?
o: The main energy level that the valence electron occupies
The number of isotopes known for that particular element
The number of protons only, ignoring electron shells
The group number multiplied by two consistently
questions.e: The period number refers to the main energy level that the valence electron occupies.

questions.q: How many periods are there on the periodic table, and how many elements does the longest period contain?
questions.e: There are 7 periods on the periodic table. The shortest period has 2 elements, and the longest has 32 elements.

questions.q: Elements whose valence electrons fill the 4f-orbitals are placed in a separate row called the:
o: Actinides, filling the 5f-orbitals near the bottom row
Transition metals, filling the d-orbitals in the middle
Lanthanides, filling the 4f-orbitals in a separate row
Halogens, the reactive nonmetals in group seventeen
questions.e: Elements with valence electrons filling the 4f-orbitals are placed in a separate row at the bottom of the periodic table, forming the Lanthanides (Lanthanum to Lutetium).

questions.q: The periodic table can be classified into how many main 'blocks'?
questions.e: The periodic table can be classified into four main blocks: s, p, d, and f.

questions.q: Which block do the transition elements belong to, and what orbitals do their valence electrons fill?
questions.e: The d-block elements (transition elements) have valence electrons filling d-orbitals, e.g. Sc–Zn in the 4th period form the 1st transition series.

questions.q: Effective nuclear charge is defined as:
o: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
The decreased attraction of protons for valence electrons by core electrons
The energy released when an electron is added to an atom
The net attraction of a proton in the nucleus for the valence electrons
questions.e: Effective nuclear charge is the net attraction of a proton in the nucleus for the valence electrons. It increases across the period.

questions.q: The screening (shielding) effect, caused by core electrons decreasing the attraction of protons for valence electrons, generally:
questions.e: Screening effect increases down the group, as more core electron shells lie between the nucleus and the valence electrons.

questions.q: Atomic radius is defined as:
o: The full distance between two bonded nuclei
The radius of the nucleus itself, excluding electron shells
The distance from the nucleus to the first energy level only
Half the distance between two bonded nuclei in a molecule
