questions.e: Atomic radius (r) is half the distance (d) between two bonded nuclei in a molecule: r = ½ × d.

questions.q: How does atomic radius change across a period, and why?
o: It stays constant regardless of the number of protons present
It decreases, because greater attraction for valence electrons pulls them closer
It increases only for metals, not for non-metals at all
It increases, because nuclear attraction weakens across the period
questions.e: The size of the atom decreases across a period because the greater the attraction for valence electrons, the smaller the size of the atom.

questions.q: From halogens to rare (noble) gases, atomic size:
o: Drops to zero once all electron shells are filled
Continues to decrease steadily across every group
Increases, due to repulsion among electrons in the outer shell
Remains exactly the same across the whole period
questions.e: From halogen to rare gases, there is an increase in atomic size due to repulsion among the electrons in the outer shell.

questions.q: Cationic radius (e.g. Li → Li⁺) is smaller than the parent atom because:
o: Cations have more electrons than protons, decreasing nuclear charge
Cations lose protons, which directly reduces the nuclear charge
Cations gain an extra electron shell, increasing overall size
Cations have fewer electrons than protons, increasing effective nuclear charge
questions.e: Cations have fewer electrons than protons, increasing their effective nuclear charge, so cationic radius is smaller than the parent atom; it decreases across a period but increases down a group.

questions.q: Anionic radius (e.g. F → F⁻) is larger than the parent atom because:
o: Anions have fewer electrons than protons, reducing repulsion
Anions have no valence electrons left in the outer shell
Anions have a smaller nucleus with fewer protons overall
Anions have more electrons than protons, increasing the screening effect
questions.e: Anions have more electrons than protons, which increases the screening effect, making anionic radius larger than the parent atom; it increases across the period and decreases down the group.

questions.q: Ionization energy (Eᵢ) is defined as the energy required to:
o: Break a covalent bond shared between two bonded atoms
Add an electron to a gaseous atom to form an anion
Form an ionic bond between a metal and a nonmetal
Remove an electron from a gaseous atom to form one mole of gaseous cation
questions.e: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom to form one mole of gaseous cation (the most loosely bound electron).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a determinant of ionization energy?
questions.e: The determinants of ionization energy include atomic radius, penetrative effect, shielding/screening effect, and stability of electronic configuration — not boiling point.

questions.q: Why does beryllium (1s² 2s²) have a higher ionization energy than boron (1s² 2s² 2p¹)?
o: Boron has more protons in its nucleus than beryllium does overall
Boron's 2p electron is at a higher, less stable energy level than beryllium's filled 2s
Beryllium is radioactive, unlike the completely stable boron atom
Boron has a larger nucleus with many more neutrons than beryllium
questions.e: 2p electrons are at a higher energy level than 2s electrons (less stable), and 2s electrons also have greater penetrative power, so Be's fully-filled 2s makes it harder to ionize than B.

questions.q: Why does nitrogen have a higher ionization energy than oxygen?
o: Oxygen's electrons are all paired up within their orbitals, which reduces its overall stability significantly
Oxygen has fewer protons in its nucleus than nitrogen does, weakening its nuclear attraction quite considerably
Nitrogen's 2p orbitals are half-filled, giving high stability, while oxygen's paired 2p electrons repel each other, lowering its Eᵢ
Nitrogen is technically a noble gas already, with a completely filled and highly stable outer electron shell
questions.e: Nitrogen's half-filled 2p³ orbitals spread single electrons out, reducing repulsion and giving high stability; oxygen's 2p⁴ has one pair of electrons that repel each other, causing lower ionization energy.

questions.q: Electron affinity (Eₐ) is defined as:
o: The attraction of an atom for bonded electrons in a molecule
The amount of energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom
The energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom
The energy needed to break an ionic bond completely apart
questions.e: Electron affinity is the amount of energy change or energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.

questions.q: Why does oxygen's second electron affinity (O⁻ + e⁻ → O²⁻, Eₐ = +798 kJ/mol) have a positive value, unlike the first (Eₐ = −141 kJ/mol)?
o: The second electron supposedly carries no charge at all, unlike every other normal electron ever added
Energy is always released whenever any single electron is added to any atom whatsoever, without exception
Oxygen supposedly becomes fully radioactive once it gains this second additional extra electron
The second electron is added against the repulsive force of the already negatively-charged ion, requiring energy input
questions.e: The second electron is added against a repulsive force of the negatively charged O⁻ ion, so energy input is required, giving a positive electron affinity value.

questions.q: Electronegativity is defined as an atom's ability to:
o: Form isotopes by changing its number of neutrons
Lose electrons easily to form a stable cation
Gain protons directly from a neighbouring atom
Attract bonded or shared electrons to itself within a molecule
questions.e: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonded or shared electrons to itself; the smaller the atom, the higher its electronegativity.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is a chemical bond?
o: The force of attraction between two atoms, formed to achieve a more stable outer electronic configuration
A physical mixture of two elements with no chemical interaction between them at all
The distance measured between the nuclei of two neighbouring atoms in a lattice arrangement
A type of chemical reaction that releases stored heat energy into the surrounding environment
questions.e: A chemical bond is defined as the force of attraction between two atoms; bonds form to achieve a more stable outer electronic configuration — the doublet or octet rule.

questions.q: Which three types of bonds were listed under 'Types of bonds' in the lecture?
o: Ionic, covalent, hydrogen bonds found in biomolecules
Sigma, pi, van der Waals interactions
questions.e: The slide lists three types of bonds: ionic or electrovalent bond, covalent bond, and coordinate bond or dative covalent bond.

questions.q: An ionic (electrovalent) bond forms due to what process?
o: Overlap of p orbitals along the internuclear axis
Donation of a lone pair by only one atom involved
Sharing of electrons equally between two atoms
Complete transfer of electrons between atoms that form the compound
questions.e: An ionic bond is a bond formation due to the complete transfer of electrons between atoms that form the compound, e.g. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻, giving Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl.

questions.q: What actually constitutes the ionic bond once Na⁺ and Cl⁻ have formed?
o: The covalent overlap of their respective atomic orbitals
Van der Waals forces acting between the two ions
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions
Hydrogen bonding occurring between the two ions
questions.e: The lecture states that the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions constitutes the ionic bond.

questions.q: Which set of conditions favours ionic bond formation, per the lecture's listed factors?
o: Low ionization energy only, with no other contributing factors
High electronegativity difference only, regardless of ionization energy
Low ionization energy, high electron affinity, high lattice energy, high EN difference
High ionization energy, low electron affinity, low lattice energy, low EN difference
questions.e: The factors affecting ionic bond formation are: low ionization energy (low positive value), high electron affinity (high negative value), high lattice energy (high negative value), and high electronegativity difference (high positive value).

questions.q: According to the lecture's note, what electronegativity (EN) difference value is generally required for a bond to be considered ionic?
questions.e: The lecture's note states: for the electronegativity (EN) difference, the value should be >= 1.7 for the bond to be considered ionic.

questions.q: Using the EN values given (Na 1.0, O 3.5), the Na–O electronegativity difference is 2.5. What type of bond does this represent?
o: Non-polar covalent bond between two identical atoms
Polar covalent bond formed between two different nonmetal atoms
The most ionic compound example given here
A coordinate bond formed by donation of electrons
questions.e: The table gives Na, O with an EN difference of 2.5, labelled as forming the 'most ionic compound' among the examples shown.

questions.q: The Al–Cl pair, with an electronegativity difference of 1.3, was classified in the lecture's table as what kind of bond?
questions.e: Al (1.5) and Cl (2.8) give an EN difference of 1.3, which the table classifies as polar covalent — below the 1.7 ionic threshold but with unequal electron sharing.

questions.q: A covalent bond forms due to which process, and what example was given?
o: Sharing of electrons between atoms; example H· + H· → H:H
Donation of a lone pair; example NH₄⁺
Loss of electrons from a metal; example Na⁺
Complete transfer of electrons; example NaCl
questions.e: A covalent bond is the bond formation due to the sharing of electrons between atoms that form the compound, illustrated with H· + H· → H:H → H₂ = H–H, and O: + :O → O:O → O₂ = O=O.

questions.q: What are the two types of covalent bonds named in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states there are two types of covalent bonds: sigma bond (σ) and pi bond (π).

questions.q: A sigma (σ) bond is formed by what kind of orbital overlap, and which of the following is true of sigma bonds per the comparison table?
o: Side-to-side overlap of parallel unhybridized p orbitals; sigma bonds are relatively weak in comparison
End-to-end overlap of hybridized orbitals; sigma bonds have no impact at all on overall molecular shape
End-to-end overlap along the internuclear line; sigma bonds are strong with high bond energies and can exist independently
Side-to-side overlap of parallel p orbitals; sigma bonds must always exist alongside an accompanying pi bond
questions.e: A sigma bond occurs via end-to-end (head-on) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear line. Per the comparison table, sigma bonds are strong with high bond energies, can exist independently, and impact molecular shape (unlike pi bonds).

questions.q: In the coordinate (dative) covalent bond of the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺), where does the shared electron pair come from, and what is a biological example of a dative bond mentioned in the lecture?
o: One atom donates both electrons of the shared pair; example is Fe²⁺ forming a dative bond with the nitrogen of the pyrrole rings in haemoglobin's haem group
Both atoms contribute exactly one electron each to the shared pair; a common example is the ordinary C–H bond found in methane itself
Neither atom contributes any electrons to the shared pair at all; an example is the ionic bond found in ordinary table salt, NaCl itself
Electrons are transferred completely from one atom to another; a biological example is glucose metabolism within living cells generally
questions.e: In a coordinate/dative covalent bond, the shared electron pair is donated by one of the bonded atoms (e.g. the lone pair on N in NH₃ donated to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺). The lecture notes that in haemoglobin, Fe²⁺ forms a dative covalent bond with the nitrogen of the pyrrole rings of the haem group.

questions.q: How does the lecture define hybridization?
o: The complete and permanent transfer of electrons between two atoms of noticeably different elements
The loss of a single electron from a neutral atom, forming a positively charged cation overall entirely
The sharing of just one lone pair of electrons between two separately bonded atoms within a molecule
The mutual mixing of atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies to form orbitals of equal energy, shape and direction
questions.e: Hybridization is the mutual mixing of atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies to form orbitals of equal energy, shape and direction.

questions.q: In methane (CH₄), why is carbon tetravalent rather than divalent as its ground-state configuration (2s²2p²) might suggest?
o: Because carbon supposedly forms only ionic bonds with hydrogen atoms in absolutely every compound it somehow forms
Because one of the valence electrons in the 2s orbital is promoted to a 2p orbital in the excited state, giving four unpaired electrons
Because carbon loses two electrons entirely to form a stable dication with a full outer shell during the reaction
Because two hydrogen atoms are somehow removed from methane during the bonding process itself somehow entirely
questions.e: Carbon's ground state (2s²2p²) has only 2 unpaired electrons, suggesting divalency. But one 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2p orbital, giving the excited state 2s¹2p³ with 4 unpaired electrons, making carbon tetravalent.

questions.q: In sp³ hybridization (e.g. methane), how many orbitals are involved, and what is the resulting shape and bond angle?
questions.e: sp³ hybridization involves four orbitals. The resulting shape is tetrahedral, with a bond angle of 109°, as shown for methane.

questions.q: In sp² hybridization (e.g. ethene, C₂H₄), how many orbitals are hybridized, and what happens to the unhybridized orbital?
o: 2 orbitals are hybridized and 2 remain unhybridized; both are directly involved in forming sigma bonds
3 orbitals are hybridized and 1 orbital is left unhybridized; the unhybridized orbital is involved in a pi bond
4 orbitals are hybridized in total; there is no unhybridized orbital left over at all in this case
All orbitals present are hybridized equally, with absolutely none left over unhybridized whatsoever
questions.e: In sp² hybridization, 3 orbitals are involved in the hybridization, leaving 1 unhybridized orbital — this unhybridized orbital is involved in a pi bond.

questions.q: What shape and bond angle does sp² hybridization give, as shown for ethene?
questions.e: The shape of sp² is trigonal, and its bond angle is 120°, as illustrated for ethene (C₂H₄).

questions.q: In sp hybridization (e.g. ethyne, C₂H₂), how many orbitals are hybridized and unhybridized, and what shape/angle results?
o: 2 hybridized, 2 unhybridized; linear shape, 180° bond angle
questions.e: sp hybridization involves 2 hybridized orbitals and 2 unhybridized orbitals (the latter form pi bonds). The resulting shape is linear with a bond angle of 180°, as shown for ethyne.

questions.q: Which set of example molecules did the lecture pair with sp³ hybridization?
questions.e: The lecture lists sp³ hybridization examples as C₂H₆ (ethane), NH₃, and H₂O — while sp is BeF₂/BeH₂/BeCl₂/C₂H₂, sp² is BCl₃/BH₃/C₂H₄, sp³d is PCl₅, and sp³d² is SF₆.

questions.q: Per the octet-rule slide, what hybridization is associated with a double bond, and what with a triple bond?
o: Double bond → sp hybridization; triple bond → sp² hybridization
Double bond → sp² hybridization; triple bond → sp hybridization
Double bond → sp³ hybridization; triple bond → sp²d hybridization
Both double and triple bonds require sp³d² hybridization
questions.e: The lecture states: for a double bond, one bond is a sigma bond and the other is a pi bond, corresponding to sp² hybridization; for a triple bond, one is a sigma bond and two are pi bonds, corresponding to sp hybridization.

questions.q: PCl₅ and BF₃ are given as examples of which exceptions to the octet rule?
o: Both are examples of the standard octet rule being obeyed
PCl₅ is an expanded octet; BF₃ is a deficient octet — neither obeys the octet rule
Neither is an exception; both strictly obey the octet rule
PCl₅ is a deficient octet; BF₃ is an expanded octet instead
questions.e: PCl₅ has a central atom whose valence shell contains more than 8 electrons — an expanded octet. BF₃ is a deficient octet example. The lecture emphasizes that neither expanded nor deficient octet configurations obey the octet rule.

questions.q: Regarding lone pairs versus bonded pairs of electrons, what does VSEPR theory state, and what is the order of decreasing repulsion?
o: Bonded pairs repel more strongly than lone pairs do; the order given is bonded:bonded > lone:bonded > lone:lone without any exceptions ever, under any circumstances
VSEPR states electron pairs arrange to minimise repulsion for molecular stability; order of decreasing repulsion: lone pair:lone pair > lone pair:bonded pair > bonded pair:bonded pair
VSEPR theory only applies to purely ionic compounds; there is supposedly no clearly defined order of repulsion or explanation of any kind whatsoever, under any circumstances
All electron pair repulsions are considered exactly equal in magnitude, regardless of whether the pairs are bonded or lone pairs under every possible circumstance
questions.e: VSEPR (valence shell electron pair repulsion) theory states that the arrangement of electron pairs should minimise repulsion to ensure molecular stability. The order of decreasing repulsion given is: lone pair:lone pair > lone pair:bonded pair > bonded pair:bonded pair.

questions.q: Comparing bond angles: CH₄ is 109°, NH₃ is 107°, and H₂O is 104.5°. Why does the angle decrease from CH₄ to H₂O?
o: Because oxygen and nitrogen atoms are somewhat smaller in overall size than carbon atoms are overall
Because NH₃ and H₂O simply have fewer valence electron pairs overall than CH₄ happens to have overall
Because each additional lone pair increases repulsion on the bonded pairs, progressively compressing the tetrahedral angle
Because H₂O and NH₃ supposedly use sp² hybridization while CH₄ instead uses sp³ hybridization throughout
questions.e: CH₄ has no lone pairs (109°, ideal tetrahedral). NH₃ has one lone pair, whose greater repulsion decreases the angle to 107°. H₂O has two lone pairs, decreasing the angle further to 104.5°. All three are sp³-hybridized but 'distorted' tetrahedra.

questions.q: Why is the shape of a molecule described as significant in the lecture, with reference to enzymes?
o: Enzymes react with absolutely any molecule regardless of its shape, since molecular shape has no bearing whatsoever on enzyme specificity, binding affinity, or catalytic activity at all, indeed

Molecular shape affects a molecule's behaviour — including odour, taste, reactivity and drug action — and underlies the 'lock and key' hypothesis where an enzyme has a shape complementary only to its specific substrate
Shape has no biological relevance whatsoever, only aesthetic or artistic interest to those who study molecular models purely for fun and personal curiosity about their structure in particular indeed
Shape only matters for ionic compounds, not for covalent ones, since covalent molecules are believed to react identically regardless of their three-dimensional shape at all, regardless of any context
questions.e: The shape of a molecule is a significant property because it affects the molecule's behaviour (odour, reactivity, taste, and drug action). The enzyme-substrate interaction is explained by the 'lock and key' hypothesis: the enzyme is a lock with a specific shape, so it has only a complementary substrate (key) — giving catalysis its specificity.

questions.q: Why are molecules such as H₂, Cl₂, and O₂ described as nonpolar?
o: Because they are simply gases at ordinary room temperature and standard atmospheric pressure conditions overall
Because they supposedly have no covalent bonds at all connecting any of their constituent atoms together at all
Because they are made of similar atoms, so there is no tendency for either atom to attract the shared electrons more than the other
Because they are believed to contain ionic bonds formed by complete electron transfer instead of sharing overall
questions.e: Covalent molecules made of similar atoms (H₂, Cl₂, O₂) are nonpolar because neither atom has a greater tendency to attract the shared electrons.

questions.q: What is the decreasing order of polarity given for the hydrogen halides?
questions.e: The lecture states the greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the resulting covalent bond, giving the decreasing order of polarity for hydrogen halides: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

questions.q: What two factors does the lecture identify as determining the polarity of a molecule?
o: Electronegativity difference and the shape of the molecule
Atomic mass and boiling point of the substance
Number of protons and number of neutrons
Temperature and pressure of the surroundings
questions.e: The two factors that determine the polarity of a molecule, per the lecture, are electronegativity difference and the shape of the molecule.

questions.q: Why is CO₂ (O=C=O) a nonpolar molecule overall, despite each C=O bond being polar?
o: Because CO₂ is believed to contain only single bonds between its carbon and oxygen atoms throughout
Because carbon and oxygen supposedly have identical electronegativities within this particular molecule
Because the molecule is linear, so the two equal and opposite bond-dipole vectors cancel out, giving no net polarity
Because CO₂ apparently has no lone pairs at all present on its central carbon atom in this structure
questions.e: In CO₂, each C=O bond is polar, but because the molecule's linear shape places the two dipoles directly opposite each other, they cancel out — since both sides are polar 'in opposite directions', it cancels, hence no overall polarity.

questions.q: According to the lecture, ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds are examples of what kind of force, in contrast to van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding?
o: Both are considered to be exactly the same type of intermolecular or intramolecular force in every case indeed
Ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds are intramolecular forces, while van der Waals and hydrogen bonding are intermolecular forces
Intermolecular forces are always considered far stronger than intramolecular forces in every situation indeed
There is supposedly no distinction made at all between these two entirely different types of forces whatsoever
questions.e: The lecture states that ionic, covalent, and coordinate bonds are intramolecular forces, while van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding are the two types of intermolecular forces, which can account for differences in physical state (e.g. CH₄/H₂S are gases, H₂O/CHCl₃ are liquids, benzoic acid is a solid).

questions.q: What causes van der Waals forces of attraction, and in which type of molecules are they most predominant?
o: A temporary, instantaneously induced dipole from distortion of the electron cloud, inducing a dipole in a neighbouring atom/molecule; very predominant in non-polar molecules
Nuclear attraction directly between protons in the nucleus of neighbouring atoms; predominant mainly in metallic bonding systems found throughout metals
Complete electron transfer between two atoms of very different elements entirely; predominant mainly in ionic compounds such as common table salts indeed
Permanent charge separation spread across the whole molecule structure; predominant only in strongly polar molecules with large dipole moments overall
questions.e: Van der Waals forces arise when the electron cloud of a non-polar molecule becomes distorted, creating a temporary (instantaneous) dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. They are very predominant in non-polar molecules.

questions.q: Why do F₂ and Cl₂ exist as gases, Br₂ as a liquid, and I₂ as a solid at room temperature, according to the lecture's note on van der Waals forces?
o: Because larger molecular size means more electrons, giving a greater tendency for electron cloud distortion and thus stronger van der Waals forces down the group
Because I₂ supposedly forms ionic bonds with metals while F₂ and Cl₂ form only ordinary covalent bonds instead entirely under all conditions
Because they simply have very different electronegativities from one another across the whole halogen group under all conditions studied
Because Br₂ and I₂ supposedly undergo hydrogen bonding while F₂ and Cl₂ do not undergo it at all in any way under any circumstances studied
questions.e: The larger the molecular size, the more electrons in the molecule, and the greater the tendency for distortion of the electron cloud to generate a temporary dipole. This increased molecular size accounts for the increased van der Waals forces down the halogen group: F₂, Cl₂ (gases) < Br₂ (liquid) < I₂ (solid).

questions.q: What is hydrogen bonding, as defined in the lecture, and between which atoms does it occur?
o: A true covalent bond to a hydrogen atom, occurring between any two nonmetals
A unique permanent dipole-dipole attraction occurring between hydrogen and N, O, or F
A weak van der Waals force present in absolutely all molecules
A type of ionic bond that only occurs within ordinary liquid water
questions.e: Hydrogen bonding is described as a unique permanent dipole-dipole attraction, occurring between hydrogen and (N, O, F). The lecture explicitly notes it is 'not a covalent bond to a hydrogen atom'.

questions.q: Why is HF a liquid while HCl, HBr, and HI are gases at room temperature?
o: HF has the highest overall molecular mass among all four of the hydrogen halides listed here indeed
HF has the strongest overall ionic bond of the group of four hydrogen halides listed here overall indeed
HF has the weakest overall van der Waals forces of the four hydrogen halides listed here overall indeed
Hydrogen bonding is strongly possible in HF; the resulting strong hydrogen bonding gives HF an associated, liquid nature
questions.e: Hydrogen bonding is possible in HF, slightly possible in HCl, and non-existent in HBr and HI. The strong hydrogen bonding in HF results in the associated nature of its molecules, accounting for its liquid state, unlike the other hydrogen halides.

questions.q: Using the maxim 'like dissolves like', why does NaCl dissolve in water but not in ether?
o: Because the attraction between the Na⁺/Cl⁻ particles and the polar water is greater than the attraction between the ions themselves, while nonpolar ether cannot attract the ions this way
Because ether reacts chemically with NaCl, supposedly destroying its ionic lattice structure completely and irreversibly on every single occasion without exception
Because NaCl is actually considered by some to be a covalent compound that only dissolves in nonpolar solvents like ether, never in polar ones under any conditions
Because ether is simply and consistently much denser than water at the exact same room temperature and pressure conditions overall without any exception whatsoever
questions.e: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents but not nonpolar ones ('like dissolves like'). NaCl dissolves in water because the attraction between the Na⁺/Cl⁻ particles and water is greater than the attraction between the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions themselves; in nonpolar ether, the ions cannot be attracted in the same way, so NaCl does not dissolve.

questions.q: Which biological structures does the lecture credit to hydrogen bonding among its 'other effects'?
o: Only ionic bonds are responsible for maintaining DNA's helical structure and a protein's secondary structure, and the great strength of these supposed ionic bonds prevents the two DNA strands from ever unwinding, even during replication of the genetic material in every single case

Hydrogen bonding has no role whatsoever in any biomolecules at all, and proteins as well as DNA are believed to rely entirely on covalent bonds alone for their three-dimensional secondary and helical structures, without any exception whatsoever under any circumstances

A protein's secondary structure and the helical structure of DNA are maintained by hydrogen bonding, and the weak nature of these bonds allows the two DNA strands to unwind during DNA replication; cellulose's greater degree of hydrogen bonding also makes it more rigid than starch or glycogen

Only the primary structure of proteins is influenced by hydrogen bonding at all, while DNA's helical shape and any higher-order protein structure supposedly depend entirely on covalent and ionic bonding alone, never on hydrogen bonds of any kind whatsoever at all whatsoever
questions.e: The lecture states hydrogen bonding maintains a protein's secondary structure and DNA's helical structure; because these bonds are weak, the two DNA strands can unwind — essential for DNA replication. It also notes cellulose's higher degree of hydrogen bonding among its glucose chains makes it more rigid than starch or glycogen, which have a lower degree of hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: How does the lecture define isomerism?
o: A phenomenon where the exact same structure represents entirely different molecular formulas
The ordinary process of forming a coordinate bond between two entirely separate atoms
A phenomenon where different structures can be used to represent compounds of the same molecular formula
A phenomenon that is unique only to ionic compounds formed between metals and nonmetals
questions.e: Isomerism is a phenomenon where different structures can be used to represent compounds of the same molecular formula; such structures are called isomers.

questions.q: What are the two main branches of isomerism shown in the lecture's diagram?
questions.e: The isomerism diagram branches into structural isomerism (chain, positional, functional, tautomerism) and stereoisomerism (conformational, configurational — which further splits into geometric and optical).

questions.q: How do structural isomers differ from one another, and which four subtypes were listed?
o: They differ only in overall molecular mass; the subtypes are cis, trans, meso, and racemic forms
They differ only in 3D spatial arrangement; subtypes are conformational, geometric, optical, and racemic
They are identical in every single respect except for their overall colour and appearance indeed
They differ in the way the constituent atoms are connected; subtypes are chain, positional, functional, and tautomerism
questions.e: Structural isomers differ in the way the constituent atoms are connected. The lecture lists four subtypes: chain isomerism, positional isomerism, functional isomerism, and tautomerism.

questions.q: Butane (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) and 2-methylpropane (CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃) — both C₄H₁₀ — are examples of which type of isomerism?
o: Positional isomerism, because the OH group moves position
Functional isomerism, because they have different functional groups
Chain isomerism, because they differ in the type of carbon chain
questions.e: Chain isomerism is when isomers differ in the chain type. Butane (a straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (a branched chain) are both C₄H₁₀ but differ in how the carbon chain is arranged.

questions.q: Propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) and propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃) are the lecture's example of which type of structural isomerism?
o: Functional isomerism, since the functional groups present clearly differ
Chain isomerism, since the carbon chain itself is branched differently
Tautomerism, since they exist together in dynamic chemical equilibrium
Positional isomerism, since they differ in the placement of the functional group on the chain
questions.e: Positional isomerism is when isomers differ in the placement of the functional group. Propan-1-ol has –OH on carbon 1, while propan-2-ol has –OH on carbon 2 — both are C₃H₇OH.

questions.q: Dimethyl ether (CH₃–O–CH₃) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), both C₂H₆O, illustrate which type of structural isomerism?
o: Chain isomerism, since the carbon skeleton itself is arranged differently
Functional isomerism, since they differ in the functional group present
Geometric isomerism, since the groups are arranged differently in space
Positional isomerism, since the substituent sits at a different position
questions.e: Functional isomerism is when isomers differ in the functional group itself. Dimethyl ether contains an ether linkage (C–O–C) while ethanol contains a hydroxyl group (–OH); both share the formula C₂H₆O.

questions.q: What defines tautomerism, and what example (C₃H₆O) did the lecture use?
o: A form of geometric isomerism that is seen only in rigid ring compounds with restricted internal rotation
Functional groups in dynamic equilibrium, with isomers being mutually interconvertible; example is the keto form and enol form
Functional groups that are permanently fixed and never interconvert; example is butane/2-methylpropane
The mirror-image relationship that exists between two entirely separate optically active compounds indeed
questions.e: Tautomerism occurs when functional groups are in dynamic equilibrium, with the isomers (tautomers) mutually interconvertible. The example given is 2-propanone (keto form) and propen-2-ol (enol form), both C₃H₆O.

questions.q: In the keto–enol tautomer example given, which form is more stable, and by roughly what proportion?
o: The enol form is entirely absent under all normal conditions
The enol form is more stable overall, at roughly 99.9 percent
Both forms are equally stable, present at fifty percent each
The keto form is more stable, at about 99.9%, versus about 0.001% for the enol form
questions.e: The slide shows the keto form (2-propanone) as more stable at 99.9%, while the enol form (propen-2-ol) is less stable at only about 0.001%.

questions.q: What distinguishes positional isomers from functional isomers?
o: Positional isomers are always optically active in every case, while functional isomers never show any optical activity at all without exception
Positional isomers have identical functional groups but at different positions on the chain, while functional isomers have entirely different functional groups
There is supposedly no real difference at all between the two; the terms are considered completely interchangeable by some without exception
Positional isomers always involve a ring system structurally in every case, while functional isomers never involve one at all without exception
questions.e: Positional isomerism keeps the same functional group but changes its position on the carbon skeleton (e.g. propan-1-ol vs propan-2-ol), whereas functional isomerism changes the functional group entirely while keeping the same molecular formula (e.g. dimethyl ether vs ethanol).

questions.q: Why are butane and 2-methylpropane both considered structural isomers rather than the same compound?
o: Because one of them is simply a gas at room temperature and the other is a liquid
Because one of them contains an oxygen atom and the other does not contain any at all
Because although they share the molecular formula C₄H₁₀, their constituent atoms are connected differently
Because they have completely and entirely different molecular formulas from one another
questions.e: Isomers share the same molecular formula (C₄H₁₀ for both butane and 2-methylpropane) but differ in how their atoms are connected — in this case, a straight chain versus a branched chain, which is chain isomerism.

questions.q: Which statement best captures why structural isomerism is grouped separately from stereoisomerism?
o: Structural isomers differ in atom connectivity, while stereoisomers share identical atom connectivity but differ in 3D spatial arrangement
Stereoisomers always have completely different molecular formulas from one another in every single case without exception
There is supposedly no meaningful distinction at all between these two entirely separate categories whatsoever indeed
Structural isomers supposedly only occur in inorganic compounds, never in organic ones at all whatsoever indeed, ever
questions.e: Structural isomerism concerns differences in how atoms are connected to one another, whereas stereoisomerism (covered separately) concerns compounds with identical connectivity but different three-dimensional spatial arrangements.

questions.q: A compound in tautomeric equilibrium is best described as which of the following?
o: Two enantiomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of one another entirely
A racemic mixture containing exactly two isomers in precisely equal proportions indeed
Two isomers that dynamically interconvert into one another, such as the keto and enol forms of a molecule
A single fixed structure that never changes at all under any conditions whatsoever
questions.e: Tautomerism specifically involves functional groups in dynamic equilibrium, where the isomeric forms (tautomers) are mutually interconvertible — as with the keto and enol forms of 2-propanone/propen-2-ol.

questions.q: How does the lecture define stereoisomerism?
o: A subtype of tautomerism involving ongoing dynamic chemical equilibrium between two forms indeed
Differences in the way atoms are connected to one another within the overall molecule altogether
Differences in the arrangement of atoms in the three-dimensional space of a compound, while connectivity stays the same
The complete and total transfer of electrons between two entirely separate stereo centres indeed
questions.e: Stereoisomerism refers to the differences in the arrangement of atoms in the three-dimensional space of a compound (connectivity is unchanged).

questions.q: What causes conformational stereoisomerism, and what are its two named conformer types (illustrated with C₂H₃Cl₃)?
o: Free rotation about a C–C single covalent bond; conformers are staggered and eclipsed
Ring rigidity within the molecule; conformers are chiral and achiral
Hindered rotation about a C=C double bond; conformers are cis and trans
Mirror-image relationships between molecules; conformers are dextro and laevo
questions.e: Conformational stereoisomerism arises from the possibility of free rotation about C–C single covalent bonds. The individual structures are called conformers, of which there are two types: staggered and eclipsed conformers, illustrated with C₂H₃Cl₃.

questions.q: What are the two subtypes of configurational stereoisomerism named in the lecture?
questions.e: Configurational stereoisomerism (arrangement about a C=C double bond or a ring system) has two subtypes: geometric isomerism and optical isomerism.

questions.q: For geometric isomerism to occur about a C=C double bond, what condition must be met?
o: The attached groups on each double-bonded carbon must be different from one another
The molecule must contain a coordinate bond somewhere within it
The two carbons of the double bond must each carry two identical groups
There must be free rotation possible about the C=C double bond
questions.e: Geometric isomerism is due to hindered rotation about a C=C double bond or a ring system, and requires that the attached groups on the double-bonded carbon(s) be different — as in cis-2-butene versus trans-2-butene.

questions.q: Why is trans-2-butene more stable than cis-2-butene, according to the lecture?
o: Cis-2-butene is not considered to be a real, physically existing compound at all in nature indeed
Trans-2-butene has a noticeably and measurably higher molecular mass than the cis form does indeed
The bulky groups in the trans isomer are wide apart, giving minimum repulsion, whereas in cis they are on the same side
Trans-2-butene has considerably more hydrogen bonds present than the cis isomer does overall indeed
questions.e: The trans isomer is more stable than the cis isomer because its bulky groups are wide apart, giving minimum repulsion — this is illustrated further with maleic acid (cis-butenedioic acid) versus the more stable fumaric acid (trans-butenedioic acid).

questions.q: Besides C=C double bonds, what other structural feature can cause geometric (cis/trans) isomerism, as shown with 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane?
o: A tautomeric equilibrium existing between two mutually interconvertible chemical forms
A ring system, which can make a molecule rigid enough to prevent free rotation and allow cis/trans isomers
A coordinate bond that is formed somewhere within the ring structure itself entirely
An ionic bond present within the ring structure, restricting any free rotation entirely
questions.e: Ring compounds can make a molecule rigid and cause geometric isomerism, as shown with cis- and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane.

questions.q: In the E/Z system of nomenclature for naming geometric isomers, what do 'E' and 'Z' mean, and how are priorities assigned?
o: E and Z both mean 'across' within this system; priority is based on atomic mass alone indeed
E means 'across' and Z means 'together'; the higher the atomic number of the attached atom, the higher its priority
E means 'together' and Z means 'across' in this system; priority assignment is essentially random
E/Z nomenclature supposedly only applies to optical isomers, never at all to geometric ones
questions.e: In the E/Z system, E represents 'across' and Z represents 'together'. Priorities are assigned by atomic number — the higher the atomic number, the higher the priority (increasing priority order given: F < Cl < Br < I).

questions.q: What makes a compound 'optically active', and what structural feature (chirality) is required for a carbon to give rise to optical isomerism?
o: An achiral carbon, with at least two similar groups attached, is what causes optical activity
An optically active compound rotates plane-polarised light; a chiral carbon must have four different groups attached
An optically active compound absorbs ppl completely; chirality requires two identical groups attached to carbon
Optical activity has absolutely nothing to do with a molecule's three-dimensional structure
questions.e: Optically active compounds interact with plane-polarised light (ppl) by rotating it, to the right (dextro-rotatory) or left (laevo-rotatory). This requires a chiral centre — a tetrahedral (sp³) carbon bonded to four different groups. An achiral molecule, by contrast, is bonded to at least two similar groups and is not optically active.

questions.q: What are enantiomers, and what example (with D/L forms) illustrates them in the lecture?
o: Compounds that cannot rotate plane-polarised light in any direction at all
Isomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other; example is L and D lactic acid
Isomers that differ only in the position of a double bond; example is cis/trans-2-butene
Isomers with completely different molecular formulas; example is butane and 2-methylpropane
questions.e: Enantiomers are mirror images of each other. The lecture's example is lactic acid (2-hydroxylpropanoic acid), which exists as L(+) and D(-) lactic acid — labelled by whether the –OH group is on the right (dextro) or left (laevo).

questions.q: How do the physical, chemical, and physiological properties of enantiomers compare, according to the lecture?
o: They have identical physical properties except for the direction they rotate plane-polarised light; identical chemical properties with optically inactive reagents; and different physiological properties — e.g. one form of nicotine is more poisonous than the other

Enantiomers always have completely identical physiological effects on the human body in every case, since the body cannot distinguish between mirror-image molecules at the level of receptor binding or metabolism under any circumstances whatsoever

They are identical in absolutely every single respect, with no differences at all in physical, chemical, or physiological properties under any circumstances whatsoever, according to this view under any circumstances whatsoever, without exception

They differ only in molecular formula, so no meaningful comparison of their physical, chemical or physiological properties ever applies in any real situation according to this claim under any circumstances whatsoever, without any exception at all
questions.e: Enantiomers share the same physical properties except that the direction of rotation of plane-polarised light differs. Their chemical properties are identical when reacting with optically inactive compounds, but differ with optically active compounds. They also have different physiological properties, e.g. (–)-nicotine is more poisonous than (+)-nicotine.

questions.q: In the 2,3-dihydroxybutanoic acid example (structures A, B, C, D), what relationship exists between A and C (or A and D)?
o: A and C are completely identical structures in every way
A and C cannot be meaningfully compared since they have different formulas
A and C are diastereoisomers, while A/B and C/D are each enantiomer pairs
A and C are enantiomers, exactly just like A and B are
questions.e: In this example, A and B are enantiomers, and C and D are enantiomers. However, A and C (as well as A and D) are diastereoisomers — stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other. The lecture also notes the number of isomers possible = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of chiral centres.

questions.q: What is a racemic mixture, and how are its two enantiomers typically separated?
o: A mixture that can supposedly only ever be separated using simple fractional distillation under normal laboratory conditions and standard atmospheric pressure alone, with nothing else required under any circumstances whatsoever

An equimolar mixture of two structural isomers that is always assumed to be fully optically active under any measurement conditions whatsoever, without any exception at all, under any circumstances whatsoever, without exception at all

A single pure enantiomer that requires no further resolution or separation of any kind under any circumstances at all, since it is already considered perfectly pure under any circumstances whatsoever, without any exception at all indeed

An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, optically inactive because the equal and opposite rotations cancel; separation can be done via a biological system, affinity chromatography, or forming diastereomers for fractional crystallisation
questions.e: A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of two optically active isomers (enantiomers), e.g. (+/-) lactic acid, which is optically inactive because the laevo rotation is cancelled by an equal but opposite dextro rotation. Resolution (separation) examples given include using a biological system such as Penicillium glaucum media (which consumes the (+) lactic acid but not the (-) form), affinity chromatography (a ligand binds one enantiomer), and combining the racemic mixture with an optically active compound to form diastereoisomers, separable by fractional crystallisation based on solubility differences.

questions.q: How does the lecture define a functional group?
o: A synonym for a hybridized orbital that is formed by mixing together different atomic orbitals
A type of intermolecular force that acts between two entirely separate molecules nearby
A group of atoms that supposedly has no effect at all on a compound's physical properties
Atoms or groups of atoms that, when present in organic compounds, determine the physical and chemical properties
questions.e: Functional groups are defined as atoms or groups of atoms that, when present in organic compounds, determine the physical and chemical properties of that compound.

questions.q: Ethane (CH₃CH₃) is described as an unreactive gas. What happens to its properties when H is removed and a –COOH group is added (giving propionic acid), or an –OH group is added (giving ethanol)?
o: The resulting compounds become soluble in water and more reactive than ethane
The resulting compounds become less soluble and less reactive than ethane
The resulting compounds become completely insoluble gases at room temperature
No change in properties occurs at all under these conditions
questions.e: The lecture illustrates that removing an H from ethane and adding –COOH gives propionic acid, while adding –OH gives ethanol; both resulting compounds are soluble in water and more reactive than the unreactive parent gas, ethane — demonstrating how a functional group determines properties.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between an alkane and an alkene?
o: There is supposedly no structural difference at all between these two compounds
An alkane contains a triple bond; an alkene contains only a double bond
An alkane contains only C–C and C–H single bonds; an alkene contains a carbon-carbon double bond
An alkane always contains an oxygen atom; an alkene never contains any at all
questions.e: An alkane (R₁–C(H)(H)–C(H)(H)–R₂) is a saturated hydrocarbon with only single C–C and C–H bonds, while an alkene contains a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C), as shown in the functional groups diagram.

questions.q: What distinguishes an alkyne from both an alkane and an alkene?
o: Alkynes supposedly contain a benzene ring fused somewhere within their overall structure indeed
An alkyne contains only single bonds throughout its structure, just like an alkane does indeed
An alkyne contains a carbon-carbon triple bond, unlike the single bond of an alkane or the double bond of an alkene
An alkyne is simply just another name used for an aromatic arene compound entirely altogether
questions.e: An alkyne is characterised by a carbon-carbon triple bond (R–C≡C–R), distinguishing it from the single C–C bond of an alkane and the double C=C bond of an alkene.

questions.q: What defines an arene, and what does 'R–X' represent in the haloalkane functional group?
o: An arene is exactly the same as an alkane; R–X denotes an amine group
Neither arenes nor haloalkanes were ever mentioned anywhere in the lecture
An arene is built on a benzene ring; R–X denotes a halogen atom attached to a carbon chain
An arene contains only single bonds; R–X denotes a hydroxyl group instead
questions.e: An arene is an aromatic compound built around a benzene ring (R attached to the ring). A haloalkane is represented as R–X, where X is a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br, or I) replacing a hydrogen on the hydrocarbon chain.

questions.q: What structural feature distinguishes an aldehyde (R–CHO) from a ketone (R₁COR₂)?
o: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen, while a ketone's carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon-containing groups
There is supposedly no structural difference at all between aldehydes and ketones in any respect whatsoever entirely
Ketones supposedly only occur within ring-shaped compounds, never within open-chain structures at all whatsoever indeed
Aldehydes never contain a C=O carbonyl group at all in their structure, but ketones always do entirely altogether indeed
questions.e: Both aldehydes and ketones contain a carbonyl group (C=O). In an aldehyde, this carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen and sits at the end of the chain (R–CHO); in a ketone, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon-containing groups (R₁–CO–R₂), placing it within the chain.

questions.q: What is the structural difference between an alcohol (R–OH) and an ether (R₁–O–R₂)?
o: An alcohol has a hydroxyl group bonded to a carbon chain, while an ether has an oxygen atom bonded between two carbon-containing groups with no O–H bond
Alcohols and ethers are considered by some to be structurally identical to one another entirely, with no distinction at all indeed
Alcohols contain a nitrogen atom somewhere within their structure; ethers supposedly never contain one at all altogether indeed
An ether molecule always contains more carbon atoms overall than an alcohol molecule does in every case without exception at all
questions.e: An alcohol carries a hydroxyl group (–OH) attached to a carbon chain (e.g. ethanol), while an ether has an oxygen atom bonded between two carbon-containing groups (e.g. dimethyl ether, CH₃–O–CH₃), with no O–H bond present.

questions.q: A carboxylic acid (R–COOH) and an amide (R–CONH₂) both derive from the carbonyl group. What differentiates them?
o: A carboxylic acid has –OH attached to the carbonyl carbon, while an amide has –NH₂ attached to the carbonyl carbon
A carboxylic acid supposedly has no carbonyl group present at all anywhere in its structure
An amide contains a halogen atom instead of an oxygen atom entirely within its structure indeed
They are actually considered the same functional group, just given two different names indeed
questions.e: Both are carbonyl (C=O) derivatives, but a carboxylic acid has a hydroxyl group (–OH) on the carbonyl carbon, while an amide has an amine group (–NH₂) on the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: An ester (R₁COOR₂) and an acyl halide (R–COX) are both carbonyl-containing functional groups. What replaces the –OH of a carboxylic acid in each case?
o: Esters and acyl halides do not contain any carbonyl group at all
In an ester, –OH is replaced by –OR₂; in an acyl halide, –OH is replaced by a halogen, X
Both functional groups replace the –OH with an amine group instead
Nothing at all is replaced in either of these two functional groups
questions.e: An ester replaces the carboxylic acid's –OH with an –OR₂ group (from an alcohol), giving R₁–CO–O–R₂. An acyl halide replaces the –OH with a halogen (X), giving R–CO–X.

questions.q: What is an acid anhydride, structurally, in the functional groups chart?
o: A halogen bonded to an alkane chain
An amine bonded directly to a benzene ring
A single carbonyl group bonded to a hydroxyl
Two acyl groups joined together through a shared oxygen atom
questions.e: An acid anhydride consists of two acyl groups joined by a shared oxygen atom, represented as R₁–C(=O)–O–C(=O)–R₂ in the functional groups chart.

questions.q: An amine (R–NH₂) is characterised by which atom being bonded to the carbon chain?
questions.e: An amine functional group is characterised by a nitrogen atom (as –NH₂) bonded to a carbon chain, distinguishing it from oxygen-based groups such as alcohols and ethers.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula pattern that describes carbohydrates in general?
questions.e: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy carbonyl compounds and their derivatives, with the general molecular formula Cx(H2O)y, as stated in the lecture's opening definition.

questions.q: What is the general formula for a monosaccharide, and what is the typical range of n?
questions.e: Monosaccharides are composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen and are characterised by the general formula (CH2O)n, in which n is any integer from 3 to 7.

questions.q: Why is the general formula (CH2O)n for monosaccharides described as 'oversimplified'?
o: Because monosaccharides never contain oxygen atoms at all
Because n can only equal exactly 6 for all monosaccharides
Because monosaccharides are always considered disaccharides
Because several biologically important monosaccharides are chemically modified
questions.e: The lecture notes that the general formula is oversimplified because several biologically important monosaccharides are chemically modified (e.g. substituted with amino groups, or missing an oxygen as in deoxyribose).

questions.q: A monosaccharide with an aldehyde functional group is called a(n):
questions.e: Monosaccharides are named by their functional group: those with a ketone group are called ketoses, whereas those with an aldehyde group are called an aldose.

questions.q: A monosaccharide with a ketone functional group is called a(n):
questions.e: A ketone group defines a ketose, as distinguished from an aldose (aldehyde group), per the functional-group naming system given in the lecture.

questions.q: Because monosaccharides contain many hydroxyl groups, they are sometimes also called:
o: Fatty acid esters found in cell membranes
questions.e: The lecture states that because monosaccharides contain many hydroxyl groups, they are sometimes called polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones.

questions.q: What is the name given to a 3-carbon sugar, based on the carbon-count naming system?
questions.e: The carbon-count naming system names a 3-carbon sugar a triose, a 4-carbon sugar a tetrose, a 5-carbon sugar a pentose, and so on.

questions.q: D-glyceraldehyde, the simplest aldose, has how many carbons?
questions.e: D-glyceraldehyde is the aldotriose from which all other D-aldoses in the family tree (erythrose, threose, ribose, glucose, etc.) are built; a triose has 3 carbons.

questions.q: Which pair of monosaccharides are the simplest examples of an aldose and a ketose, respectively?
questions.e: The lecture's diagram contrasts the aldose glyceraldehyde with the ketose dihydroxyacetone as the two simplest trioses, one bearing a CHO group and the other a C=O group at carbon-2.

questions.q: What kind of chemical reaction produces a hemiacetal?
o: An alcohol reacting with a carboxylic acid
An alcohol reacting with an aldehyde
An amine reacting with a ketone
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows an alcohol (R-OH) reacting with an aldehyde to yield a hemiacetal — the reaction that allows monosaccharides such as glucose to cyclise.

questions.q: What kind of chemical reaction produces a hemiketal?
o: An alcohol reacting with an aldehyde
An alcohol reacting with a ketone
An acid reacting with a base
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows an alcohol reacting with a ketone to yield a hemiketal — the reaction underlying fructose's cyclisation (the C-2 keto group reacting with the C-5 hydroxyl).

questions.q: When D-glucose cyclises, which two carbons react intramolecularly to form the six-membered pyranose ring?
questions.e: In D-glucose, the C-1 aldehyde group reacts with the C-5 hydroxyl group intramolecularly (cyclisation) to form the six-membered pyranose ring, giving rise to α- and β-D-glucopyranose.

questions.q: Oxidation of D-glucose at carbon-1 produces which sugar acid?
questions.e: The lecture's diagram on sugar acids shows that oxidation of D-glucose at C-1 gives D-gluconic acid, which exists in equilibrium with D-δ-gluconolactone.

questions.q: Oxidation of D-glucose at carbon-6 produces which sugar acid?
questions.e: Oxidation at C-6 of D-glucose produces D-glucuronic acid (GlcUA), as shown in the derivative-forms slide on sugar acids.

questions.q: Oxidation of D-glucose at BOTH carbon-1 and carbon-6 produces which sugar acid?
questions.e: Oxidation at both C-1 and C-6 produces D-glucaric acid, which carries a COOH group at each end of the chain.

questions.q: Sugar alcohols such as D-glucitol (sorbitol) and D-mannitol are produced by what kind of reaction?
questions.e: The lecture lists sugar alcohols as a derivative form produced by reduction of the carbonyl groups of sugars, listing examples such as D-glucitol (sorbitol), D-mannitol, D-xylitol, D-glycerol, myo-inositol, and D-ribitol.

questions.q: 2-Deoxy-α-D-ribose is an example of which derivative class of monosaccharides?
questions.e: 2-Deoxyribose is a deoxy sugar — a hydroxyl group (at C-2) is replaced by hydrogen; this class also includes α-L-rhamnose and α-L-fucose.

questions.q: α-D-Glucose-1-phosphate and adenosine-5'-triphosphate (ATP) are examples of which class of sugar derivative?
questions.e: These are phosphate esters of sugars, one of the seven derivative forms described in the lecture; intermediate monosaccharides in carbohydrate metabolism commonly carry phosphate groups.

questions.q: β-D-glucosamine and β-D-galactosamine belong to which class of sugar derivatives, and where are they found?
o: Sugar acids; found in blood plasma
Sugar esters found in ATP molecules
Deoxy sugars found in DNA strands
Amino sugars; found in polysaccharides of cell membranes
questions.e: These are amino sugars — a hydroxyl group replaced by an amino group — and the lecture notes they are found in the polysaccharides of cell membranes.

questions.q: What distinguishes a ketal from a hemiketal?
o: A ketal forms when a hemiketal reacts with a further alcohol, releasing water
A ketal is a hemiketal with an added phosphate group
A ketal and a hemiketal are exactly the same molecule
A ketal forms by simple reduction of a hemiketal group
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows a hemiketal reacting with a second alcohol (R''-OH) to release water and form a ketal, mirroring the hemiacetal-to-acetal reaction.

questions.q: What is a glycosidic bond?
o: The bond formed when the anomeric hydroxyl of a cyclic sugar reacts with an -OH of another molecule
An ionic bond formed between a sugar molecule and a positively charged metal ion
A peptide bond formed between two separate amino sugar residues in a chain
A double bond formed between C-1 and C-2 of a single monosaccharide ring unit
questions.e: Glycosides form when the anomeric (hemiacetal/hemiketal) hydroxyl of a cyclic sugar reacts with an -OH group of another molecule, as illustrated by methyl-α-D-glucoside and methyl-β-D-glucoside.

questions.q: Which molecule is described as 'the most essential sugar in the human body' and is also known as dextrose or blood sugar?
questions.e: Glucose (C6H12O6, an aldohexose) is described as the most essential sugar in the human body, found in foods under names such as dextrose and blood sugar.

questions.q: What is the normal range for blood glucose concentration given in the lecture?
questions.e: Normal blood glucose levels are 3.9–5.5 mmol/L, with the highest concentrations appearing after a meal (postprandial), and the level is controlled by insulin and glucagon.

questions.q: Which sugar is described as 'the sweetest simple sugar' and is also known as levulose or fruit sugar?
questions.e: Fructose, also called levulose and fruit sugar, is described as the sweetest simple sugar, found in large amounts in honey, corn syrup, and sweet fruits.

questions.q: How does the lecture define an oligosaccharide?
o: A single isolated sugar unit alone
A chain of more than 10 simple sugars
A chain of exactly 100 simple sugars
A chain of 2 to 10 simple sugars
questions.e: Oligosaccharides are defined in the lecture as chains of 2–10 simple sugars, with disaccharides being the simplest oligosaccharides.

questions.q: What is the glycosidic linkage in maltose?
questions.e: Maltose is glucose-α-1,4-glucose (Glcα1→4Glc); it is a component of malt and is produced from starch by diastase during germination.

questions.q: Which enzyme, produced during germination, catalyses the hydrolysis of starch to maltose?
questions.e: The lecture states that diastase, produced during germination, catalyses the hydrolysis of starch to maltose, which is then fermented by yeast — crucial in the brewing of beer.

questions.q: What is the glycosidic linkage in lactose?
questions.e: Lactose is galactose-β-1,4-glucose (Galβ1→4Glc), the main carbohydrate in milk.

questions.q: What enzyme deficiency causes lactose intolerance?
questions.e: Lactose intolerance occurs when people lack lactase, so lactose cannot be hydrolysed; it remains undigested in the gut and causes cramping and diarrhoea, and is metabolised by bacteria to release organic acids and CO2.

questions.q: What is the glycosidic linkage in sucrose, and which enzyme hydrolyses it in the human intestine?
questions.e: Sucrose is glucose-α-1,2-fructose (Glcα1→2Fru), and it is hydrolysed by sucrase in the human intestine into glucose and fructose.

questions.q: Why is sucrose classified as a non-reducing sugar, unlike maltose or lactose?
o: It cannot be hydrolysed at all under any normal laboratory conditions whatsoever, ever
Both anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are joined in the glycosidic bond, leaving no free reducing end
It contains no oxygen atoms anywhere within its molecular structure at all, ever indeed
It has an extra phosphate group blocking reduction of its anomeric carbon entirely indeed
questions.e: The lecture's diagram highlights that sucrose has 'no reducing end' because the glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose, unlike maltose, lactose, and cellobiose which retain a free anomeric (reducing) carbon.

questions.q: What is cellobiose, in terms of its monosaccharide composition and bond?
questions.e: Cellobiose is glucose-β-1,4-glucose (Glcβ1→4Glc), the repeating disaccharide unit that makes up the polysaccharide cellulose.

questions.q: What is isomaltose, and where does this type of linkage typically occur in polysaccharides?
o: Galactose-β-1,4-glucose; found abundantly in milk sugar
Glucose-α-1,6-glucose; found at branch points of starch/glycogen
Glucose-α-1,4-glucose; found abundantly in malt sugar
questions.e: Isomaltose (Glcα1→6Glc) reflects the type of linkage found at the branch points of starch (amylopectin) and glycogen.

questions.q: Why should sucrose intake, per the lecture, be minimised in the diet even though it is a natural sugar?
o: It contains toxic heavy metals absorbed from contaminated soil entirely indeed
It cannot be digested by humans at all under any circumstances entirely indeed
It represents 'empty calories' with no vitamins or minerals, and is linked to obesity and tooth decay
It is radioactive and decays slowly over a long period of time entirely indeed
questions.e: The lecture states sucrose in the diet is undesirable because it represents empty calories, containing no vitamins or minerals, and that large intakes promote obesity and tooth decay, with links to diabetes, NAFLD and cardiovascular disease.

questions.q: What recommended limit does the lecture give for sucrose as a percentage of daily caloric intake?
questions.e: The lecture states that 45–65% of dietary calories should come from carbohydrates, and that no more than 10% of the daily caloric intake should be sucrose.

questions.q: Bleomycin A2 and Streptomycin, mentioned in the lecture as containing oligosaccharide components, are examples of what kind of compounds?
o: Drugs used to treat serious infections
questions.e: The lecture notes that oligosaccharides occur widely as components of drugs, citing Bleomycin A2 (an antitumor agent used against specific tumours) and Streptomycin (a broad-spectrum antibiotic).

questions.q: How does the lecture define a polysaccharide?
o: A chain of more than 10 simple sugars
A single isolated sugar unit alone
Any molecule containing carbon and oxygen
questions.e: Polysaccharides (glycans) are defined as chains of more than 10 simple sugars, distinguishing them from oligosaccharides (2–10 units).

questions.q: What distinguishes a homopolysaccharide from a heteropolysaccharide?
o: A homopolysaccharide contains only one kind of monosaccharide; a heteropolysaccharide contains more than one kind
A heteropolysaccharide is always found only in plant cell walls specifically and nowhere else
A homopolysaccharide always contains amino acid residues within its overall structure entirely
A homopolysaccharide is always a simple two-unit disaccharide overall and nothing more indeed
questions.e: Homopolysaccharides (homoglycans) are built from one kind of monosaccharide (e.g. glucans, mannans), while heteropolysaccharides (heteroglycans) contain more than one kind of monosaccharide.

questions.q: What proportion of starch is typically amylose versus amylopectin?
questions.e: The lecture states that starch is 10–30% amylose and 70–90% amylopectin.

questions.q: What colour does helical amylose produce when combined with iodine, and why is this test useful?
o: Green colour, indicating the presence of glycogen
Red colour, indicating the presence of cellulose
No colour change occurs at all when tested
Blue colour, characteristic and diagnostic of starch
questions.e: Iodine inserts into the middle of the amylose helix to give a blue colour that is characteristic and diagnostic of starch, because amylose adopts a helical conformation in water.

questions.q: Approximately how frequently do α(1→6) branch points occur in amylopectin?
questions.e: Amylopectin has α(1→6) branch points approximately every 12–30 residues, as shown in the branched-structure diagram of starch.

questions.q: Which enzyme acts as an endoamylase in the mouth, splitting only α(1→4) glycosidic linkages, and is inactivated by the low pH of the stomach?
questions.e: Salivary α-amylase is an endoamylase active in the mouth that splits α(1→4) glycosidic linkages only, and is inactivated in the stomach due to the low pH.

questions.q: Which enzyme specifically cleaves the α(1→6) branch points of starch (in amylopectin)?
questions.e: The lecture states that α(1→6)-glucosidase splits the α(1→6) glycosidic linkage, cleaving at the branch points of starch (in amylopectin).

questions.q: Where is glycogen mainly stored in animals, and roughly what percentage of that tissue's mass does it represent?
questions.e: Glycogen, the key form of stored polysaccharide in animals, is mainly found in the liver (about 10% of liver mass) and skeletal muscle (1–2% of muscle mass).

questions.q: How does the branching frequency of liver glycogen compare to that of starch's amylopectin?
o: Liver glycogen never branches at all, ever, under any conditions
Liver glycogen branches more frequently, roughly every 8–12 residues
Liver glycogen branches only every 100 residues
Glycogen and amylopectin have identical branching frequency
questions.e: Liver glycogen is highly branched, with α(1→6) branch points every 8–12 residues — more frequent than amylopectin's 12–30 residues.

questions.q: What type of glycosidic bond links glucose units in cellulose, and what conformation does this give the polymer?
o: β bonds, giving an extended conformation
α bonds, giving a helical conformation
β bonds, giving a globular conformation
α bonds, giving a branched conformation
questions.e: Cellulose is a homopolymer of D-glucose linked by β(1→4) glycosidic bonds, which allow the chain to adopt an extended (rather than helical) conformation stabilised by hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: Why can't humans digest cellulose, even though we can digest starch and glycogen?
o: Humans lack a stomach acid strong enough
Humans cannot synthesise the enzyme cellulase
questions.e: The lecture states that unlike glycogen, amylose, and amylopectin, humans cannot digest cellulose because we cannot synthesise cellulase; termites, cows and goats can digest it via symbiotic organisms.

questions.q: Approximately how many glucose units does typical cellulose contain, and how many does the alga Valonia's cellulose contain?
o: About 3,000,000 units typically; Valonia's has 26 units
About 10 units typically; Valonia's cellulose has about 100 units
About 3,000 units typically; Valonia's cellulose has about 26,000 units
Cellulose always contains exactly 100 glucose units
questions.e: The lecture states cellulose typically contains about 3,000 glucose units, but the alga Valonia produces cellulose containing 26,000 glucose units.

questions.q: What is a glycoprotein?
o: An enzyme that only digests starch molecules
A lipid molecule bound covalently to a sugar
A protein to which carbohydrate groups are covalently linked
A carbohydrate with no protein component
questions.e: Glycoproteins are molecules in which carbohydrate groups link to polypeptide chains, including structural proteins, enzymes, membrane receptors, transport proteins, and immunoglobulins.

questions.q: In O-linked glycoproteins, the carbohydrate attaches to which amino acid side chains?
o: The -OH of serine, threonine, or hydroxylysine
questions.e: O-linked saccharides attach to the -OH group of serine, threonine, or hydroxylysine residues, as distinguished from N-linked saccharides.

questions.q: In N-linked glycoproteins, the carbohydrate attaches to which functional group?
questions.e: N-linked saccharides attach to the amide nitrogen of asparagine, distinguishing them from O-linked saccharides attached via serine/threonine/hydroxylysine hydroxyls.

questions.q: What are proteoglycans, according to the lecture?
o: Polysaccharides with no protein component at all present anywhere
A family of glycoproteins whose carbohydrate moieties are predominantly glycosaminoglycans
Lipids conjugated chemically to fatty acid chains present in membranes
Simple disaccharides found only in cow's milk and nowhere else indeed
questions.e: Proteoglycans are defined as a family of glycoproteins whose carbohydrate moieties are predominantly glycosaminoglycans (GAGs).

questions.q: How are glycosaminoglycans typically linked to the protein core in proteoglycans?
o: Through an ester bond to a fatty acid
questions.e: The lecture states that glycosaminoglycans are O-linked to Ser-Gly, and that the resulting proteoglycans may be soluble and located in the extracellular matrix.

questions.q: What body function are proteoglycans specifically credited with in the lecture?
o: The flexibility and resilience of cartilage tissue
Carrying oxygen in red blood cells
Digesting starch in the small intestine
questions.e: Proteoglycans modulate cell growth processes and are responsible for the flexibility and resilience of cartilage tissue in the body.

questions.q: Peptidoglycan, described in the lecture as a protective bacterial cell-wall layer, is built from alternating units of N-acetylglucosamine and:
questions.e: Peptidoglycan is a peptide-polysaccharide built from alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid units, cross-linked through short peptide chains.

questions.q: How does the peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria differ structurally from that of Gram-negative bacteria?
o: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick layer cross-linked by a pentaglycine bridge; Gram-negative bacteria have a thin, single layer with direct cross-links
Peptidoglycan thickness is exactly identical in both bacterial types studied here, without exception, under any circumstances whatsoever
Only Gram-positive bacteria have any peptidoglycan layer at all present, none in the other, under any circumstances whatsoever indeed
Gram-negative bacteria have thicker peptidoglycan than Gram-positive bacteria overall, under any circumstances whatsoever indeed
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows Gram-positive bacteria with a thick peptidoglycan layer (about 25 nm) cross-linked via a pentaglycine bridge, while Gram-negative bacteria have a thin single layer (2–3 nm) with direct cross-links, sandwiched between two lipid membranes.

questions.q: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), found in the outer membrane of which type of bacteria, includes a repeating chain called the:
questions.e: Lipopolysaccharides occur in Gram-negative bacteria and include a repeating O-antigen chain (built from sugars such as mannose, rhamnose, abequose and D-galactose) attached to a core oligosaccharide.

questions.q: Chitin, found in fungal cell walls and the exoskeletons of crustaceans and insects, is composed of which repeating unit and linkage?
questions.e: Chitin is described in the lecture as being composed of β(1→4)-linked N-acetyl-D-glucosamine units, found in fungal cell walls and the exoskeletons of crustaceans and insects.

questions.q: Molisch's test is described as what kind of test, and what colour result indicates a positive result?
o: A test for pentoses only; a green colour
A general test for carbohydrates; a purple ring/complex
A test for proteins; a blue colour
A test specific to ketoses only; a cherry-red colour
questions.e: Molisch's test is a general test for carbohydrates: sulfuric acid dehydrates the sugar to furfural or hydroxymethylfurfural, which reacts with sulfonated α-naphthol to give a purple (violet-red) coloured complex.

questions.q: In Molisch's test, which furfural derivative is formed from a pentose sugar, and which is formed from a hexose sugar?
o: Both pentose and hexose give the same furfural product
Neither pentose nor hexose reacts in this test
Hydroxymethyl furfural from pentose; furfural from hexose
Furfural from pentose; hydroxymethyl furfural from hexose
questions.e: The lecture states that when treated with conc. H2SO4, furfural is formed from pentose sugar, and hydroxymethyl furfural is formed from hexose sugar; both react with α-naphthol to give the purple ring.

questions.q: Bial's test is used to distinguish which two categories of sugar, and what colour indicates a positive result?
o: Reducing sugars from non-reducing sugars; a blue colour
Pentose sugars from hexose sugars; a green complex
Aldoses from ketoses; a cherry-red complex
Monosaccharides from disaccharides; a brick-red precipitate
questions.e: Bial's test distinguishes pentose sugars from hexose sugars: pentoses form furfural in an acidic medium, which condenses with orcinol in the presence of ferric ion to give a green-coloured complex, soluble in butanol.

questions.q: In Bial's test, what reagent does the furfural condense with, in the presence of ferric ion, to form the coloured complex?
questions.e: Bial's test uses orcinol; the furfural formed from pentoses condenses with orcinol in the presence of ferric ion to give a green condensation product.

questions.q: Seliwanoff's test distinguishes aldoses from ketoses. What colour do ketoses give, and how quickly?
o: A cherry-red colour, in a shorter time of heating than aldoses
A green colour, faster than aldoses overall
No colour change at all observed here
A cherry-red colour, but only after cooling for 24 hours
questions.e: In Seliwanoff's test, ketoses are dehydrated more readily to give furfural derivatives that condense with resorcinol to give a cherry-red complex, forming in a shorter heating time than the brownish colour given by aldoses.

questions.q: What reagent does furfural condense with in Seliwanoff's test to give the cherry-red colour?
questions.e: Seliwanoff's test uses resorcinol: on condensation with resorcinol, the furfural derivatives formed from ketoses give a cherry-red complex.

questions.q: Benedict's test detects which category of sugars, and what colour change indicates a positive result?
o: Reducing sugars; colour changes from green to dark red or rusty brown
Polysaccharides only; colour changes to yellow
Ketoses only; colour changes to a deep purple
Non-reducing sugars; colour stays completely blue
questions.e: Benedict's test is a test for reducing sugars: when mixed with Benedict's reagent and heated, a reduction reaction changes the colour from green to dark red (brick) or rusty brown, depending on the amount and type of sugar.

questions.q: In Benedict's test, what happens chemically to cause the colour change?
o: Sugar is oxidised to carbon dioxide and water only
Copper ions in the reagent are reduced to copper ions
Iron ions are reduced to iron ions
Sodium ions are reduced to sodium metal
questions.e: The copper (II) ions in Benedict's solution are reduced to copper (I) ions by the reducing sugar, which causes the observed colour change.

questions.q: What three components make up Benedict's reagent solution?
o: Copper acetate, sodium chloride, and citric acid
Cupric sulphate, sodium carbonate, and sodium citrate
Sodium potassium tartrate and copper sulphate only
questions.e: Benedict's test is carried out in a solution containing cupric sulphate, sodium carbonate, and sodium citrate.

questions.q: What are the two components of Fehling's reagent, and what role does sodium potassium tartrate play?
questions.e: Fehling's reagent comprises Fehling's solution A (aqueous copper sulphate) and solution B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate), mixed in equal amounts before the test; the sodium potassium tartrate acts as the chelating agent.

questions.q: How does Fehling's test compare to Benedict's test in terms of reagent stability and result?
o: Fehling's reagent is far more stable and gives a completely different colour entirely indeed
Fehling's and Benedict's tests detect completely unrelated compounds altogether indeed truly
