Vitamins required for coenzyme synthesis only, and nothing else whatsoever, under any circumstances at all
Substrates that are always in excess relative to the enzyme, under any circumstances whatsoever, ever, always
questions.e: Modulator proteins bind to enzymes and influence their activity; cAMP-dependent protein kinase exists as dimers of catalytic and regulatory subunits, and dissociation of the regulatory subunits (modulator proteins) activates the catalytic subunits, while reassociation suppresses activity.

questions.q: How is a metabolic pathway defined in the lecture?
o: A random sequence of substrate collisions with no defined order
Any chemical reaction occurring inside a cell, unrelated to a pathway
A single enzyme reaction that produces energy directly
A series of connected enzymatic reactions that produce a specific product
questions.e: A metabolic pathway is defined as a series of connected enzymatic reactions that produce a specific product, consisting of sequential steps with over 2,000 reactions catalysed by distinct enzymes.

questions.q: Approximately how many distinct enzyme-catalysed reactions make up the full set of metabolic pathways described in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that metabolic pathways consist of sequential steps, with over 2,000 reactions catalysed by distinct enzymes.

questions.q: What are the substrates of the enzymes that make up metabolism called?
questions.e: Enzymes are the basic units of metabolism, and the substrates of these enzymes are called metabolites.

questions.q: What holds together the temporary structural-functional complexes that usually form between sequential enzymes of a pathway?
o: Non-covalent interactions with structural cell elements
Strong covalent bonds formed between the adjacent enzymes
Hydrogen bonds formed directly with DNA strands
Disulfide bridges linking cysteine residues together
questions.e: Temporary structural-functional complexes form between sequential enzymes of a pathway, held together by non-covalent interactions and structural elements of the cell such as integral membrane proteins and cytoskeletal proteins.

questions.q: What term does the lecture use for multi-enzyme complexes formed when consecutively acting soluble enzymes are organised into cellular ultra-structures?
questions.e: Recent research reveals that soluble enzymes are organised into ultra-structures in the cell, where consecutively acting enzymes are associated with multiple enzyme complexes called metabolons.

questions.q: In one arrangement of a metabolic pathway, enzymes are physically separated from one another. What must happen for the pathway to proceed in this case?
o: Intermediate metabolites must diffuse from one active site to the next
The pathway must stop after just one single step
The enzymes must fuse permanently into one single protein
The substrate must be actively transported using ATP energy
questions.e: When enzymes are physically separated, the intermediate metabolites must diffuse from one active site to the next active site before the next reaction can occur.

questions.q: In a multi-enzyme complex arrangement of a pathway, how are intermediate metabolites handled?
o: They diffuse freely throughout the cytosol of the cell
They are passed directly from one active site to the next
They are exported from the cell entirely and permanently
They are stored in the nucleus for later use
questions.e: When enzymes form a multi-enzyme complex, intermediate metabolites are passed directly from one active site to the next, avoiding free diffusion.

questions.q: For metabolic pathways that reside within membranes, how do the enzyme and its substrates move?
o: They diffuse in the two dimensions of the membrane
They are transported by vesicles only
They do not move; the membrane moves around them
They diffuse in the three dimensions of the cytosol
questions.e: Some pathways reside within membranes; in this case, the enzyme and the substrates diffuse in the two dimensions of the membrane rather than in free 3-D solution.

questions.q: Why are metabolic pathways described as irreversible?
o: Because every individual reaction step is irreversible
Because enzymes cannot be reused after a single catalytic cycle
Because pathways are highly exergonic, which gives the pathway direction
Because ATP is never regenerated within the pathway itself
questions.e: Metabolic pathways are highly exergonic, which gives the pathway direction. This overall exergonic character is what makes the pathway effectively irreversible, even though individual steps may be near equilibrium.

questions.q: If two metabolites A and B are interconvertible, what does the irreversibility principle imply about the pathway from A to B versus from B to A?
o: They must be exactly the same pathway run in reverse
They must differ, allowing the two pathways to be independently regulated
They must use the same first committed step regardless
They cannot both exist within the same cell simultaneously
questions.e: If two metabolites are interconvertible, the pathway from the first to the second must differ from the reverse pathway. This allows the two pathways to be independently regulated.

questions.q: What characterises the 'first committed step' of a metabolic pathway?
o: It is a step that never involves an enzyme catalyst of any kind at all
It is an irreversible reaction that commits the intermediate to continue down the pathway
It is a reversible step that remains near equilibrium conditions
It is always the very last reaction occurring in the entire pathway
questions.e: Although most reactions in a pathway are near equilibrium, every pathway has an irreversible reaction committing the intermediate it produces to continue down the pathway; beyond this committed step the reaction proceeds to completion.

questions.q: How is control of the metabolic flux through a pathway typically accomplished?
o: By destroying the enzyme completely after just one use
By regulating the rate-determining step, often the first committed step
By regulating every single reaction in the pathway equally
By randomly varying substrate concentration levels
questions.e: Control of the metabolic flux of metabolites through a pathway is accomplished by regulating the rate-determining step of the pathway, which often is the first committed step.

questions.q: Why do eukaryotic cells compartmentalise metabolic pathways into organelles?
o: To reduce the number of enzymes needed for catalysis overall entirely
Because organelles cannot contain any enzymes whatsoever at all, ever
To allow different pathways to occur in specific locations and be independently regulated
To prevent any pathway from ever finishing its reactions at all, ever
questions.e: Eukaryotes use organelles to compartmentalise metabolic pathways, allowing different metabolic pathways to occur in specific locations and allowing for independent regulation, e.g. in mitochondria, cytosol, and the nucleus.

questions.q: Which pathway architecture is illustrated by the conversion 3-Phosphoglycerate → 3-Phosphohydroxypyruvate → 3-Phosphoserine → Serine?
questions.e: This is a linear pathway: a series of independent enzymes in which the product of one reaction becomes the substrate for the next reaction.

questions.q: What key feature distinguishes a cyclic pathway, such as the citric acid cycle, from a linear pathway?
o: It only occurs in bacteria and nowhere else
The product is never used again by the cell
Intermediates are regenerated every turn of the cycle
No enzymes are required for this pathway type
questions.e: In a cyclic pathway such as the citric acid cycle, intermediates (e.g. oxaloacetate) are regenerated every turn. The lecture notes that very few pathways are actually cyclic.

questions.q: Fatty acid synthesis is given as an example of which pathway architecture, in which the same set of enzymes is used repeatedly for polymerisation reactions?
questions.e: Fatty acid synthesis is a spiral pathway: the same set of enzymes is used repeatedly, and the reactions are polymerisation reactions that build up the fatty acid chain.

questions.q: Which class of metabolic reaction is responsible for deriving valuable energy from the oxidation of carbon compounds?
questions.e: Oxidation-reduction reactions are crucial components of many pathways; valuable energy is often derived from the oxidation of carbon compounds, and they are catalysed by oxidoreductases or dehydrogenases.

questions.q: Which enzyme family catalyses oxidation-reduction reactions in metabolism?
questions.e: Oxidation-reduction reactions are catalysed by oxidoreductases or dehydrogenases, such as succinate dehydrogenase.

questions.q: In the citric acid cycle reaction catalysed by succinate dehydrogenase, what happens to succinate and to FAD?
o: Succinate is reduced to fumarate; FAD is oxidised
Succinate is phosphorylated; FAD is released
Succinate is oxidised to fumarate; FAD is reduced to FADH2
Succinate is hydrolysed; FAD is unaffected
questions.e: Succinate dehydrogenase removes two hydrogen atoms from succinate, oxidising it to fumarate, while reducing flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to FADH2.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of a ligation reaction in metabolism?
o: It forms bonds using free energy from ATP cleavage
It rearranges atoms within a molecule
It cleaves a bond using water
It transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to a sugar
questions.e: Ligation reactions form bonds by using free energy released from ATP cleavage; they are catalysed by synthases or ligases.

questions.q: In the ATP-dependent formation of oxaloacetate from pyruvate and CO2, which type of chemical bond is being formed?
questions.e: The reaction pyruvate + CO2 + ATP + H2O ⇌ oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi + H+ illustrates the ATP-dependent formation of a carbon-carbon bond, required to combine smaller molecules into larger ones, catalysed by synthases or ligases.

questions.q: Which enzyme class catalyses ligation reactions such as the ATP-dependent formation of oxaloacetate from pyruvate?
questions.e: Ligation reactions, which form carbon-carbon or other bonds using energy from ATP cleavage, are catalysed by synthases or ligases.

questions.q: What do isomerisation reactions accomplish in a metabolic pathway?
o: They rearrange atoms within a molecule to prepare it for later reactions
They release two hydrogen atoms to reduce FAD directly
They transfer a phosphoryl group directly between molecules
They add water to break a bond within the molecule
questions.e: Isomerisation reactions rearrange atoms within a molecule, preparing it for subsequent reactions such as oxidation-reduction reactions; they are catalysed by isomerases or epimerases.

questions.q: Aconitase catalyses which conversion in the citric acid cycle, illustrating an isomerisation reaction?
questions.e: Aconitase catalyses citrate → cis-aconitate → isocitrate, moving the hydroxyl group of citrate from a tertiary to a secondary position, preparing the molecule for subsequent oxidation and decarboxylation.

questions.q: Why does the isomerisation of citrate to isocitrate matter for the citric acid cycle?
o: It releases ATP directly during the isomerisation step without any oxidation occurring at all
It moves the hydroxyl group from a tertiary to a secondary position, enabling subsequent oxidation and decarboxylation
It hydrolyses citrate into two smaller molecules using a water molecule instead of shifting groups
It converts citrate directly into a fat molecule for long-term storage without any change in oxidation
questions.e: By moving the hydroxyl group of citrate from a tertiary to a secondary position, the isomerisation prepares the molecule for the oxidation and decarboxylation steps that follow later in the citric acid cycle.

questions.q: Which enzyme class is responsible for group-transfer reactions in metabolism?
questions.e: Group-transfer reactions, in which a functional group is transferred from an activated carrier to an acceptor molecule, are catalysed by transferases.

questions.q: In the reaction catalysed by hexokinase, what is transferred, and to what molecule?
o: A methyl group is transferred from SAM to DNA
A hydroxyl group is transferred to fructose
A phosphoryl group is transferred from ATP to glucose
An amino group is transferred from glutamate to pyruvate
questions.e: Hexokinase transfers a phosphoryl group from the activated phosphoryl-group carrier ATP to glucose, forming glucose-6-phosphate.

questions.q: What is the biological purpose of phosphorylating glucose to glucose-6-phosphate via hexokinase?
o: It releases glucose from the cell into the bloodstream
It traps glucose in the cell so further catabolism can occur
It prevents glucose from ever being used by the cell
It converts glucose directly into a lipid for storage
questions.e: The group-transfer reaction catalysed by hexokinase traps glucose in the cell (as glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot cross the membrane as easily) so that further catabolism of glucose can occur.

questions.q: Which class of reaction cleaves bonds by adding water across them?
questions.e: Hydrolytic reactions cleave bonds by adding water. Hydrolysis breaks down large molecules to facilitate further metabolism or to reutilise components for biosynthetic purposes.

questions.q: Which enzyme family catalyses hydrolytic reactions such as the breakdown of sucrose into glucose and fructose?
questions.e: Hydrolases catalyse hydrolytic reactions. In the lecture's example, sucrose + H2O yields glucose and fructose.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how are proteins broken down for reuse or further metabolism?
o: By isomerisation into amino acid isomers
questions.e: The lecture states that proteins are digested by hydrolytic cleavage, which is catalysed by hydrolases.

questions.q: What is the sixth class of metabolic reaction described in the lecture, involving double bonds?
o: Hydrolysis of double bonds using a water molecule to cleave them
Addition of functional groups to double bonds, or removal of groups to form double bonds
Ligation of double bonds only, using ATP energy for the reaction
Reduction of double bonds by NADH exclusively and completely, always
questions.e: The sixth class of metabolic reaction is the addition of functional groups to double bonds, or the removal of groups to form double bonds; such reactions are catalysed by lyases.

questions.q: Aldolase converts fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into which two three-carbon products?
questions.e: Aldolase, a lyase, converts the six-carbon molecule fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon fragments: dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.

questions.q: Which enzyme class catalyses the aldolase-type cleavage of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon fragments?
questions.e: Lyases catalyse the addition of functional groups to double bonds or removal of groups to form double bonds, as in aldolase splitting fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.

questions.q: Enolase converts 2-phosphoglycerate into phosphoenolpyruvate by which type of chemical change?
o: Dehydration to form a double bond
questions.e: Enolase catalyses dehydration to form a double bond: 2-phosphoglycerate loses water (via enolase) to become phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP).

questions.q: What is the significance of forming phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) from 2-phosphoglycerate?
o: It sets up the next pathway step, a group-transfer reaction that uses PEP's high phosphoryl transfer potential to form ATP
It ends the pathway with no further use of the product at all, since no group-transfer reaction follows this step
It converts PEP into a fat molecule for long-term storage instead of being used in any further group-transfer reaction
It hydrolyses PEP immediately into pyruvate and water only, without forming any ATP or high-energy phosphate bond
questions.e: This dehydration reaction sets up the next pathway step, a group-transfer reaction that uses the high phosphoryl transfer potential of PEP to form ATP.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a metabolic reaction class with its catalysing enzyme family?
questions.e: Group-transfer reactions, such as hexokinase transferring a phosphoryl group from ATP to glucose, are catalysed by transferases.

questions.q: Sucrose + H2O → Glucose + Fructose is an example of which reaction class?
questions.e: This reaction adds water to cleave the glycosidic bond in sucrose, which is the defining feature of a hydrolytic reaction, catalysed by a hydrolase.

questions.q: Which of these reactions is catalysed by a synthase or ligase rather than a transferase?
o: Pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → Oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi
questions.e: The ATP-dependent carbon-carbon bond-forming conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is a ligation reaction, catalysed by a synthase/ligase, not a transferase.

questions.q: A student observes an enzyme using the free energy of ATP cleavage to join two smaller carbon-containing molecules into one larger molecule. Which reaction class and enzyme family best describes this?
questions.e: Using free energy from ATP cleavage to form a new bond that combines smaller molecules into a larger one is the defining feature of a ligation reaction, catalysed by synthases or ligases.

questions.q: What is the primary reason the level of a single enzyme varies under different environmental conditions, according to the lecture?
o: Fluctuation in ATP concentration only within the cell
Variation in the enzyme's rate of synthesis
Random degradation of mRNA transcripts within the cell
Variation in overall cell size and volume
questions.e: The level of a single enzyme varies under different environmental conditions primarily because of variations in the enzyme's rate of synthesis, a phenomenon particularly well understood in bacteria.

questions.q: What is the term for the phenomenon where a bacterium synthesises new enzyme molecules, from less than one per cell to thousands per cell, when a usable substrate is added to its growth medium?
questions.e: When a usable substrate is added to a bacterial growth medium, the abundance of enzymes needed to process the substrate may increase sharply by synthesising new proteins — this phenomenon is called enzyme induction.

questions.q: In the lac operon, what happens when lactose is absent from the bacterial cell?
o: The active repressor protein binds the operator, and RNA polymerase cannot attach to the promoter
The operon is permanently turned on regardless of conditions or lactose availability
RNA polymerase binds the promoter freely without any repressor interference
The lactose-processing genes are transcribed at their maximum rate continuously
questions.e: When lactose is absent, the active repressor protein binds to the operator. This blocks RNA polymerase from attaching to the promoter, so the operon is turned off.

questions.q: In the lac operon, what effect does the presence of lactose have on the repressor protein?
o: It inactivates the repressor protein, allowing RNA polymerase to bind the promoter
It destroys RNA polymerase completely and irreversibly, permanently
It has no effect on the repressor protein whatsoever, ever
It converts the repressor into a second messenger molecule
questions.e: When lactose is present, it inactivates the repressor protein (repressor protein inactivated by lactose). RNA polymerase can then bind to the promoter and transcribe the lactose-processing genes into mRNA, which is translated into lactose-processing enzymes.

questions.q: The lac operon example illustrates control of metabolism at which level?
o: Control of enzyme levels via regulated gene transcription
Control of enzyme activity via allostery
Control via a steroid hormone receptor
Control via compartmentation in the mitochondria
questions.e: The lac operon example illustrates control of enzyme levels: whether the lactose-processing genes are transcribed (and thus whether the enzymes are synthesised) depends on whether lactose is present.

questions.q: According to the lecture, in how many distinct ways can the catalytic activity of an existing enzyme be controlled?
questions.e: The lecture states that the catalytic activity of an enzyme can be controlled in two ways: (a) reversible interaction with ligands, and (b) covalent modification of enzyme structure.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a ligand that can reversibly interact with an enzyme to control its activity?
o: An operon controlling transcription of nearby genes
A DNA promoter sequence recognised by RNA polymerase
An allosteric effector binding a regulatory site
A ribosome translating mRNA into protein
questions.e: Control of enzyme activity by reversible interaction with ligands can involve substrates, products, or allosteric modifiers/effectors, especially low molecular weight ones.

questions.q: Where do allosteric effectors typically bind on an enzyme, and what is the effect?
o: They bind DNA directly and block transcription entirely without any enzyme
They bind specific regulatory sites, altering subunit-subunit interactions within the enzyme
They bind the enzyme's mRNA and prevent its translation into protein
They bind the active site directly and are converted to product entirely
questions.e: Allosteric effectors bind to specific regulatory sites (not the active site), thereby altering subunit-subunit interactions within the enzyme and controlling product formation. This usually acts on the committed step of the pathway.

questions.q: In allosteric inhibition, what happens to the enzyme's active site when the allosteric inhibitor binds the allosteric site?
o: Nothing changes at the active site of the enzyme at all
The active site is duplicated elsewhere on the enzyme
The active site becomes covalently modified by phosphorylation
The active site becomes distorted so the substrate cannot bind productively
questions.e: In allosteric inhibition, binding of the allosteric inhibitor to the allosteric site distorts the active site, so that when the substrate later arrives it cannot bind productively.

questions.q: In allosteric activation, what is the effect of the allosteric activator binding the allosteric site?
o: It causes hydrolysis of the enzyme, destroying its structure
It restores or opens up the active site so the substrate can bind productively
It permanently destroys the enzyme beyond any possible repair
It converts the enzyme into a completely different enzyme entirely
questions.e: In allosteric activation, the allosteric activator binds the allosteric site and this converts a previously distorted active site into a form that can properly bind the substrate, activating the enzyme.

questions.q: Which amino acid residues are most commonly phosphorylated as a means of covalently modifying and controlling enzyme activity?
questions.e: Covalent modification of enzyme structure to control activity is mainly through phosphorylation of serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues of the enzyme protein.

questions.q: What is adenylation, as a form of covalent enzyme regulation?
o: The removal of an adenine base from RNA
The binding of adenylyl cyclase to a receptor
The transfer of the adenylate moiety of ATP to the enzyme
The transfer of a phosphoryl group from ADP to glucose
questions.e: Adenylation is a complex covalent regulation mechanism involving the transfer of the adenylate moiety of ATP to the enzyme being regulated.

questions.q: What is ADP-ribosylation, as described in the lecture's discussion of covalent enzyme regulation?
o: The oxidation of ADP directly into ATP molecules
The hydrolysis of ADP into AMP and free phosphate
The transfer of a ribose sugar from RNA to DNA
The transfer of the ADP-ribosyl moiety from NAD+ to the enzyme
questions.e: ADP-ribosylation is described as the transfer of the ADP-ribosyl moiety from NAD+ to the enzyme, another form of complex covalent regulation.

questions.q: What is the regulatory basis of compartmentation as a metabolic control mechanism?
o: The random distribution of enzymes throughout the cell with no membrane barriers at all, ever
The complete impermeability of all cellular membranes to every metabolite without exception
The selective permeability of membranes to metabolites, controlling passage of intermediates between compartments
The absence of membranes within eukaryotic cells entirely, leaving no compartments at all
questions.e: The regulatory function of compartmentation is due to the selective permeability of membranes to metabolites, thereby controlling the passage of intermediates from one compartment to another.

questions.q: Which organelle houses the enzymes of the electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation, illustrating compartmentation as a control mechanism?
questions.e: Enzymes of the electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation are all found in the mitochondria, illustrating how compartmentation localises and regulates specific pathways.

questions.q: Which organelle houses RNA polymerases, where DNA transcription to RNA occurs, illustrating compartmentation?
questions.e: RNA polymerases are found in the nucleus, where DNA transcription to RNA occurs — an example of enzymes participating in the same process being localised to a particular compartment.

questions.q: In the glucose metabolism example, glycolysis occurs in the cytosol while the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation occur in the mitochondria. What kind of control mechanism does this represent?
o: Control of enzyme levels via induction
questions.e: The spatial separation of glycolysis (cytosol) from the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation (mitochondria) is an example of compartmentation, which allows independent regulation of each pathway.

questions.q: A bacterium is grown without lactose and then lactose is added to its medium. Predict what happens to the lac repressor and to transcription of the lactose-processing genes.
o: The repressor is destroyed permanently and can never re-form under any condition
The repressor becomes more active and transcription stops entirely and permanently
Lactose inactivates the repressor, allowing RNA polymerase to bind the promoter and transcribe the genes
Transcription begins without any change to the repressor protein or the operator
questions.e: Lactose inactivates the active repressor protein. With the repressor inactivated, RNA polymerase can bind the promoter, and the lactose-processing genes are transcribed — this is enzyme induction via control of enzyme levels.

questions.q: How are hormones defined in the lecture?
o: Substances synthesised by specialised cells and circulated through the blood to remote target cells
Allosteric effectors that bind only within the same cell that produced them
Enzymes that catalyse ligation reactions using ATP energy exclusively always
Metabolites that simply diffuse between active sites of nearby enzymes only
questions.e: Hormones are substances synthesised by specialised cells and circulated through the blood to remote target cells, where they trigger a metabolic response.

questions.q: How many major types of metabolic response to hormones does the lecture describe?
questions.e: The lecture describes two types of metabolic responses to hormones: (a) the steroid hormone response involving intracellular receptors and gene regulation, and (b) responses involving synthesis of intracellular second messengers.

questions.q: With steroid hormones such as oestrogen, where does the hormone first interact with its receptor?
o: On ribosomes directly during protein synthesis
In the mitochondrial matrix only, never elsewhere
Intracellularly, with an intracellular protein receptor
On the outer surface of the plasma membrane
questions.e: With steroid hormones such as oestrogen, the hormone enters the target cell and interacts with intracellular protein receptors, since steroid hormones can cross the plasma membrane.

questions.q: After a steroid hormone binds its intracellular receptor, where does the resulting hormone-receptor complex migrate?
o: To the lysosome for degradation and complete destruction
Out of the cell entirely, never to return
To the Golgi complex for further processing
To the nucleus, where it binds specific sites in the genome
questions.e: The hormone-receptor complex migrates to the nucleus, where it binds to specific sites in the genome and either activates or represses the transcription of genes.

questions.q: What is the ultimate metabolic effect of a steroid hormone-receptor complex binding to genomic DNA?
o: It activates or represses transcription of genes, altering protein synthesis
It converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate directly
It hydrolyses membrane phospholipids into fatty acids
It directly phosphorylates cytoplasmic enzymes only
questions.e: In the nucleus, the steroid hormone-receptor complex binds specific genomic sites and either activates or represses transcription of genes, ultimately changing which proteins are made via subsequent transcription and translation.

questions.q: In the steroid hormone signalling diagram, what molecules assist in releasing the receptor from a receptor-chaperonin complex before it binds hormone?
questions.e: The diagram shows molecular chaperones associated with the receptor-chaperonin complex; once the steroid hormone binds, the receptor is released from this complex to form the receptor-hormone complex.

questions.q: After the steroid hormone-receptor complex binds chromatin and drives transcription, what are the next two steps shown in the pathway?
o: Export of chromatin from the nucleus
Direct conversion of DNA into protein without RNA
Translation of mRNA at the ribosome to make new protein
questions.e: Following transcription (production of mRNA from the DNA-associated receptor complex on chromatin), the mRNA is translated at the ribosome in the cytoplasm to produce new protein.

questions.q: For nonsteroid hormones, where does the hormone (the 'first messenger') act?
o: Inside the mitochondrial matrix, never elsewhere at all
Extracellularly, by binding to a receptor in the plasma membrane
Inside the nucleus, bound directly to genomic DNA
On the Golgi complex only, never elsewhere at all
questions.e: For nonsteroid hormones, the hormone (first messenger) acts extracellularly by binding to receptors in the plasma membrane, unlike steroid hormones which act intracellularly.

questions.q: In the nonsteroid hormone signalling pathway shown in the lecture, what happens immediately after the hormone receptor is activated?
o: The hormone is hydrolysed by a lyase
The receptor's G-protein exchanges GDP for GTP
The receptor moves to the nucleus
questions.e: After the nonsteroid hormone binds its receptor, the receptor-associated G-protein exchanges GDP for GTP, which then goes on to activate adenylyl cyclase in the membrane.

questions.q: In the nonsteroid hormone signal pathway, which membrane enzyme converts ATP into the second messenger?
o: Adenylyl cyclase, activated via the G-protein pathway
Aldolase, which cleaves fructose bisphosphate instead
Succinate dehydrogenase, part of the citric acid cycle
questions.e: Adenylyl cyclase, activated via the GTP-bound G-protein, converts ATP into the second messenger cAMP, which then produces the effect on cellular function.

questions.q: What is the second messenger generated by adenylyl cyclase in the nonsteroid hormone signalling pathway?
questions.e: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP (cyclic AMP), which serves as the second messenger that goes on to produce the effect on cellular function.

questions.q: In the glycogen mobilisation example, what happens after the hormone glucagon binds its receptor?
o: Glucagon is hydrolysed immediately and has no further effect
Synthesis of the second messenger cAMP is activated, resulting in glycogen breakdown
Glycogen synthesis is directly activated by glucagon without any messenger
The receptor migrates to the nucleus like a steroid hormone receptor
questions.e: In glycogen mobilisation, the hormone glucagon, after binding to its receptor, activates the synthesis of the second messenger cAMP, which in turn results in the breakdown of glycogen.

questions.q: Which set of elements does the lecture say lipids always contain?
o: CHO, meaning carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
questions.e: Lipids are heterogeneous groups of organic compounds related to fatty acids that contain CHO and may also have PNS (phosphorus, nitrogen, sulphur).

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the most crucial function of lipids?
questions.e: Lipids play many vital roles, but their most crucial function is to build cellular membranes; others are energy storage, communication, insulation and protection.

questions.q: Lipids are defined as a class of biomolecules by which property?
o: Insolubility in all solvents, both polar and nonpolar
High solubility in water and low solubility in nonpolar solvents
Low solubility in water and high solubility in nonpolar solvents
Equal solubility in polar and nonpolar solvents
questions.e: The slide states lipids are a class of biomolecules defined by low solubility in water and high solubility in nonpolar solvents.

questions.q: A lipid that possesses only nonpolar groups is described as:
questions.e: Lipids in biosystems are either hydrophobic (possessing only nonpolar groups) or amphipathic (possessing both polar and nonpolar groups).

questions.q: A lipid that possesses both polar and nonpolar groups is described as:
questions.e: Amphipathic lipids possess both polar and nonpolar groups, unlike hydrophobic lipids which possess only nonpolar groups.

questions.q: Why are lipids the molecules of choice for metabolic energy storage?
o: They are highly reduced forms of carbon that yield large amounts of energy on oxidation
They contain nitrogen atoms that store energy within peptide bonds
They cannot be metabolised at all, so they simply persist unused
They dissolve readily in water, allowing for easy transport in blood
questions.e: Lipids (largely hydrocarbons in nature) represent highly reduced forms of carbon and, upon oxidation in metabolism, yield large amounts of energy.

questions.q: How does the hydrophobic nature of lipid molecules benefit membranes?
o: It makes membranes fully permeable to water and ions
It allows membranes to act as effective barriers to more polar molecules
It prevents membranes from ever forming at all, ever
It allows membranes to dissolve in the cytoplasm
questions.e: The hydrophobic nature of lipid molecules allows membranes to act as effective barriers to more polar molecules.

questions.q: Which is the first of the three broad classes of lipids described in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture classifies lipids into simple lipids, compound lipids and derived lipids.

questions.q: Simple lipids that are esters of fatty acids with glycerol are called:
questions.e: Simple lipids include true fats (esters of fatty acids with glycerol) and waxes (esters of fatty acids with a higher molecular weight monohydric alcohol).

questions.q: What distinguishes compound lipids from true fats?
o: Compound lipids never contain any alcohol component at all, unlike true fats which always do
Compound lipids contain an additional group such as phosphate, carbohydrate, sulphate or protein
Compound lipids contain no fatty acids at all, unlike true fats which are fatty acid esters
Compound lipids are always gaseous at room temperature, unlike true fats which are solid or liquid
questions.e: Compound lipids are esters of fatty acids with alcohol that, besides this, contain another group (phosphate, carbohydrate, sulphate or protein).

questions.q: Derived lipids are produced by which process?
o: Hydrolysis of simple and compound lipids
questions.e: Derived lipids are derived from simple and compound lipids by hydrolysis, yielding fatty acids, glycerol, sphingosine, cholesterol and steroid derivatives.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the learning objectives of this lecture?
o: Derive the equations of stellar nucleosynthesis
Explain the process of DNA replication
Explain the classification and reactions of lipids
questions.e: The three learning objectives given are to identify the functions of lipids, explain the classification and reactions of lipids, and understand the structural features and properties of lipids.

questions.q: A fatty acid is composed of which two structural parts?
o: A long hydrocarbon chain and a terminal carboxyl group
A ring system and an amino alcohol
A steroid nucleus and a sugar residue
A phosphate group and a glycerol backbone
questions.e: Fatty acids are composed of a long hydrocarbon chain ("tail") and a terminal carboxyl group (or "head"), which is usually ionised under physiological conditions.

questions.q: Why are free fatty acids rare in biological systems?
o: They evaporate quickly at body temperature
They are esterified to glycerol or other backbone structures
They are toxic and immediately degraded
They cannot form covalent bonds of any kind
questions.e: Fatty acids occur in large amounts in biological systems but are rarely free; they are esterified to glycerol or other backbone structures.

questions.q: Most naturally occurring fatty acids have carbon chains in which range, with an even number of carbons?
questions.e: Most fatty acids in nature have an even number of carbon atoms, usually 14 to 24; certain marine organisms contain substantial amounts with odd numbers of carbon atoms.

questions.q: A fatty acid with more than one double bond in its hydrocarbon chain is called:
questions.e: If a fatty acid has one double bond it is monounsaturated, and if it has more than one, it is polyunsaturated.

questions.q: What is the shorthand notation 18:0 used to describe?
o: Stearic acid — an 18-carbon chain with no double bonds
A fatty acid with 18 double bonds
Oleic acid — an 18-carbon chain with one double bond
questions.e: A fatty acid composed of an 18-carbon chain with no double bonds is called stearic acid (systematic name octadecanoic acid), shorthand notation 18:0.

questions.q: Which fatty acid is described as the most common unsaturated fatty acid, notated 18:1(9)?
questions.e: The most common unsaturated fatty acid is oleic acid, or 18:1(9), with a double bond between carbons 9 and 10.

questions.q: What configuration are the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids nearly always found in?
o: Trans, keeping the chain perfectly straight
Cis, causing a bend or "kink" in the chain
questions.e: The double bonds are nearly always in the cis configuration, causing a bend or "kink" in the heavy acid chain, with significant consequences for membrane structure.

questions.q: Which two fatty acids are identified as essential fatty acids that mammals must obtain from the diet?
questions.e: Mammals do not synthesise some fatty acids necessary for normal growth (essential fatty acids): linoleic acid and γ-linolenic acid, which must be obtained in the diet from plant sources.

questions.q: Arachidonic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid, is synthesised by mammals from which precursor?
questions.e: Arachidonic acid is not found in plants but can be synthesised by mammals from linoleic acid.

questions.q: A triacylglycerol in which all three fatty acid groups are identical, such as trioleoylglycerol, is called a:
questions.e: If all three fatty acid groups are the same, the molecule is called a simple triacylglycerol, e.g. trioleoylglycerol (triolein); mixed triacylglycerols contain two or three different fatty acids.

questions.q: About how much energy does complete oxidation of 1 gram of triacylglycerols yield, compared with proteins/carbohydrates?
o: About 4 kJ, versus about 38 kJ/g for proteins and carbohydrates
About 38 kJ, versus about 17 kJ/g for proteins and carbohydrates
No usable energy at all is released upon oxidation
Exactly the same energy as proteins and carbohydrates
questions.e: Complete oxidation of 1 g of triacylglycerols yields about 38 kJ of energy, whereas proteins and carbohydrates release about 17 kJ/g.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of an acylglycerol with alkali, yielding salts of free fatty acids and glycerol, is called:
questions.e: Hydrolysis with alkali is saponification and yields salts of free fatty acids and glycerol; one historical method used potassium hydroxide (potash) from wood ashes.

questions.q: What is the parent compound for glycerol-based phospholipids, consisting of glycerol-3-phosphate with fatty acids esterified at the 1- and 2-positions?
questions.e: Phosphatidic acid, the parent compound for the glycerol-based phospholipids, consists of glycerol-3-phosphate with fatty acids esterified at 1- and 2-positions — the simplest glycerophospholipid.

questions.q: Which two phosphatides, formed with choline or ethanolamine head groups, are described as two of the most common constituents of biological membranes?
questions.e: Phosphatides with choline or ethanolamine are phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) or phosphatidylethanolamine (cephalin), two of the most common constituents of biological membranes.

questions.q: Diphosphatidylglycerol, first observed in heart tissue, is also known as:
questions.e: Glycerol phosphatide found in many tissues is diphosphatidylglycerol, first observed in heart tissue, where it is called cardiolipin.

questions.q: In cardiolipin, the two phosphatidylglycerols are esterified through which positions of the glycerol moiety?
o: The C-4 and C-5 hydroxyl groups
The C-1 and C-3 hydroxyl groups
questions.e: In cardiolipin, the two phosphatidylglycerols are esterified through the C-1 and C-3 hydroxyl groups of the glycerol moiety.

questions.q: Ether glycerophospholipids differ from ordinary glycerophospholipids by having what at the C-1 position?
o: An ether linkage instead of an acyl group
A steroid ring fused to it
questions.e: Ether glycerophospholipids possess an ether linkage instead of an acyl group at the C-1 position of glycerol.

questions.q: Platelet-activating factor (PAF) is unusually water-soluble for a lipid because of what feature at its C-2 position?
o: A 2-carbon acetate unit as the acyl group
questions.e: The alkyl group at C-1 of PAF is typically a 16-carbon chain, but the acyl group at C-2 is a 2-carbon acetate unit, making PAF much more water-soluble and able to act as a soluble messenger.

questions.q: What 18-carbon amino alcohol forms the backbone of sphingolipids, replacing glycerol?
questions.e: An 18-carbon amino alcohol, sphingosine, forms the backbone of sphingolipids rather than glycerol.

questions.q: Sphingomyelins, which are especially important in nervous tissue, are formed by esterifying phosphorylcholine or phosphorylethanolamine to which structure?
o: The carboxyl group of a fatty acid
questions.e: Esterification of a phosphorylcholine or a phosphorylethanolamine to the 1-hydroxy group of a ceramide forms sphingomyelin.

questions.q: A neutral glycosphingolipid containing a single glucose or galactose residue is called a:
questions.e: Neutral glycosphingolipids contain only neutral sugar residues; a cerebroside occurs for a single glucose or galactose.

questions.q: Gangliosides are complex glycosphingolipids whose ceramide backbone carries three or more sugars, one of which is typically a:
o: Sialic acid such as N-acetylneuraminic acid
questions.e: Gangliosides consist of a ceramide backbone with three or more sugars esterified, one of these being a sialic acid such as N-acetylneuraminic acid (NAA).

questions.q: Compounds containing N-acetylneuraminic acid (NAA) are classified as which type of glycosphingolipid, carrying a net negative charge at neutral pH?
questions.e: Compounds containing NAA are called acidic glycosphingolipids, and they have a net negative charge at neutral pH.

questions.q: Tay-Sachs disease, a rare but fatal genetic disease of infants and children, results from accumulation of which ganglioside?
questions.e: Tay-Sachs disease involves accumulation of ganglioside GM2 in victims' brains due to an absent degrading enzyme, characterised by a red-spotted retina, gradual blindness and weight loss.

questions.q: Waxes are defined in the lecture as esters of which combination?
o: Glycerol with three short-chain fatty acids
Long-chain alcohols with long-chain fatty acids
questions.e: Waxes are esters of long-chain alcohols with long-chain fatty acids, with weakly polar heads (the ester moiety) and a long nonpolar tail.

questions.q: In waxes, what is typical of the fatty acid component versus the alcohol component?
o: The fatty acids are usually saturated, while the alcohols may be saturated or unsaturated
The fatty acids contain nitrogen and the alcohols contain sulphur
Both components are always identical simple sugars in every case
The fatty acids are always unsaturated, and the alcohols are always aromatic
questions.e: Fatty acids in waxes are usually saturated, whereas the alcohols may be saturated or unsaturated and include sterols such as cholesterol.

questions.q: Carnauba wax, used for high-gloss finishes such as boat and automobile wax, comes from which source?
o: Fronds of palm trees in Brazil
questions.e: Carnauba wax, from the fronds of palm trees in Brazil, is a tough wax used for high gloss finishes such as boat wax, automobile wax, floor wax and shoe polish.

questions.q: Lanolin, used as a base for pharmaceutical and cosmetic products, is a component of which material?
questions.e: Lanolin, a wool wax component, is used as a base for pharmaceutical and cosmetic products because human skin rapidly assimilates it.

questions.q: Terpenes are built from combinations of which five-carbon repeating unit?
questions.e: Terpenes are a class of lipids formed from combinations of two or more molecules of isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene), a five-carbon unit abbreviated C5.

questions.q: A monoterpene, made of two isoprene units (C10), is described as occurring:
questions.e: Monoterpenes occur in all higher plants, whereas sesquiterpenes and diterpenes are less widely known.

questions.q: Squalene and lanosterol, precursors of cholesterol and other steroids, belong to which terpene class (C30, six isoprene units)?
questions.e: The triterpenes (C30: six isoprene units) include squalene and lanosterol, precursors of cholesterol and other steroids.

questions.q: β-Carotene and lycopene, colourful photosynthetic pigments, belong to which terpene class (C40, eight isoprene units)?
questions.e: Tetraterpenes (C40: eight isoprene units) are uncommon but include carotenoids; β-carotene is the precursor of vitamin A, and lycopene is a pigment found in tomatoes.

questions.q: Dolichols, polyprenols of 16 to 22 isoprene units, function as dolichyl phosphates to carry out which role?
o: Carrying carbohydrate units in the biosynthesis of animal glycoproteins
Absorbing dietary lipids in the small intestine
Transmitting nerve impulses across the synapse gap
Neutralising free fatty acids in rancid fat fully
questions.e: The dolichols (16 to 22 isoprene units) are polyprenols which, when in the form of dolichyl phosphates, carry carbohydrate units in the biosynthesis of animal glycoproteins.

questions.q: The steroid nucleus, consisting of three fused cyclohexane rings plus a cyclopentane ring, is formally named:
questions.e: The steroid nucleus has three fused cyclohexane rings together with the cyclopentane ring, known as cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene.

questions.q: Which statement about cholesterol is accurate according to the lecture?
o: It has no role in atherosclerosis and is never found in any arterial plaque deposits whatsoever at all
It is a carbohydrate, not a lipid, and is built entirely from repeating chains of glucose sugar units
It is found only in plant cell walls and never occurs anywhere in animal tissues or membranes at all
It is the most common animal steroid and precursor for all other steroids, and a principal component of animal cell membranes
questions.e: Cholesterol is the most common animal steroid and precursor for all other steroids; it is a principal component of animal cell membranes and is among the constituents of plaques in atherosclerosis.

questions.q: Bile acids such as cholic and deoxycholic acid, derived from cholesterol, function mainly as:
o: Antioxidants that prevent oxidative rancidity in stored fats
Hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle in females
Membrane anchors for polyprenyl proteins in the cell
Detergent molecules that assist absorption of dietary lipids in the intestine
questions.e: The bile acids (cholic and deoxycholic acid) are detergent molecules that assist in the absorption of dietary lipids in the intestine.

questions.q: Soaps are chemically described as:
o: Esters of cholesterol with fatty acids
Sodium and potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids
questions.e: Soaps are sodium and potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, commonly formed when acylglycerols are heated in the presence of an alkali (saponification).

questions.q: Between sodium and potassium soaps, which is described as less soluble and cheaper?
questions.e: Sodium soaps are less soluble and cheaper than potassium soaps; liquid soaps and shaving creams usually contain potassium soaps.

questions.q: Detergents are chemically described as sodium and potassium salts of long-chain:
questions.e: Detergents are sodium and potassium salts of long-chain alkyl sulphates or sulphonates, such as sodium p-dodecylbenzene sulphonate and sodium lauryl (dodecyl) sulphate.

questions.q: Both soaps and detergents are described as amphipathic molecules because they are composed of:
o: Equal amounts of protein and carbohydrate
questions.e: Detergents and soaps are amphipathic molecules composed of hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts (polar heads and hydrophobic tails).

questions.q: During the cleansing action of a detergent, what are the tiny droplets that dirt is broken into called?
questions.e: With agitation, the dirt is removed and broken into tiny droplets called micelles, in which the hydrophobic tail interacts with dirt and the polar head interacts with water.

questions.q: In a micelle formed during cleansing, where is the carboxylate head positioned?
o: Dissolved separately in the dirt phase, away from any water molecules
Attached directly to another micelle nearby within the mixture
Buried inside the dirt droplet, fully shielded from the aqueous medium
Exposed to the aqueous medium, while the hydrocarbon tail extends into the greasy dirt
questions.e: In the micelle, the carboxylate head is exposed to the aqueous medium while the hydrocarbon tail extends into the greasy dirt.

questions.q: What prevents micelles from coalescing with one another during cleansing?
o: The presence of cholesterol embedded within the micelle structure itself
Attractive covalent bonds forming between micelles
High temperature keeping the micelles apart from one another
Repulsive forces from negative charges on the head groups at the surface
questions.e: Due to negative charges on the head portion at the surface, repulsive forces prevent the micelles from coalescing.

questions.q: What overall action does soap perform on organic dirt so that it can be rinsed away?
o: It hydrolyses the dirt into glycerol
questions.e: The soap emulsifies the organic dirt to be rinsed away.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of soaps mentioned in the lecture?
o: They dissolve completely in water and leave no residue behind at all
They are too expensive to manufacture on any industrial scale at all
They precipitate in hard water containing Ca2+ and Mg2+, wasting soap and leaving deposits
They cannot form micelles at all under any water conditions whatsoever
questions.e: The main drawback of soaps is that they precipitate in hard water with Ca2+ and Mg2+; metallic ions must precipitate before any lather forms, wasting soap and forming undesirable deposits.

questions.q: Which named example is given as a detergent (an alkyl sulphonate)?
questions.e: Sodium p-dodecylbenzene sulphonate and sodium lauryl (dodecyl) sulphate are given as examples of detergents.

questions.q: Saponification, the process that produces soap, is achieved by heating acylglycerols in the presence of:
questions.e: Soaps are commonly formed when acylglycerols are heated in the presence of an alkali — this alkaline hydrolysis is called saponification.

questions.q: Rancidification is defined in the lecture as:
o: The formation of micelles in soap solutions
The esterification of glycerol with fatty acids
The chemical decomposition of fats, oils and other lipids
questions.e: Rancidification, the product of what is described as rancidity, is the chemical decomposition of fats, oils and other lipids.

questions.q: How many pathways for rancidification are recognised in the lecture?
questions.e: Three pathways for rancidification are recognised: hydrolytic rancidity, oxidative rancidity and microbial rancidity.

questions.q: Hydrolytic rancidity occurs through which chemical process?
o: Iodine is absorbed at the double bonds
Oxygen cleaves double bonds via free radicals
Bacteria synthesise new fatty acid chains
Water splits fatty acid chains away from the glycerol backbone
questions.e: Hydrolytic rancidity occurs when water splits fatty acid chains away from the glycerol backbone — the chemical term is ester hydrolysis, which usually goes unnoticed.

questions.q: Oxidative rancidity mainly affects which type of fat, and what does it release?
o: Unsaturated fats, releasing volatile aldehydes and ketones
questions.e: Through a free radical process, double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids can undergo cleavage, releasing volatile aldehydes and ketones; oxidation mainly occurs with unsaturated fats.

questions.q: Microbial rancidity is caused by microbes using which type of enzyme to break down fat?
questions.e: Microbial rancidity is a process in which microbes, like bacteria, use their enzymes (lipases) to break down fat; it can be prevented by sterilisation.

questions.q: Which pair are given as examples of natural antioxidants that delay rancidity?
questions.e: Natural antioxidants include polyphenols (flavonoids), ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and tocopherols (vitamin E).

questions.q: Which are named as synthetic antioxidants used to delay rancidity?
questions.e: Synthetic antioxidants named in the lecture are butylated hydroxyanisole and hydroxytoluene, propyl gallate and ethoxyquin.

questions.q: What storage condition is recommended to decrease (though not eliminate) rancidification?
o: A warm, sunlit place with maximum air exposure
A cool, dark place with little exposure to oxygen
questions.e: Rancidification can be decreased by storing fats and oils in a cool, dark place with little exposure to oxygen, since heat and light accelerate the reaction rate of fats with oxygen.

questions.q: The acid number of a fat or oil measures:
o: The mg of KOH required to saponify 1 g of fat completely into glycerol and soap
The mmol of oxygen taken up per kilogram of oil during storage and handling overall
The mg of KOH required to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of fat, giving a measure of rancidity
The grams of iodine absorbed by 100 grams of fat during the iodine number analysis
questions.e: The acid number is the milligrams of KOH required to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 gram of fat or oil, giving a measure of the extent of rancidity of fats.

questions.q: The iodine number of a fat or oil indicates:
o: The degree of unsaturation of the fat or oil
The freshness of the oil sample
The chain length of its fatty acids
questions.e: The iodine number is the grams of iodine absorbed by 100 grams of fat or oil; since absorbed iodine adds to double bonds, it shows the degree of unsaturation of the fat or oil.

questions.q: The thiobarbituric acid (TBA) test measures the presence of which secondary lipid peroxidation product?
questions.e: The TBA test measures the secondary lipid peroxidation product malonaldehyde, which reacts with thiobarbituric acid to give coloured products whose intensity indicates the degree of peroxidation.

questions.q: Which four elements together make up the vast majority of living matter?
questions.e: C, H, O, and N together account for roughly 96% of the mass of most living organisms.

questions.q: A trace element is best defined as one that:
o: Is required by organisms only in very small amounts
Cannot be found in the periodic table
questions.e: Trace elements such as zinc, iodine, and copper are essential but needed only in minute quantities.

questions.q: Which mineral is a key component of hemoglobin, essential for oxygen transport?
questions.e: Iron sits at the center of the heme group in hemoglobin, enabling reversible oxygen binding.

questions.q: Dehydration synthesis differs from hydrolysis in that it:
questions.e: Dehydration synthesis builds polymers by releasing a water molecule for each new bond formed; hydrolysis is the reverse.

questions.q: A functional group consisting of -COOH is called a:
questions.e: The carboxyl group (-COOH) is acidic and found in amino acids, fatty acids, and many other biomolecules.

questions.q: Magnesium commonly functions in cells as a:
questions.e: Magnesium ions are required cofactors for many enzymes involved in phosphate transfer and ATP metabolism.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes a macroelement from a trace element?
o: The quantity required by the organism
Whether the element is found in DNA
questions.e: Macroelements like carbon and oxygen are needed in large amounts; trace elements are needed in only minute amounts.

questions.q: The Miller-Urey experiment is significant because it demonstrated that:
o: Organic molecules can form from simple inorganic gases under early-Earth conditions
Life definitely began in hydrothermal vents
RNA cannot act as a catalyst
questions.e: The experiment simulated early-Earth conditions and produced amino acids from inorganic starting materials, supporting abiogenesis.

questions.q: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life relied on RNA because RNA can:
o: Both store genetic information and catalyze reactions
Only catalyze reactions, never store information
Only exist in modern eukaryotic cells
questions.e: RNA's dual capability as both an informational and catalytic molecule makes it a plausible candidate for early self-replicating systems.

questions.q: According to endosymbiotic theory, chloroplasts most likely originated from:
o: A fragment of the host cell's nucleus
questions.e: Chloroplasts share key features, such as their own circular DNA and double membranes, with free-living photosynthetic bacteria.

questions.q: Homologous structures across different species are evidence of:
questions.e: Homologous structures share an underlying anatomical or genetic origin, even when their current functions differ.

questions.q: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment is historically important because it:
o: Disproved the theory of spontaneous generation
Proved the theory of spontaneous generation
questions.e: Pasteur demonstrated that microorganisms did not arise spontaneously from sterile broth, supporting the principle of biogenesis.

questions.q: The biochemical unity of life refers to the observation that:
o: All organisms share fundamental biochemical processes and molecules
All organisms have identical DNA sequences
Only animals share a common ancestor
questions.e: Despite vast diversity, all known life shares core biochemistry: DNA/RNA, the genetic code, ATP, and similar central metabolic pathways.

questions.q: Convergent evolution describes a situation where:
o: Unrelated species independently evolve similar traits
Related species diverge into different forms
questions.e: Convergent evolution produces similar adaptations, such as wings, in lineages that are not closely related, due to similar selective pressures.

questions.q: The atomic number of an element is defined by its number of:
questions.e: Atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus and uniquely identifies each element.

questions.q: Isotopes of an element differ in their number of:
questions.e: Isotopes share the same number of protons (and thus the same element identity) but differ in neutron number, and therefore mass.

questions.q: Electronegativity is best described as a measure of:
o: An atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond
The number of electron shells an atom has
The number of neutrons in a nucleus
questions.e: Higher electronegativity means an atom pulls bonding electrons more strongly toward itself, contributing to bond polarity.

questions.q: Valence electrons are located in:
questions.e: Valence electrons occupy the outermost shell and are primarily responsible for an atom's chemical bonding behavior.

questions.q: Noble gases are chemically unreactive mainly because they:
o: Have a complete valence electron shell
questions.e: A full valence shell gives noble gases very low reactivity, since they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.

questions.q: Moving down a group on the periodic table, atomic radius generally:
o: Increases, due to additional electron shells
questions.e: Each successive period adds a new electron shell, increasing the overall size of the atom despite increasing nuclear charge.

questions.q: The Aufbau principle states that electrons:
o: Fill lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy ones
Are found only in the nucleus
questions.e: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy orbitals first, building up the electron configuration of an atom systematically.

questions.q: An ionic bond forms primarily through the:
questions.e: Ionic bonds arise when one atom donates electrons to another, producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other.

questions.q: A hydrogen bond is best described as:
o: A weak attraction between a hydrogen atom and an electronegative atom on another molecule
A strong covalent bond within a single molecule
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds, though individually weak, are critical for water's properties and for stabilizing DNA and protein structures.

questions.q: A molecule described as amphipathic contains:
questions.e: Amphipathic molecules, such as phospholipids, have a polar (hydrophilic) head and a nonpolar (hydrophobic) tail.

questions.q: The octet rule describes atoms' tendency to:
o: Achieve eight electrons in their valence shell
questions.e: Achieving a stable octet (like the noble gases) drives much of the bonding behavior observed in main-group elements.

questions.q: A nonpolar covalent bond occurs when electrons are shared:
o: Equally between two atoms of similar electronegativity
questions.e: When bonded atoms have similar electronegativities, the shared electron pair is distributed roughly evenly.

questions.q: Van der Waals forces are best described as:
o: Weak, short-range attractions between molecules or atoms
questions.e: These weak forces arise from transient shifts in electron distribution and contribute to interactions between nonpolar molecules.

questions.q: Glycosidic bonds link together which type of molecules?
questions.e: Glycosidic bonds are the covalent linkages joining sugar units in disaccharides and polysaccharides.

questions.q: Starch and glycogen both serve primarily as:
questions.e: Plants store glucose as starch, while animals store it as the more highly branched glycogen.

questions.q: Cellulose differs from starch mainly in its:
o: Type of glycosidic bond linking glucose units
questions.e: Cellulose is linked by beta-1,4-glycosidic bonds, forming straight, rigid chains, unlike starch's alpha-linked helical chains.

questions.q: A reducing sugar is one that:
o: Has a free aldehyde or ketone group able to donate electrons
Cannot be digested by the body
questions.e: Reducing sugars, detected by tests such as Benedict's, have a free carbonyl group available to reduce other compounds.

questions.q: Benedict's test is used to detect the presence of:
questions.e: A positive Benedict's test produces a color change from blue to orange/red, indicating a reducing sugar is present.

questions.q: The main structural difference between amylose and amylopectin is that amylopectin is:
o: Made of fructose, while amylose is glucose-based
questions.e: Amylopectin contains alpha-1,6 branch points in addition to alpha-1,4 linkages, unlike the linear chain of amylose.

questions.q: A nucleotide is composed of a sugar, a phosphate group, and a:
questions.e: These three components join together to form the repeating monomer unit of DNA and RNA.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine always pairs with:
questions.e: Complementary base pairing links adenine with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and guanine with cytosine (three hydrogen bonds).

questions.q: RNA differs chemically from DNA by containing which sugar and base?
o: Ribose and uracil (instead of deoxyribose and thymine)
questions.e: RNA uses ribose as its sugar and uracil in place of DNA's thymine as one of its four nitrogenous bases.

questions.q: The two strands of a DNA double helix run:
questions.e: DNA's two strands run in opposite 5' to 3' directions, an arrangement essential for correct base pairing and replication.

questions.q: Purine bases are distinguished from pyrimidines by having:
questions.e: Purines (adenine, guanine) have a fused double-ring structure, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring.

questions.q: Which type of RNA carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome?
questions.e: mRNA is transcribed from DNA and carries the coding sequence to ribosomes, where it is translated into protein.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because each new molecule:
o: Contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand
questions.e: Each daughter DNA molecule retains one parental strand, conserving half of the original genetic material in each copy.

questions.q: Amino acids are linked together in a protein chain by:
questions.e: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing water.

questions.q: The primary structure of a protein refers to its:
o: Specific linear sequence of amino acids
questions.e: Primary structure is simply the order of amino acids, which ultimately determines all higher levels of folding.

questions.q: Denaturation of a protein results in:
o: Loss of its native structure and function, without breaking peptide bonds
Complete breakdown into free amino acids
No change in the protein at all
questions.e: Heat, extreme pH, or other stresses can unfold a protein's secondary/tertiary structure while its primary sequence stays intact.

questions.q: An alpha helix and a beta sheet are both examples of protein:
questions.e: These are common local folding patterns stabilized largely by hydrogen bonds along the polypeptide backbone.

questions.q: Hemoglobin's four polypeptide subunits together exemplify:
o: A simple protein with no structure
questions.e: Quaternary structure describes how multiple separate polypeptide chains associate to form one functional protein complex.

questions.q: The Biuret test is used to detect the presence of:
questions.e: A positive Biuret test produces a violet color when peptide bonds react with copper ions in an alkaline solution.

questions.q: A disulfide bond that stabilizes tertiary protein structure forms between two:
questions.e: Disulfide bonds form when the sulfur-containing side chains of two cysteine residues become covalently linked.

questions.q: An enzyme's active site is best described as the region where:
o: The substrate binds and the reaction is catalyzed
questions.e: The active site's shape and chemistry are specifically suited to bind a particular substrate and lower the reaction's activation energy.

questions.q: Competitive inhibitors work by:
o: Binding the active site and blocking substrate access
questions.e: Because competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate, they compete for the same active site, and their effect can be reduced by raising substrate concentration.

questions.q: A coenzyme is best described as:
o: A small organic molecule that assists an enzyme's catalytic activity
A protein that never interacts with enzymes
An inhibitor that always blocks catalysis
questions.e: Coenzymes, often derived from vitamins, participate directly in the catalytic mechanism alongside the enzyme.

questions.q: Vmax in an enzyme reaction represents:
o: The maximum rate of reaction when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate
The minimum substrate concentration needed for any activity
questions.e: Once every active site is occupied, adding more substrate cannot increase the reaction rate further, defining Vmax.

questions.q: Allosteric regulation of an enzyme occurs when a molecule binds:
o: A site other than the active site, changing enzyme shape and activity
Directly and only at the active site
To a completely unrelated molecule with no effect
questions.e: Allosteric effectors bind regulatory sites and induce conformational changes that can activate or inhibit the enzyme.

questions.q: Most enzymes lose activity at extreme temperatures because they become:
questions.e: Extreme heat disrupts the weak bonds maintaining an enzyme's three-dimensional structure, destroying its catalytic ability.

questions.q: Glycolysis breaks down one molecule of glucose into two molecules of:
questions.e: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and yields two pyruvate molecules along with a small net gain of ATP and NADH.

questions.q: The electron transport chain generates the majority of a cell's ATP through:
o: Oxidative phosphorylation, driven by a proton gradient
questions.e: Electrons passed along the chain pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and ATP synthase uses this gradient to make ATP.

questions.q: Anabolic reactions are characterized by:
o: Building complex molecules from simpler ones, requiring energy input
Breaking complex molecules down and releasing energy
questions.e: Anabolism, such as protein or glycogen synthesis, consumes ATP to construct larger molecules from smaller building blocks.

questions.q: Fermentation allows glycolysis to continue in the absence of oxygen mainly by:
o: Regenerating NAD+ needed for glycolysis to proceed
Producing large amounts of ATP directly
questions.e: Fermentation pathways, such as lactic acid or alcoholic fermentation, regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen.

questions.q: Beta-oxidation is the metabolic pathway responsible for breaking down:
questions.e: Beta-oxidation sequentially removes two-carbon units from a fatty acid chain, generating acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle.

questions.q: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to:
o: Fix carbon dioxide into organic sugar
questions.e: The Calvin cycle is the carbon-fixing stage of photosynthesis, converting CO2 into glucose using energy captured earlier.

questions.q: A triglyceride is composed of glycerol bonded to:
questions.e: Ester bonds link each of the three fatty acid tails to the glycerol backbone, forming a triglyceride.

questions.q: Phospholipids are the primary structural component of:
questions.e: Their amphipathic nature allows phospholipids to spontaneously form the bilayer structure of biological membranes.

questions.q: Saturated fatty acids differ from unsaturated fatty acids in that they:
o: Are always liquid at room temperature
questions.e: The absence of double bonds allows saturated fatty acid chains to pack tightly, typically making them solid at room temperature.

questions.q: Cholesterol is classified as a lipid because it is:
o: Hydrophobic, despite its ring rather than chain structure
questions.e: Though structurally distinct from fatty-acid-based lipids, cholesterol is nonpolar and hydrophobic, qualifying it as a steroid lipid.

questions.q: Emulsification of dietary fat is important because it:
o: Increases surface area for digestive enzymes to act on fat droplets
Removes the need for bile salts
questions.e: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets, allowing lipase enzymes to access and digest them more efficiently.

questions.q: The Sudan test is used in the laboratory to detect the presence of:
questions.e: Sudan dyes selectively stain lipid droplets, producing a visible red-orange color that indicates lipids are present in a sample.

questions.q: Coenzymes which are tightly bound to their enzymes are referred to as:
questions.e: A coenzyme (or cofactor) so tightly, often covalently, bound to its enzyme that it doesn't dissociate is called a prosthetic group.

questions.q: Life is a process of sustenance. This means that life must be:
o: Capable of maintaining itself through the use of sustainable mechanisms for survival
Capable of ensuring continuity in order to prevent extinction
Able to make up for damage or loss of materials that may occur
Capable of adapting to changing conditions in order to survive and ensure continuance
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: life must be able to make up for damage or loss of materials that may occur.

questions.q: The Colonisation Theory supposes that:
o: The earth was colonised by ex-terrestrial organisms who evolved over a long period to become what they are today
Intelligent forces subdued the earth and released their spores onto it to generate life
Life reached earth in the form of living spores from elsewhere and was driven to the earth by pressure
Multiple spores arrived on earth with emerging progeny competing under the pressures of natural selection after which the most dominant species colonised the earth
questions.e: The Colonisation (Panspermia) Theory holds that living spores travelling through space reached Earth, driven here by radiation pressure, and then began to colonise the planet.

questions.q: At physiological pH, amino acids are best described as:
questions.e: At physiological pH, an amino acid's carboxyl group is deprotonated (-COO⁻) and its amino group is protonated (-NH3⁺), giving it both a positive and negative charge simultaneously — a zwitterion.

questions.q: Tertiary structure is maintained by:
questions.e: A protein's tertiary (3D folded) structure is stabilized by a combination of interactions — hydrogen bonds, disulfide linkages, and the covalent peptide backbone that holds the chain together — along with hydrophobic and ionic interactions.

questions.q: The enzyme glucose isomerase catalyses the conversion of glucose to fructose. The enzyme belongs to the EC enzyme class:
questions.e: Isomerases, which rearrange atoms within a single molecule (like converting glucose to its isomer fructose), are EC class 5.

questions.q: Which statement below best defines the “quaternary structure” of a protein?
o: The arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits in a single functional complex
The folding of a polypeptide backbone in three dimensional space
The interaction of amino acid chains
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain
questions.e: Quaternary structure describes how multiple, separately-folded polypeptide subunits come together to form one functional multi-subunit protein complex.

questions.q: Disulphide bonds are formed between:
o: Cysteine residues that are close together
Cystine residues that are closed together
Proline residues that are close together
Histidine residues that are close together
questions.e: Two cysteine residues brought close together in the folded protein can oxidize to form a covalent disulfide (S-S) bond; the resulting linked pair is what's then called cystine.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true regarding primary structure of proteins?
o: Primary structure denotes the number of amino acids in a protein
Primary structure denotes the sequence of amino acids in a protein
Primary structure determines the biological activity of a protein
questions.e: Primary structure is the linear sequence (and hence number) of amino acids in a protein, and since this sequence dictates all higher-order folding, it ultimately determines the protein's biological activity — making all three statements true.

questions.q: The amyloid protein deposition with Alzheimer's disease is composed of:
questions.e: Amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's disease are characterized by misfolded protein aggregating into cross-β pleated sheet structures.

questions.q: The first amino acid in a polypeptide chain is:
questions.e: Translation always begins at the start codon AUG, which codes for methionine, so every new polypeptide chain begins with a methionine residue (later often cleaved).

questions.q: According to Christians, Muslims and Traditionalists, life originated by:
questions.e: These religious traditions are grouped together under the doctrine of “special creation” — the view that a deity created life directly and deliberately, rather than through natural processes.

questions.q: Which of the following concepts is most plausible?
o: Proteins and nucleic acids evolved from carbohydrate condensation
Proteins and nuclei acids must have evolved in parallel
questions.e: The widely favored “RNA World” hypothesis holds that self-replicating, catalytic RNA (a nucleic acid) predates proteins, which is the most broadly accepted answer among these options.

questions.q: When a boundary or membrane is formed around catabolically active molecules, such a structure is termed:
questions.e: A protobiont is the prebiotic-chemistry term for an aggregate of organic molecules enclosed by a membrane-like boundary, capable of maintaining an internal chemical environment distinct from its surroundings.

questions.q: Condensation agents used in the formation of prebiotic polymers were advantageous because they:
o: Formed more reactive intermediates that increased the rate of reaction
Removed water molecules from the prebiotic soup thereby shifting the equilibrium towards product formation
Acted as catalysts to allow product formation in an aqueous medium
questions.e: Condensation (dehydrating) agents work by pulling water out of the reaction system, which shifts the condensation equilibrium toward polymer (product) formation even in a dilute aqueous “prebiotic soup.”

questions.q: Bacteriorhodopsin, a unique light-driven proton-pumping protein, contains which of the following derived amino acids?
questions.e: Pyroglutamic acid (formed by cyclization of glutamine/glutamate residues) is the derived amino acid most commonly cited in this context among these four options; the other three are derived amino acids associated with different specialized proteins (elastin, GABA-related signaling, and blood-clotting factors respectively).

questions.q: Corn contains an uncommon amino acid called:
questions.e: Aminoadipic acid is a non-standard amino acid found accumulated in corn (maize) seed proteins.

questions.q: Since most proteins in the body contain the full complement of amino acids, young animals fail to grow on a diet deficient in all the following amino acids EXCEPT:
questions.e: Asparagine is a non-essential amino acid that the body can synthesize itself, so a diet lacking it doesn't stunt growth; histidine, methionine and valine are all essential amino acids that must come from the diet.

questions.q: According to the Big Bang theory:
o: Hydrogen and helium were formed in the centre of the stars
All other elements apart from hydrogen and helium were formed in the centre of the stars
Accumulation of hydrogen and helium caused the collapse of a primordial ball of matter
Explosion of the stars resulted in the formation of hydrogen and helium
questions.e: Hydrogen and helium formed directly from the Big Bang itself; every heavier element was subsequently forged by nuclear fusion inside the cores of stars.
