questions.q: Californium was produced by …………… by the fusion of ……………… and ………………
questions.e: Californium is one of the transuranium elements co-discovered by Glenn Seaborg's team, produced via heavy-ion bombardment/fusion reactions of this type.

questions.q: Silicon is more abundant in the earth's crust than it is in living cells because it is:
questions.e: Silicon's stable oxide (silica/silicate minerals) is chemically inert and doesn't readily participate in the reactive, carbon-based chemistry of life, so despite its crustal abundance it's largely excluded from biological molecules.

questions.q: Some elements were not incorporated into cells because they are:
questions.e: Many heavier elements have atomic/ionic radii too large to form the compact, stable covalent bonds needed for the small, versatile biomolecules that life is built from.

questions.q: Use the following Key to answer: Used in the treatment of Schizophrenia. (Key: A. Lithium Carbonate, B. Platinum, C. Kaolin, D. Gold conjugates)
questions.e: Lithium carbonate is a psychiatric medication (mood stabilizer) used in the management of major psychiatric conditions, matching this option among the four.

questions.q: Use the following Key to answer: Employed as an anticancer agent. (Key: A. Lithium Carbonate, B. Platinum, C. Kaolin, D. Gold conjugates)
questions.e: Platinum-based compounds (e.g. cisplatin) are classic chemotherapy (anticancer) agents that work by cross-linking DNA.

questions.q: Use the following Key to answer: Used in the management of diarrhoea. (Key: A. Lithium Carbonate, B. Platinum, C. Kaolin, D. Gold conjugates)
questions.e: Kaolin (a clay mineral) is a traditional over-the-counter antidiarrheal agent, often combined with pectin.

questions.q: Si-Si bonds are rare because they are:
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: Si-Si bonds are rare because they are too big.

questions.q: Several factors enable proteins to participate in a wide range of functions EXCEPT: I. Proteins are linear polymers built of monomer units. II. Proteins contain only one functional group. III. Proteins do not occur as complexes with other biomolecules. IV. Proteins could exist as rigid and globular forms.
questions.e: Statements II and III are false — proteins actually carry many different functional groups (from their varied side chains) and frequently do form complexes with other biomolecules (nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates), so these two are the factors that do NOT enable their functional versatility.

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics best describes glycine?
questions.e: Glycine's side chain is just a single hydrogen atom, so its alpha carbon isn't a stereocenter — making glycine the only optically inactive (non-chiral) standard amino acid.

questions.q: Some proteins contain additional amino acids that arise by modification of an amino acid already present in a peptide. Examples of such modified amino acids include:
questions.e: 4-Hydroxyproline (in collagen), β-alanine (in some peptides), and GABA are all examples of non-standard amino acids produced by post-translational or metabolic modification of a standard amino acid.

questions.q: A mutation has changed an Isoleucine residue of a protein to glutamic acid. Which statement best describes its location in a hydrophilic exterior?
o: On the surface since it is hydrophilic in nature
Inside the core of the protein since it is hydrophobic in nature
Inside the core of the protein since it has a polar but charged side chain
questions.e: Glutamic acid's charged, hydrophilic side chain is energetically favored at the water-exposed surface of a globular protein, unlike the hydrophobic core.

questions.q: The highest concentration of cystine can be found in:
questions.e: Keratin (found in hair, nails and skin) is exceptionally rich in cysteine residues that form extensive disulfide (cystine) cross-links, giving it its characteristic toughness.

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids may be considered hydrophobic at physiological pH?
questions.e: Isoleucine's branched aliphatic side chain is strongly nonpolar/hydrophobic, unlike the charged (arginine, aspartic acid) or polar (threonine) side chains of the other options.

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids is a precursor for the mediation of allergies and inflammation?
questions.e: Histidine is decarboxylated to histamine, the classic mediator of allergic and inflammatory responses.

questions.q: All the following are metalloproteins EXCEPT:
questions.e: Carbonic anhydrase, xanthine oxidase and superoxide dismutase all require a bound metal cofactor; lactate dehydrogenase does not.

questions.q: The greatest buffering capacity at physiological pH would be provided by a protein rich in which of the following amino acids?
questions.e: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa near physiological pH, giving it the greatest buffering capacity of the options at that pH.

questions.q: Biotin is involved in the transfer of:
questions.e: Biotin is the coenzyme for carboxylase enzymes, carrying and transferring a single carbon unit in the form of CO2.

questions.q: Boron can form dative covalent bonds because it:
o: Bears a lone pair of electrons after bonding
questions.e: Boron has only 3 valence electrons and an empty p-orbital, which can accept a lone pair from a donor atom to form a dative (coordinate) covalent bond.

questions.q: When the initial reducing agents were exhausted, the photosynthetic machinery utilized …………… instead.
questions.e: Once early reducing agents like H2S ran out, photosynthetic organisms evolved the ability to use the far more abundant H2O as an electron donor (oxygenic photosynthesis).

questions.q: Oxygen was a minor component of the atmosphere until:
o: Photosynthetic organisms began to produce oxygen from the oxidation of water
Multiple photosynthetic cells were produced from parent cells
Photochemical splitting of water by the sun released O2 from sea water
questions.e: The rise of atmospheric oxygen (the Great Oxidation Event) is attributed to oxygenic photosynthesis, in which organisms split water and release O2 as a byproduct.

questions.q: The glucosidic linkage present in sucrose is:
questions.e: Sucrose is formed by an α1→β2 glycosidic bond between the anomeric carbons of glucose (C1, α) and fructose (C2, β).

questions.q: Of all the disaccharides, …………… is a non-reducing sugar.
questions.e: Sucrose's glycosidic bond joins both sugars' anomeric carbons, leaving no free anomeric hydroxyl to reduce — making it the classic non-reducing disaccharide.

questions.q: The principal storage carbohydrate in plants is ……………, whereas its equivalent in animals is ……………
questions.e: Plants store glucose as starch, while animals store it as the analogous branched polymer glycogen.

questions.q: Anomers are isomers which differ in the:
o: Spatial arrangement of atoms around a single carbon
Arrangement of bonds around the hemiacetal
Arrangement of -OH on the penultimate carbon
Arrangement of -OH on the carbon of interest
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: anomers differ in the arrangement of bonds around the hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon formed on ring closure.

questions.q: The reaction between an alcohol and a ketone yields a/an:
questions.e: An alcohol adding across a ketone's carbonyl produces a hemiketal (the ketone analogue of a hemiacetal, which instead forms from an alcohol and an aldehyde).

questions.q: Fructose, despite being a hexose, forms a 5-membered ring structure because the structure:
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: the furanose ring protects the anomeric carbon.

questions.q: Biological evolution refers to the:
o: Biological processes by which life evolved
Theory that unicellular organisms were the first forms of life and evolved over complex evolutionary trends to form multiple species
Formation of living matter from chemical agents
Formation of living cells from complex organic molecules
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: biological evolution refers to the formation of living cells from complex organic molecules.

questions.q: Prebiotic monosaccharides could have been formed by the …………… reaction.
questions.e: The formose reaction (formaldehyde self-condensing under basic/catalytic conditions) is the classic proposed prebiotic route to simple sugars.

questions.q: Nucleotide bases in the prebiotic atmosphere were synthesized by the polymerization of:
questions.e: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) polymerization is the classic proposed prebiotic pathway to purine and pyrimidine bases (as shown in Oro's and related experiments).

questions.q: The primitive atmosphere was said to be reducing because:
o: There was little or no oxygen present
Meteorites contained iron either as Fe or Fe2+
Carbon was present as elemental carbon
The matter from which the earth was formed was mostly hydrogen
questions.e: A “reducing” atmosphere is defined by the absence of free oxygen (which would otherwise oxidize reactive prebiotic molecules), matching this option directly.

questions.q: In animals, triacylglycerols are mostly found in the:
questions.e: Adipose (fat) tissue is the body's dedicated storage depot for triacylglycerols.

questions.q: Carbohydrates are mainly produced by plants through the process of:
questions.e: Photosynthesis is how plants fix atmospheric CO2 into carbohydrates using light energy.

questions.q: The primary energy source for the brain and nervous system is:
questions.e: The brain and nervous system rely almost exclusively on glucose for their energy needs under normal conditions.

questions.q: Starch and cellulose belong to a class of carbohydrates usually referred to as ………… carbohydrates.
questions.e: As large polysaccharides built of many linked monosaccharide units, starch and cellulose are both classified as complex carbohydrates.

questions.q: A labourer who indulges in intensive manual work may prefer complex carbohydrates for breakfast because they:
o: Are digested over a longer period and thus supply a sustained flow of energy
questions.e: Complex carbohydrates break down more slowly during digestion, releasing glucose gradually for a sustained energy supply well-suited to prolonged manual labour.

questions.q: Monosaccharides contain a single …………… unit.
questions.e: By definition, a monosaccharide (“mono” = one) is the simplest single sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller carbohydrates.

questions.q: The phosphate group of a nucleotide may either be bonded at the ……… or ……… positions.
questions.e: The phosphate of a nucleotide is esterified to the sugar's 3′ or 5′ hydroxyl carbon (the primed numbering distinguishes the sugar ring positions from the base's own numbering).

questions.q: Base stacking is possible in nucleic acids because the constituent nucleotides are:
questions.e: The flat, planar geometry of the nitrogenous bases allows adjacent bases in a nucleic acid strand to stack closely on top of one another, stabilizing the helix.

questions.q: DNA is usually associated with basic proteins such as:
questions.e: DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone is neutralized and packaged by binding to basic (positively charged) proteins, chiefly histones (in somatic cells) and protamines (in sperm).

questions.q: The basic composition of a given organism is dependent on its age, nutritional state and other environmental factors.
questions.e: An organism's biochemical composition genuinely shifts with age, diet, and environment, making this statement true.

questions.q: The increase in UV absorbance of DNA by about 40% when it is denatured is termed:
questions.e: The rise in UV absorbance seen when double-stranded DNA denatures into single strands is called the hyperchromic effect/shift.

questions.q: An enzyme is said to be saturated when:
o: Its rate is proportional to the concentration of substrate
Its rate increases only slightly when substrate concentration is increased
It cannot dissolve any more substrate at a particular temperature
The rate of catalysis becomes independent of substrate concentration
questions.e: At saturation, all enzyme active sites are occupied, so the reaction rate plateaus (Vmax) and becomes independent of further increases in substrate concentration.

questions.q: Consumption of raw egg can lead to a deficiency in:
questions.e: Raw egg white contains avidin, which tightly binds biotin and prevents its absorption, causing a biotin deficiency.

questions.q: Pernicious anaemia can result from a deficiency in vitamin:
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia is the classic disease of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, typically due to lack of intrinsic factor for its absorption.

questions.q: NAD(H) is usually involved in …………… reactions while NADP(H) is involved in …………… reactions.
questions.e: NAD+/NADH mainly shuttles electrons in catabolic (energy-releasing) pathways, while NADPH is the reducing power used in anabolic (biosynthetic) pathways.

questions.q: Proper functioning of the enzyme glucokinase is dependent on the presence of …………… ions.
questions.e: Like most kinases, glucokinase requires Mg2+ to coordinate the ATP phosphate groups during phosphoryl transfer.

questions.q: Which of the following vitamins is critical for the hydroxylation of proline and hence collagen formation?
questions.e: Vitamin C is a required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, the enzyme that hydroxylates proline residues during collagen synthesis.

questions.q: Vitamin E typically functions as an:
questions.e: Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membrane lipids from oxidative damage.

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids is most compatible with an α-helix?
questions.e: Leucine's simple, unbranched-at-Cβ side chain fits well within the α-helix geometry, unlike bulky Trp or helix-breaking Proline.

questions.q: In scurvy, which amino acid that is normally part of collagen is not synthesized?
questions.e: Vitamin C is a required cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase, which produces hydroxyproline in collagen; without it (scurvy), hydroxyproline synthesis fails and collagen becomes structurally weak.

questions.q: On the basis of functional groups, monosaccharides are either ……… or …………
questions.e: Monosaccharides are classified by their carbonyl functional group as either aldoses (containing an aldehyde) or ketoses (containing a ketone).

questions.q: Fructose is a:
questions.e: Fructose carries a ketone carbonyl group along with multiple hydroxyls, making it a polyhydroxyketone.

questions.q: The 3-C aldehyde sugar is known as a/an:
questions.e: A 3-carbon sugar bearing an aldehyde group is named an aldotriose (e.g. glyceraldehyde).

questions.q: The amino acids are carried to the ribosome for incorporation into the growing peptide chain by:
questions.e: Transfer RNA (tRNA) is the adaptor molecule that ferries specific amino acids to the ribosome, matching each to its corresponding mRNA codon.

questions.q: Pre-mRNA is processed by:
questions.e: Small nuclear RNA (snRNA), as part of the spliceosome, processes pre-mRNA by removing introns and joining exons.

questions.q: All the following are nucleotide analogs EXCEPT:
questions.e: “5-Methylthymine” isn't a therapeutic analog at all — thymine is already the natural 5-methyl derivative of uracil, whereas the other three are genuine synthetic nucleotide-analog drugs.

questions.q: Nucleotides and nucleic acids play all the following metabolic roles EXCEPT that they:
o: Can supply energy to drive metabolic reactions
questions.e: Nucleotides/nucleic acids do act as catalysts (ribozymes), coenzymes (e.g. NAD+, FAD, CoA), and energy carriers (ATP) — but protein synthesis itself is catalyzed by the ribosome's rRNA-based peptidyl transferase machinery, not by nucleotides directly in the way the other roles describe.

questions.q: Nucleosides differ from nucleotides in that they lack a:
questions.e: A nucleoside is simply a base attached to a sugar; adding a phosphate group converts it into a nucleotide.

questions.q: Respiration was one of the metabolic pathways developed to:
o: Ensure efficient use of primary metabolites
Generate ATP to drive other metabolic reactions
Use up excess oxygen to circumvent oxidative damage
Generate CO2 to balance the amount of oxygen
questions.e: Cellular respiration's central purpose is to generate ATP, the energy currency that powers the cell's other metabolic reactions.

questions.q: The naturally occurring isomer of amino acids in proteins is/are:
questions.e: With rare bacterial exceptions, the amino acids incorporated into proteins by ribosomal translation are exclusively the L-isomer.

questions.q: All these amino acids exhibit significant UV absorption above 250 nm EXCEPT:
questions.e: The three aromatic amino acids (Trp, Tyr, Phe) absorb UV light strongly due to their ring systems; arginine has no aromatic ring and doesn't show this absorption.

questions.q: In the peptide bond formation, the carbonyl oxygen and the amide hydrogen are in ………………… configuration.
questions.e: The peptide bond's partial double-bond character locks it in a planar arrangement, and the carbonyl O and amide H are almost always oriented trans to one another.

questions.q: A peptide bond is:
o: Rigid with partial double bond character
questions.e: The peptide bond is a covalent linkage that, due to resonance with the adjacent carbonyl, has partial double-bond character, making it both rigid and planar — all three descriptions are correct.

questions.q: Even-number elements are far more abundant than odd-numbered elements because:
o: They are formed from mainstream reactions
Their nuclei are more stable when formed
Their mechanisms of formation are simple
They are evolutionarily selected for incorporation into cells
questions.e: Nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons tend to be more tightly bound and stable (the Oddo-Harkins rule), which is why even-numbered elements are cosmically more abundant.

questions.q: Laboratory synthesis has been employed in the formation of:
questions.e: Elements beyond uranium on the periodic table (transuranium elements) don't occur naturally in appreciable quantities and have all been created through laboratory nuclear synthesis.

questions.q: Which of the following is not found in the fluids that bathe the cells?
questions.e: Tin is not one of the trace elements normally present in extracellular/interstitial fluid, unlike nickel, copper, and silicon which do occur in trace amounts.

questions.q: Nucleic acids absorb UV light maximally at ………… nm.
questions.e: The purine/pyrimidine bases of nucleic acids give DNA and RNA their characteristic UV absorption maximum at 260 nm, which is the standard wavelength used to quantify nucleic acid concentration.

questions.q: Nucleic acids have a high negative charge due to the presence of:
questions.e: Each nucleotide's phosphate group ionizes to carry a negative charge, and the repeating phosphodiester backbone is what gives nucleic acids their overall strong negative charge.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a form of vitamin K?
questions.e: Phylloquinone (K1), menaquinone (K2), and menadione (K3, a synthetic precursor) are the recognized forms of vitamin K; “phyllodione” is not a real vitamin K form.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a form of vitamin B6?
questions.e: Pyridoxal, pyridoxine, and pyridoxamine are the three genuine vitamin B6 vitamers; “pyridoxone” is not a real form.

questions.q: The coenzyme THF catalyses the transfer of 1-carbon components. It does this using the ………… positions.
questions.e: Tetrahydrofolate (THF) carries and transfers one-carbon units attached at its N5 and/or N10 nitrogen positions.

questions.q: Which of the following do you think is most critical for the function of transaminases?
questions.e: Transaminase (aminotransferase) enzymes absolutely require pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) as their coenzyme to shuttle amino groups.

questions.q: Coenzyme A is usually involved in:
o: Group transfer to or from amino acids
questions.e: Coenzyme A's reactive thiol group forms high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups (like acetyl-CoA), making acyl group transfer its defining role.

questions.q: Most of the major elements:
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: most of the major elements are found in the p-block.

questions.q: All the following are reasons why carbon is uniquely suited for incorporation into living cells EXCEPT:
o: It has the power of catenation
It forms multiple bonds with itself and other elements
questions.e: Tetravalency, the ability to form long self-linked (catenated) chains, and the capacity for multiple (double/triple) bonds are the three classic textbook reasons for carbon's biochemical versatility; “ideal size” on its own isn't typically cited as a distinct, separate reason.

questions.q: The specific site on the enzyme where substrates bind and catalysis occurs is known as the:
questions.e: The active site is the specific pocket on an enzyme where substrate binding and the catalytic chemistry both take place.

questions.q: One international unit, as defined by the International Commission on Enzymes, is:
o: The amount of enzyme that catalyses the formation of one micromole of product in one minute
The amount of enzyme that catalyses the conversion of one mole of substrate to product in one second
The amount of enzyme that catalyses the formation of one micromole of product in one second
The amount of enzyme that catalyses the formation of one mole of product in one minute
questions.e: One international unit (IU) of enzyme activity is formally defined as the amount that converts one micromole of substrate to product per minute under standard conditions.

questions.q: The analogy that an enzyme is specific for only one substrate is best explained by the ………… hypothesis.
questions.e: The classic “lock and key” model is the analogy used to explain an enzyme's strict, rigid specificity for one particular substrate shape.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a proenzyme?
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: proelastase is not a proenzyme in this list (trypsinogen, pepsinogen and fibrinogen are the zymogens/precursors).

questions.q: A mother of a malnourished child has been instructed to include a complete protein in the diet of the child. Which of the following should be recommended?
questions.e: Milk is a complete protein source, containing all essential amino acids in adequate amounts, unlike plant sources like pulses and wheat which are typically limiting in one or more essential amino acids.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a fibrous protein?
questions.e: Carbonic anhydrase is a compact, globular enzyme, unlike collagen, fibrinogen, and keratin, which are all elongated, structural fibrous proteins.

questions.q: Lowering pH to about 3 or increasing it to about 12 can cause DNA to denature due to:
o: Disruption of the sugar phosphate backbone
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: disruption of the sugar phosphate backbone.

questions.q: Thymine is also referred to as:
questions.e: Thymine is structurally identical to uracil except for a methyl group at the 5-position, so it is chemically known as 5-methyluracil.

questions.q: The stability of nucleic acids is attributable to:
o: Extensive hydrogen bonding and base stacking
questions.e: Nucleic acid double-helix stability comes from the combined contribution of hydrogen bonding between complementary bases AND the stacking interactions between adjacent stacked base pairs.

questions.q: Sequence specific proteins usually interact with DNA at the:
questions.e: The major groove of the DNA double helix exposes more distinguishing chemical information about the base sequence, which is where sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins (like transcription factors) typically make contact.

questions.q: The forms of DNA are: I. A II. B III. C IV. D
questions.e: A-DNA and B-DNA are the two principal, well-established right-handed helical conformations of DNA (alongside the distinct left-handed Z-DNA); “C” and “D” forms are not standard recognized forms.

questions.q: Membrane proteins serve all of the following functions EXCEPT:
questions.e: Signal transduction, enzyme catalysis, and transport are all classic, well-established membrane protein functions; cell sorting is primarily mediated by vesicular trafficking signals rather than being a core membrane-protein function in this list.

questions.q: The various blood groups in the ABO system differ from each other by virtue of the membrane …………… they possess.
questions.e: ABO blood type is determined by the specific carbohydrate (sugar) antigens attached to glycoproteins/glycolipids on the red blood cell surface.

questions.q: All the following are characteristics of membrane transporters EXCEPT they:
o: Facilitate the movement of molecules through the membrane at a very fast rate
Always transport molecules along a concentration gradient
Have a high degree of structural and stereospecificity
questions.e: Many membrane transporters (active transporters/pumps) move molecules AGAINST their concentration gradient using energy, so “always along a concentration gradient” is false; the other three properties are general hallmarks of transporters.

questions.q: In flavin coenzymes, the chemically functional part is the ………… ring.
questions.e: The isoalloxazine ring system of FAD/FMN is the redox-active part of the flavin coenzyme that actually accepts and donates electrons.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a component of folic acid?
questions.e: Folic acid (folate) is built from a pterin ring, PABA, and one or more glutamate residues; aspartate is not part of its structure.

questions.q: Catalytic power is defined as:
o: The ratio of the catalysed to the uncatalysed rate of reaction
The tendency for a catalysed reaction to proceed
The amount of catalyst present in a catalysed reaction
The alternative reaction path provided by the catalyst
questions.e: Catalytic power quantifies how much faster a reaction proceeds with the catalyst compared to without it — the ratio of catalysed to uncatalysed rate.

questions.q: A prosthetic group of a protein is a non-protein structure that is:
o: A part of the secondary structure of the protein
questions.e: Unlike a transient ligand or substrate, a prosthetic group is a non-protein component that is permanently (tightly/covalently) bound to its protein.

questions.q: Protein purification refers to:
o: Separation of proteins from other biomolecules
Separation of particular proteins from other contaminants
questions.e: Protein purification broadly covers isolating proteins from other biomolecules and from other contaminating proteins alike — all of the listed descriptions apply.

questions.q: In which of the following separation methods are proteins separated on the basis of their net charge?
questions.e: Ion exchange chromatography separates proteins according to their net surface charge, which determines their binding to the charged resin.

questions.q: Galactose is an epimer of glucose with respect to carbon:
questions.e: Galactose and glucose differ only in the configuration at carbon 4, making them C-4 epimers.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct? I. Lactose is a component of galactose. II. Galactose is a component of lactose. III. Lactose is also called milk sugar. IV. Galactose is also called milk sugar.
questions.e: Lactose (milk sugar) is built from galactose + glucose, so galactose is a component of lactose (II) and lactose is indeed called milk sugar (III).

questions.q: DNA, the molecule that contains the genetic information of the cell, contains:
questions.e: DNA's sugar is 2-deoxyribose — ribose lacking the 2′-hydroxyl group.

questions.q: The disaccharide maltose is produced by the combination of:
o: An α-D-glucose and either α- or β-D-glucose
A β-D-glucose and either α- or β-D-glucose
questions.e: Maltose is formed from an α-D-glucose (donating its anomeric carbon in an α1→4 bond) linked to a second glucose that may end up as either the α or β anomer at its own free anomeric carbon.

questions.q: The disaccharide linkage in amylose is:
questions.e: Amylose is a linear glucose polymer linked entirely by α(1→4) glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: A class of lipid that exerts a hormone-like effect are:
questions.e: Prostaglandins are the classic lipid signalling molecules that act locally with hormone-like effects.

questions.q: Chemical evolution refers to the:
o: Chemical processes by which life evolved
Theory that compounds were formed from pre-biotic elements
Formation of complex organic molecules from simple molecules
Formation of living cells from complex organic molecules
questions.e: Chemical evolution describes the prebiotic build-up of complex organic molecules (monomers, then polymers) from simpler starting molecules, prior to the origin of life itself.

questions.q: In the Strecker synthesis:
o: Ammonia reacts with an aldehyde to form an imine
Ammonia reacts with an aldehyde to form an imide
Ammonia reacts with a ketone to form an imine
Ammonia reacts with a carbonyl to form an imide
questions.e: The Strecker synthesis begins with ammonia condensing with an aldehyde to form an imine, which subsequently reacts with cyanide en route to an amino acid.

questions.q: A dipeptide has:
questions.e: Joining two amino acids requires exactly one peptide bond, forming a dipeptide.

questions.q: Myoglobin is a protein with: I. Primary structure II. Secondary structure III. Tertiary structure IV. Quaternary structure
questions.e: As a single polypeptide chain, myoglobin has primary, secondary and tertiary structure, but no quaternary structure (which requires multiple subunits).

questions.q: Fibrous proteins like silk fibroin consist of polypeptide chains arranged in:
questions.e: Silk fibroin is a classic example of a fibrous protein built from stacked β-pleated sheets.

questions.q: All the following are α-amino acids EXCEPT:
questions.e: Proline is an imino acid (its amino group is secondary, forming a ring with its own side chain), not a standard primary α-amino acid like the other three.

questions.q: Aspartic and glutamic acids have a net negative charge at physiological pH and serve several functions including: I. Binding to metal ions for structural and functional purposes. II. Acting as electrophiles in certain enzymes. III. Participating in electrostatic bonding interactions.
questions.e: Negatively charged carboxylate side chains readily coordinate metal cations and form electrostatic (ionic) interactions (statements I and III); being electron-rich, they act as nucleophiles in catalysis rather than electrophiles, making statement II false.

questions.q: The functional groups of histidine and arginine are referred to as:
questions.e: Histidine's side chain is an imidazole (protonated to imidazolium), while arginine's side chain is a guanidino group (protonated to guanidinium).

questions.q: Fusion reactions were possible because:
o: Matter from the primordial ball could combine at high temperatures
Gravitational forces drew atomic nuclei together to form other atoms
High temperatures caused the elements formed after the Big Bang to fuse forming other elements
Head-on collisions between atoms forced them to combine
questions.e: The extreme temperatures inside stellar cores (generated after the Big Bang's initial light elements formed) provide the energy needed to overcome nuclear repulsion and fuse nuclei into heavier elements.

questions.q: Explosion of stars occurs:
o: As energy released by fusion reactions gets too high
Due to repulsive forces between the positively charged nuclei in their centres
When the atomic nuclei contained in their centres collapsed
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: explosion occurs as energy released by fusion reactions gets too high.

questions.q: The source of the light emitted by stars is:
o: From the burning of hydrogen to form helium
Burning of numerous gases in their centres
Conservation as heat is converted to light energy
questions.e: Stars shine because nuclear fusion, chiefly the fusion of hydrogen into helium, releases enormous energy that is emitted as light.

questions.q: Two enantiomers which are identical to one another in all other chemical and physical properties will rotate plane polarized light:
o: To different degrees but in the same direction
To the same degree but in opposite directions
questions.e: Correction (verified against a second source of this same question, a clean typed 100-question midsem paper): enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarized light by the exact same magnitude but in opposite directions — this is the defining optical property distinguishing a pair of enantiomers. The originally-recorded answer (from the earlier marked-answer-key scan) was corrected here.

questions.q: A triacylglycerol is said to be simple if it contains:
o: The same fatty acid esterified at all three positions
questions.e: A “simple” triacylglycerol has the identical fatty acid esterified at all three glycerol positions; a “mixed” triacylglycerol carries two or more different fatty acids.

questions.q: The presence of free fatty acids in the bloodstream may be indicative of:
questions.e: Elevated circulating free fatty acids are a recognized marker associated with fatty liver disease (hepatic steatosis), among other metabolic disturbances.

questions.q: Linoleic and γ-linolenic acids are examples of …………… fatty acids.
questions.e: Linoleic and γ-linolenic acid are polyunsaturated fatty acids the body cannot synthesize itself, so they must be obtained from the diet — classifying them as essential fatty acids.

questions.q: Tuberculostearic acid escapes enzymatic degradation in man because it:
o: Cannot pass through the plasma membrane
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: it escapes degradation because it is modified.

questions.q: Cellulose is effective as a structural polysaccharide because it:
o: Can absorb a lot of water
questions.e: Cellulose's linear β(1→4)-linked glucose chains pack together with extensive interchain hydrogen bonding, forming the rigid, strong microfibrils that give plant cell walls their structural strength.

questions.q: Levorotatory sugars are designated as:
questions.e: A sugar's rotation of plane-polarized light to the left (levorotatory) is denoted with a minus sign (-), which is distinct from the unrelated D/L configurational labeling.

questions.q: Glycine and proline are the most abundant modifiable amino acids in the structure of:
questions.e: Collagen's characteristic repeating Gly-X-Y sequence is rich in glycine and proline (much of the latter modified to hydroxyproline).

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids carries a net positive charge at physiological pH?
questions.e: Valine, leucine and isoleucine are all nonpolar, uncharged branched-chain amino acids; none of them carries a charge at physiological pH.

questions.q: The 3D structure of a protein can be determined by:
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: X-ray crystallography.

questions.q: D-amino acids occur naturally in small amounts in:
questions.e: Bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan is one of the few places D-amino acids (like D-alanine and D-glutamate) occur naturally, helping protect it from host proteases.

questions.q: Maltose is a reducing sugar because:
o: It has a free hemiacetal hydroxyl group
It is a strong reducing agent
It reacts with Benedict's and Fehling's reagents
It reduces the sweetness of substances to which it is added
questions.e: Maltose retains one free anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon that can open to expose a reactive aldehyde group, which is what makes a sugar a “reducing sugar.”

questions.q: Lactose is produced via a/an:
o: α(1→4) glycosidic linkage between α-D-galactose and β-D-glucose
α(1→4) glycosidic linkage between β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose
β(1→4) glycosidic linkage between α-D-galactose and either α-D-glucose or β-D-glucose
β(1→4) glycosidic linkage between β-D-galactose and either α-D-glucose or β-D-glucose
questions.e: Lactose is galactose linked β(1→4) to glucose; since glucose's own anomeric carbon is left free, it can exist as either the α or β anomer.

questions.q: Infants who lack the enzyme for metabolizing galactose suffer from:
questions.e: A deficiency in galactose-metabolizing enzymes (e.g. GALT) causes galactose and its metabolites to accumulate, a condition called galactosemia.

questions.q: Lactose intolerance is common in adults who lack the enzyme:
questions.e: Lactase is the enzyme that breaks lactose down into glucose and galactose; its decline in adulthood causes lactose intolerance.

questions.q: The transport sugar in plants is ……………, whereas its equivalent in animals is ……………
questions.e: Plants transport sugar through the phloem mainly as sucrose, while animals circulate sugar in the bloodstream mainly as glucose.

questions.q: Starch is said to be heterogeneous because:
o: It is made up of different sugars
Depending on its source, its ratio of amylose to amylopectin may differ
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: starch is heterogeneous because it contains two different polymers (amylose and amylopectin).

questions.q: The earth is ideal for the sustenance of life because it has:
o: Water, oxygen gas and solar energy (heat)
The ozone layer, suitable temperature and air
questions.e: Liquid water, an oxygen-containing atmosphere, and solar energy input are the fundamental physical/chemical conditions that make Earth suitable for supporting life.

questions.q: The Colonisation Theory is also called the Theory of:
questions.e: The Colonisation Theory of life's origin is more widely known by its formal name, Panspermia.

questions.q: Spontaneous generation theory asserts that life:
o: Arose when elements and matter released from the Big Bang spontaneously aggregated to generate living things
Was generated over time but cannot be observed without a microscope
questions.e: This (now-discredited) theory held that living things could spontaneously assemble directly from non-living matter and energy released after the Big Bang, without any biological parent.

questions.q: Long term spontaneous generation suggests that:
o: Raw materials present on the primitive earth were used to synthesize monomers and macromolecules for living things
Electrical charges coupled with sunlight spontaneously energized prebiotic matter to form living things over time during the course of evolution
The first few cells to be formed were brought to the earth by meteorites
Oxygen gas was evolved after the development of photosynthesis after which evolution gave rise to multiple species
questions.e: The “long-term” (chemical evolution) version of spontaneous generation envisions raw prebiotic chemicals gradually being built up, step by step, into the monomers and macromolecules needed for life.

questions.q: Gangliosides are formed when:
o: A neutral sugar residue is bound to a ceramide
A charged sugar residue is bound to a ceramide
Two neutral sugar residues are bound to a cerebroside
Three or more charged sugar residues are bound to a ceramide
questions.e: Per the source's marked answer key: three or more charged sugar residues are bound to a ceramide.

questions.q: On a per gram basis, the greatest amount of energy is obtained from oxidation of:
questions.e: Fats/lipids yield roughly 9 kcal per gram on oxidation, nearly double the ~4 kcal/g yielded by carbohydrates or proteins, making them the most energy-dense macronutrient.

questions.q: Fatty acids are …………… molecules.
questions.e: A fatty acid has both a polar carboxylic acid head group and a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail, making it amphipathic.

questions.q: The phenylthiohydantoin, a product of Edman's reagent, is derived from:
questions.e: Edman degradation sequentially cleaves and labels the N-terminal amino acid residue of a peptide as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) derivative, allowing stepwise sequencing from the N-terminus.

questions.q: Carboxypeptidase A works well in hydrolysing the C-terminal peptide bond of all residues EXCEPT:
questions.e: Carboxypeptidase A cleaves C-terminal residues with neutral or aromatic side chains but does not act efficiently on basic residues like arginine (or lysine) at the C-terminus.

questions.q: Carboxypeptidase C and Y can act on any C-terminal residue.
questions.e: Unlike the more selective carboxypeptidase A and B, carboxypeptidases C and Y have broader specificity and can cleave essentially any C-terminal residue.

questions.q: Trypsin is specific in hydrolysing only peptide bonds in which the carbonyl function is contributed by:
questions.e: Trypsin cleaves peptide bonds specifically on the carboxyl (carbonyl) side of the basic residues lysine and arginine.

questions.q: Triacylglycerols consist of glycerol esterified to:
questions.e: A triacylglycerol is glycerol with each of its three hydroxyl groups esterified to a fatty acid.

questions.q: Atoms larger than the largest atom that can be formed from nuclear fusion reactions result when the latter captures ……………… resulting from the explosion of a star.
questions.e: Elements heavier than iron are built via neutron-capture processes (the s-process and r-process) during and after a supernova explosion, not by direct fusion.

questions.q: The largest atom that can be formed from a nuclei fusion reaction is:
questions.e: Fusion releases energy only up to iron (Fe-56), the most tightly bound nucleus; fusing elements beyond iron would require energy input rather than releasing it, so iron marks the limit of energy-releasing stellar fusion.

questions.q: A single atom of C-12 is most likely formed from a fusion between:
questions.e: Carbon-12 is produced in stars via the triple-alpha process, in which three helium-4 nuclei fuse together.

questions.q: When stars begin to collapse:
o: Helium nuclei fuse to form beryllium
questions.e: As a star's core contracts and heats further after exhausting hydrogen, helium nuclei begin fusing together (initially forming unstable beryllium-8) as the next stage of stellar nucleosynthesis.

questions.q: Choose the correct category of milk protein, casein, out of the following.
questions.e: Casein is classified as a phosphoprotein because it carries multiple phosphate groups esterified to serine residues.

questions.q: Which of the following amino acids in myoglobin, a globular protein, is highly likely to be localised within the interior of the molecule?
questions.e: Valine's nonpolar, hydrophobic side chain favors burial within the hydrophobic core of a globular protein like myoglobin, unlike the charged, surface-favoring arginine, aspartic acid, and lysine.

questions.q: …………… attraction between oppositely charged ions constitutes an ionic bond.
questions.e: An ionic bond is defined by electrostatic (Coulombic) attraction between oppositely charged ions.

questions.q: The process of coacervation was employed in the synthesis of:
questions.e: Oparin's coacervate droplets — membrane-less aggregates of macromolecules held together electrostatically — are the classic model proposed for early protobionts.

questions.q: The ozone layer developed:
o: When O2 from the Big Bang condensed
Immediately after O2 generation pathways were developed
When the primitive earth lost its reductive potential
questions.e: Ozone (O3) forms from O2 via UV-driven photochemistry, so an ozone layer could only build up once atmospheric O2 (from oxygenic photosynthesis) had become abundant.

questions.q: A sugar is said to be dextrorotatory when it:
o: Has OH to the left of the penultimate carbon
Has OH to the right of the penultimate carbon
Rotates plane-polarized light to the left
Rotates plane-polarized light to the right
questions.e: Dextrorotatory (+) describes a compound that rotates plane-polarized light clockwise, i.e. to the right; this is independent of the unrelated D/L configurational (penultimate-carbon) labeling.

questions.q: Stereoisomers are usually described as being:
questions.e: Stereoisomers share the same molecular formula and atom connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement, making them non-superimposable on one another.

questions.q: Cellulose cannot be degraded by human enzymes because it contains:
questions.e: Humans lack an enzyme (cellulase) able to hydrolyse the β(1→4) glycosidic linkages joining cellulose's glucose units, unlike the α(1→4) linkages in starch.

questions.q: Glycogen differs from amylopectin by having:
questions.e: Glycogen branches roughly every 8-12 glucose residues, more frequently (and so more shortly) than amylopectin's branches every 24-30 residues.

questions.q: The glycosidic linkage(s) in amylopectin is/are:
questions.e: Amylopectin's main chains are linked α(1→4), with branch points introduced by α(1→6) linkages.

questions.q: The inert nature of Si-O bonds is attributable to their:
questions.e: The Si-O bond is unusually strong (among the strongest single bonds), which makes silicate structures chemically inert and resistant to reaction.

questions.q: How many bonding and non-bonding electron pairs are found in the PCl3 molecule?
questions.e: Phosphorus in PCl3 forms 3 bonding pairs (to the 3 chlorines) and retains 1 lone (non-bonding) pair, consistent with its trigonal pyramidal shape.

questions.q: Louis de Broglie suggested that an electron has:
questions.e: De Broglie's hypothesis (λ = h/p) relates a particle's wavelength to its momentum, proposing wave-particle duality for the electron.

questions.q: Life is a process which is capable of self-sustenance, replication and ……………
questions.e: The commonly used minimal definition of life (echoed in NASA's working definition) is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of self-sustenance, replication, and evolution — mutation being the driver of that evolutionary capacity.

questions.q: The following scientists are proponents of spontaneous generation, except……………
questions.e: Francesco Redi's classic meat-and-maggots experiment was designed to disprove spontaneous generation, unlike Van Helmont and Needham, who were historically proponents of it.

questions.q: Molecules present in the primitive atmosphere included……………
questions.e: The classic Miller-Urey model of the primitive atmosphere included hydrogen, methane, ammonia and water vapor; of the options given, hydrogen, methane and water is the closest match.

questions.q: The following are evidence of panspermia, except……………
o: Bacteria can survive in harsh environments
Maggot able to grow on meat
questions.e: Maggots growing on meat is the classic observation behind spontaneous generation (later disproved by Redi), not evidence cited in support of panspermia.

questions.q: Which of these hydrogen halides has the most negligible Van der Waals forces of attraction?
questions.e: Van der Waals (London dispersion) forces grow with molecular size/polarizability. HF is the smallest, least polarizable of these hydrogen halides, giving it the weakest dispersion (Van der Waals) contribution, even though its overall intermolecular attraction is boosted separately by hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Which sugar is linked by an α(1-2)-glycosidic bond?
questions.e: Sucrose's glycosidic bond joins C1 of glucose (α) to C2 of fructose, commonly described as an α(1→2) type linkage.

questions.q: What is the formula of the compound formed between aluminium and oxygen?
questions.e: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ combine in a 2:3 ratio to balance charge, giving aluminium oxide, Al2O3.

questions.q: The molecular formula for glucose is C6H12O6. What would be the molecular formula for a polymer that links five glucose molecules together by dehydration synthesis?
questions.e: Five glucose units (5×C6H12O6 = C30H60O30) joined by 4 dehydration (condensation) bonds lose 4 H2O molecules (−8H, −4O), giving C30H52O26.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds has an expanded octet?
questions.e: Phosphorus in PCl5 forms 5 bonds, requiring 10 electrons around it — an expanded octet only possible for elements beyond period 2.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of atoms would form a non-polar covalent bond?
questions.e: Two identical atoms (Cl-Cl) share their bonding electrons perfectly equally, with zero electronegativity difference, forming a non-polar covalent bond.

questions.q: Which of the following elements has valence electrons in the n = 4 shell?
questions.e: Potassium's electron configuration is [Ar]4s¹ — its single valence electron sits in the n = 4 shell, unlike carbon, fluorine and aluminium, whose valence electrons are all in n = 2 or n = 3.

questions.q: The following factors affect ionic bond formation, except……………
questions.e: Ionic bonding is favoured by a HIGH lattice energy (the energy released on forming the ionic solid), so a low lattice energy works against ionic bond formation rather than favouring it.

questions.q: Select the correct electronic configuration from the list below.
questions.e: (Ne)3s² correctly builds on the neon core to give magnesium's ground-state configuration. The others are invalid: an Ar core already includes 3s, and writing 3d electrons directly on an Ar or Ne core (skipping 3p, and skipping the preferred half-filled 3d⁵4s¹ configuration of chromium) does not represent a real ground-state atom.

questions.q: The following are reducing sugars, except……………
questions.e: Sucrose's glycosidic bond joins both sugars' anomeric carbons, leaving no free anomeric hydroxyl to reduce — the classic non-reducing disaccharide, unlike lactose, arabinose and cellobiose.

questions.q: The ionization energy of an element would be affected by all the following except:
questions.e: Penetration, shielding and atomic radius all directly govern the effective nuclear charge felt by an electron and hence ionization energy; electron affinity is a separate periodic property, not itself a cause of ionization energy.

questions.q: Pick the odd one out of this list.
questions.e: Hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen are all gases at room temperature; mercury is the odd one out, being a liquid metal at room temperature.

questions.q: The ability of carbohydrates to function as markers that distinguish one cell from another is because……………
o: The diversity of the molecules and their location on the cell's surface
The uniformity of the molecules and their location on the cell's surface
They can interact with other macromolecules
questions.e: Cell-surface carbohydrates (as in the glycocalyx) act as identity markers precisely because of how diverse their structures are and because they are displayed on the outer cell surface, where they can be recognized by other cells.

questions.q: The symmetrical or unsymmetrical nature of a molecule can give an idea about the …………… of a molecule.
questions.e: A molecule's overall symmetry (its 3D shape) reflects the hybridization state of its central atom(s) — e.g. a symmetric tetrahedral shape points to sp³ hybridization.

questions.q: Which of the following substances is considered to be optically inactive?
questions.e: Chloroform (CHCl3) has no stereocentre and is achiral, unlike glucose, fructose and lactic acid, which are all chiral and optically active.

questions.q: Which of the following sugars is a component of malt sugar?
questions.e: Malt sugar (maltose) is built from two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) glycosidic bond.

questions.q: The storage carbohydrate in muscle is……………
questions.e: Muscle (like liver) stores glucose as glycogen, the branched storage polysaccharide of animals.

questions.q: Which of the compounds has the highest repulsion in valence electron pairs?
questions.e: Lone pair-lone pair repulsion is the strongest type of electron-pair repulsion in VSEPR theory. Of these, H2O has the most lone pairs (2), giving it the greatest overall electron-pair repulsion (reflected in its most-compressed bond angle, 104.5°).

questions.q: Glycogen……………
questions.e: Glycogen is stored chiefly in the liver (and muscle); it is a branched homopolysaccharide of glucose linked by α, not β, bonds.

questions.q: Which compound has two hybridised and two unhybridised orbitals present in its formation?
questions.e: Each carbon in ethyne (acetylene) is sp-hybridized, using 2 hybrid (sp) orbitals for its sigma bonds while keeping 2 unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

questions.q: What is the respective maximum number of electrons in the first four shells?
questions.e: The maximum electron capacity of shell n is 2n²: 2, 8, 18, and 32 for n = 1 through 4 respectively.

questions.q: Element X has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 6, and element Y has the configuration 2, 8, 3. The formula of the covalent compound that would be formed when they combine is……………
questions.e: X (configuration 2,8,6, e.g. sulfur) has a combining valence of 2; Y (configuration 2,8,3, e.g. aluminium) has a combining valence of 3. Cross-multiplying valences gives the formula Y2X3.

questions.q: Which atom has the strongest attraction for a new electron?
questions.e: Chlorine has the highest electron affinity of any element — even slightly higher than fluorine's, since fluorine's very small 2p orbital suffers extra electron-electron repulsion that partly offsets its high nuclear charge.

questions.q: Which of these glycosaminoglycans is an essential component of cartilage?
questions.e: Chondroitin sulfate is the major glycosaminoglycan of cartilage, providing much of its compressive strength.

questions.q: Which of these scientists disproved the Spontaneous generation theory posited by Aristotle?
questions.e: Francesco Redi's controlled meat-and-maggots experiment (excluding flies with gauze) was the classic demonstration that disproved spontaneous generation.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not true?
o: Valence electrons play the same role as core electrons in the periodic properties of element
Valence electrons are responsible for the chemical properties of elements
Core electrons are responsible for the physical properties of elements
questions.e: Valence and core electrons play very different roles: valence electrons drive reactivity and periodic chemical trends, while core electrons are largely chemically inert — so it is false that they play “the same role.”

questions.q: Which of the atomic models considers the magnetic quantum number?
questions.e: The magnetic quantum number emerges from solving the Schrödinger wave equation, which describes each orbital's orientation in space — a feature absent from the earlier Rutherford, Dalton and Bohr models.

questions.q: The elements in the "P" block on the periodic table will……………
o: React with an acid to form hydrogen gas
questions.e: P-block elements sit toward the right of the periodic table and are predominantly nonmetals/metalloids, which tend to gain electrons to complete their octet.

questions.q: Excess glucose is taken up in the body by:
questions.e: Insulin, released when blood glucose rises, signals cells (especially muscle and adipose tissue) to take up the excess glucose.

questions.q: The two types of bonds found in NH4+ are …………… bonds.
questions.e: NH4+ forms from NH3's three ordinary covalent N-H bonds plus a fourth N-H bond formed when the nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H+ — a dative (coordinate covalent) bond.

questions.q: As the number of bonds increases (from single to double to triple), the bond length……………
questions.e: Higher bond order pulls the bonded atoms closer together, so bond length decreases going from single to double to triple bonds.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs of sugars are epimers at C-3?
questions.e: Working through the D-aldose configurations, D-ribose and D-xylose share the same configuration at every carbon except C-3, making them epimers specifically at that carbon (D-allose/D-gulose differ at C-4, and D-erythrose/D-threose differ at C-2).

questions.q: The following features of significant elements in the living cells are true, except they are……………
questions.e: The major bio-elements (C, H, N, O, P, S) are overwhelmingly p-block (plus hydrogen), not s-block, so "s-block elements" is the false statement here.

questions.q: The formation of an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose from sucrose is:
questions.e: Sucrose is split into its component monosaccharides, glucose and fructose, by hydrolysis — the glycosidic bond is broken with the addition of a water molecule.

questions.q: The shielding effect explains why:
o: The ionic size of oxygen is greater than that of boron
The atomic size of chlorine is smaller than that of iodine
The electronegativity of fluorine is greater than that of gallium
There is unexpected low electron affinity for fluorine among the halogens
questions.e: Fluorine's anomalously low electron affinity (lower than chlorine's) is the classic textbook example explained by poor shielding: fluorine's small 2p orbital suffers unusually strong electron-electron repulsion when it gains an extra electron.

questions.q: Pick the odd one out in options A to D
questions.e: Starch, glucose and xylose are all carbohydrates; lecithin is a phospholipid, not a carbohydrate.

questions.q: When an individual consumes large quantities of sucrose, they can be at risk of:
questions.e: Sucrose is a concentrated source of calories, and habitual excess intake is a well-established contributor to weight gain and obesity.
